bf: vals + Dashka are collaborating on two ambient sets this year at the Refuge stage. They create immersive sonic textures by weaving together sampled instruments, field recordings, and ethereal monosodium glutamate. They began playing music together in 2012 creating silly RC20 loops using ancient percussive typewriters, glottal flips, prehistoric Casios, found cassette tapes, and pianos haunted by wild ghost horses. This will be their first show together since the beforetimes. You know the ones. Rhymes with shmovid shmockdown. If you’re looking to be enveloped by a soft smooshy velvet cloud, you’ve come to the right place. Come unfurl with us like the sweet baby fern that you are.
“It’s like if Unsolved Mysteries was produced by Soul Train.”

vals is a sound artist and composer living in Portland, OR. They create composite sonic environments using audio programming techniques, field recordings, and live-instrument sampling. Their work explores the whimsicality of listening, ASMR study session playlists, and whether a hammock can be made from vibrating air particles.

Performing as Dashka, Dasha Shleyeva is a somatic educator, visual artist, and therapeutic musician weaving sound and embodiment into restorative experiences. Informed by clinical harp therapy studies and therapeutic music, their offerings blend improvised harp with otherworldly vocals and field recordings to create immersive, spell-casting loops and soundscapes. Their work centers reciprocity, autonomy, and shared joy between all beings.

Zsuzsanna has practiced yoga for over 18 years and has studied with teachers including Suniti Dernovsek, Sarahjoy Marsh, and Allegra Chabay. Her work integrates yoga, mindfulness, neuroscience, and somatic awareness, creating spaces that invite presence, curiosity, and meaningful connection. bf: Brianna Taylor (she/her) is a multidisciplinary movement artist, choreographer, facilitator, yoga instructor and bodyworker born and raised in the Pacific Northwest. Her work as an artist and educator is rooted in collaboration and community care, improvisation and experimentation, and practices of listening to and honoring the wisdom of the body. Brianna carries an eclectic movement history that has been deeply enriched by the study of many forms including Modern/Contemporary, West African and other dances, Improvisation, Yoga, Tai Chi/Qi Gong, and various somatic practices. She has been guiding Yoga, dance, somatic movement and creative experiences for 20+ years. Her intention as a facilitator/practitioner is to provide a supportive container for individuals to connect to and be present with the wisdom of their bodies, and she aims to facilitate spaces that uplift and celebrate our wholeness.

Brianna is also the visionary and co-steward of Confluence Arts Center in Scotts Mills, OR. The mission of this center is to provide a loving container for anyone seeking to reconnect to their body/mind/spirit, and to hold space for creative incubation, co-creation in community, and healing through movement, sound therapy, and bodywork offerings.

bf: Daily pickle pop-up, offering free pickles and brine for hydration. Stop into The Refuge to learn about pop up times!

Over twenty years ago Stewart Golomb (a veteran third grade teacher) started making pickles in his tiny East Village apartment in New York City. The initial goal was to see if his pickles could be better than what was currently available on the street in NYC’s Lower East Side (former pickle mecca). Batch after batch he tested and tested. Ad absurdum. The refrigerator in the small NYC apartment was constantly filled with test batches. Which necessitated the extremely popular pickle-tasting parties to make room for more test batches. The overwhelming response to the pickles fell somewhere between unbridled enthusiasm and mania. MoonBrine was born.

Armed with his love of food, fun and a mission to bring some simple joy to people’s lives, he attacks the pickling process with an intensity hard to come by unless you’re just plain intense, aka Stew.

From New York City, Stew moved to Boston, Massachusetts where he brewed and sold his fermented pickles for seven years. Continuing his mission to spread the love of pickles, Stew moved MoonBrine World Headquarters to the great Pacific Northwestern city of Portland, Oregon where he is producing out of the Historic Ford Building located in Southeast Portland. From the Great Atlantic Northeast to the Great Pacific Northwest – Pickles for all!
Stew says, “Giddy up! Pickle down!”
MoonBrine.com | Instagram

bf: LIT Sunday: Imagine Storytelling

The Imagine Storytelling show is set to return to the Woods Stage this year at 11am on Sunday. Host and curator Patricia Wheeler (The Moth) has assembled an exciting 90 minutes of stories from tellers across the country—each sharing a true, personal tale centered on this year’s theme: Belonging.

Patricia has been curating the Imagine show at Pickathon since 2017, and in that time, she’s witnessed firsthand how deeply welcoming the community on the farm is—especially on quiet, golden Sunday mornings. She couldn’t think of a more fitting theme.
So grab your coffee and find a spot on the hill—or sway gently in a hammock up high—as these gifted storytellers take you on a ride through humor, heartbreak, and everything in between.

Patricia Wheeler is a producer, storyteller, story coach, and writer from Hell, Michigan. Her stories can be found many places including on Risk!, The Great Lakes Review, and The Secret Society of Twisted Storytellers. She is the Michigan producer of The Moth. She helps the corporate world be a little less corporate by briging the power of story into their work. She received a Master’s degree in Storytelling from East Tennessee State University, where she worked with survivors of traumatic events to use personal narrative to help take back their lives. She started with her own.

Upon special request they also lend a listening ear, which at current looks like supporting agencies to better their Trans and LGBQ+ inclusion. Originally from bucolic Southern Oregon, they now call Portland home alongside their super kind and wicked smart wife, Dr. Sarah. Together they raise two exuberant and free kiddos, ages 7 and 10. Their first Pickathon was in 2011! They will never forget Ms. Mavis Staples’ way of saying “Pick uh thhon Pick uh thhhhon!”- anybody else remember that? Pictured in their arms you will find their fam’s most recent addition- Honey Bunz.

bf: Chef Angel Medina is the Founder of República & Co. and TODOS Media. Born in Southern California and raised between Guadalajara and Tijuana, Medina came to Portland in 2010 and built a path from Mexican-grown coffee to a small group of restaurants. His work treats Mexican cuisine as history and reclamation, separating what is ancestral from what colonization introduced. República has earned national recognition from the James Beard Foundation and Bon Appétit.

Established in November of 2020, República began as a humble space offering beloved classics such as Pozole, Menudo, and Cochinita Pibil. Within a matter of weeks, it gained popularity as one of the best Mexican restaurants in the city. By only its sixth month, the restaurant began to offer an evening Chef’s Tasting Dinner, which quickly caught the attention of not only the local press but also the L.A. Times.

Within its first year, República was named Restaurant of the Year by Portland Monthly, a week later Best New Restaurant by Eater Portland, and one of Oregon’s Best New Restaurants by The Oregonian. One month later it received its first James Beard Foundation nomination for Best New Restaurant. In September of 2022, Bon Appétit named República one of the 10 Best New Restaurants in America, finishing off one of the most impressive launch cycles the city of Portland had ever seen.

In February of 2023, República finished the build out of its new home, settling in on the busy corner of NW 10th and NW Couch in the bustling Pearl District. The new location wasn’t only a larger space but rather the right space, as it finally matched the quality of the food and the service it was accustomed to doing. The change served as an opportunity to curate an experience that wasn’t possible before, switching the service model and the overall style of the restaurant to one that mirrored something in Paris, New York, London, or even the restaurants of Mexico City. The presentation, the service, and overall experience brought on more recognition and attention to what was already one of the most beloved Mexican restaurants in the country.

bf: Restaurateur, Chef, and Channeler of the Soul of Italian Cuisine

Cathy Whims, a six-time James Beard Award finalist for Best Chef: Northwest, is a visionary who has profoundly shaped Portland’s culinary landscape. As Chef-Owner of Nostrana, a Portland institution approaching its 20th anniversary in 2025, Cathy has created a dining experience that seamlessly marries Italian tradition with Pacific Northwest seasonality. Her influence extends to Oven and Shaker and Enoteca Nostrana, where her passion for regional Italian cuisine continues to thrive.

Cathy’s culinary journey began over 40 years ago at Genoa, where she introduced Portland to the nuanced flavors of Italian cooking and the concept of sourcing locally. Her philosophy, rooted in the Italian ethos of celebrating food as a cornerstone of life’s relationships and rhythms, is reflected in her commitment to building lasting connections with farmers, winemakers, and artisans both locally and in Italy.

An educator at heart, Cathy shares her expertise through international culinary tours, cooking classes, and now through writing. Her debut cookbook, The Italian Summer Kitchen, launched in April 2025, showcasing her deep love of Italian culture and its interplay with seasonal cooking.
Cathy Whims will be accompanied by Nostrana’s Executive Chef, Bryan Donaldson.
chef-cathy-whims-of-nostrana.b: Restaurateur, Chef, and Channeler of the Soul of Italian Cuisine

bf: Since opening in Portland in 2006, Screen Door has become a beloved destination for Southern cooking, blending the rich foodways of South Louisiana with the Pacific Northwest’s seasonal bounty.

Born and raised in Tennessee, Screen Door Culinary Director Dominic Finzo represents a new generation of Southern chefs—one rooted in tradition while constantly looking ahead. Blending classical technique with a modern Pacific Northwest sensibility, he is passionate about preserving the soul of Southern cuisine while continuing to push it forward.

His cooking is guided by a deep respect for heirloom ingredients and the stories they carry, believing that every dish is an opportunity to honor the people, places, and traditions that have shaped Southern food. Working closely with regional farmers and producers, he creates menus that celebrate the seasons, showcase exceptional local ingredients, and reflect the rich diversity of Southern culinary heritage.

Whether exploring familiar classics or reimagining them through a contemporary lens, Dominic approaches every plate with the goal of respecting Southern cuisine’s past, embracing its present, and helping shape its future.

faq: Tent camping in the woods is included with every weekend pass, with a quiet area in Lush Camp. Cars, vans and RVs need a vehicle camping spot at Willow Camp or South Camp.
Park at the Welcome Lot, then walk about a mile in or take the free shuttle to the Farmhouse. Coming by MAX? The Pickathon Shuttle runs from Lents Town Center with a Shuttle Pass. Or bike in.
Kids 12 and under are free with a ticketed adult. Coyote is the neighborhood built for families, with its own stage all weekend.
Are there senior or student discounts?

No. Every adult pays the same price, and prices are lowest early in the year. Kids 12 and under are free with a ticketed adult, and day tickets are the most affordable way to come for part of the weekend.
Can I work for a ticket?

Yes. Work traders give about 16–24 hours of pre- or post-festival work in exchange for one adult weekend ticket. You must be 18 or older, and spots fill up. Details and the application are at worktrade.pickathon.com.

stories.x: By day they are raw wood and geometry. By night they ignite. This year the Galaxy Courtyard blooms into Habitats: two massive water lilies designed by Matt Thomas and Chris Cardoza and built by Blackbird Public Arts, glowing on the blacktop and built for the n

f: Stepping out of the Galaxy Barn, you enter the Courtyard, the open-air social plaza of the festival. Anchored by immersive art installations on the dance floor and a central fire pit, this is where the party spills out under the sky. An outdoor screen broadcasts the action from inside the barns, connecting you to the music while you grab a drink at the bar or reconnect with friends.

This year, that plaza becomes a habitat. Two massive water lilies rise from the blacktop of Galaxy Courtyard, built from layered lumber and stacked petal by petal into full bloom. By day they read as raw wood and geometry, monumental forms that invite people to sit and linger. By night, they ignite. Light pours through the slats, a DJ drops in from inside one flower, and the other opens its arms to anyone who wants to dance or get lost in the visuals projected on the screen between them. Something glowing on the blacktop, pulling you out of the forest and into the evening. A habitat built for the night.
Habitats was designed by Matt Thomas and Chris Cardoza, who have been shaping the Galaxy Courtyard together for years, and built by Blackbird Public Arts.

When the festival ends, the Courtyard’s story keeps going. Blackbird Public Arts has been repurposing the lumber from the Galaxy Courtyard for several years now. They build large public art installations at local farms and festivals while teaching basic construction skills to their volunteer builders, on a mission to bring public art out from behind paywalls and make it accessible for all, while offering a container for rapidly disappearing power-tool skills to be passed down. Their builds are temporary, and when they are disassembled the materials move on to the next art piece.

Blackbird works in partnership with the Guild of Oregon Woodworkers. Once the materials have been worked down to a smaller size after several art installations, they are donated to the Guild for their skill-building classes. From a festival dance floor, to a public art piece, to the hands of the next generation of woodworkers.

Designed by Matt Thomas (@mattomis) and Chris Cardoza (@cardozacm). Built by Blackbird Public Arts (@blackbirdpublicarts). Downstream partner: Guild of Oregon Woodworkers and Blackbird Public Arts (@blackbirdpublicarts).

stories.x: Two wooden porches rise in the fields at Pickathon’s arrival and departure points, each a facade without a building and an entry to an open horizon. The Long Porch welcomes every traveler to Pendarvis Farm, then journeys onward to a new life in the community.

f: This summer, two wooden porches appear in the fields around Pendarvis Farm. Positioned at Pickathon’s arrival and departure points, they receive travelers coming and going from the festival. Set against the open horizons of farmland, each Long Porch presents itself as an unexpected and incomplete structure: a facade without a building, a streetfront without a town, an entry to an open horizon. Conjuring memories of train stops, rural barns, storefronts, and ghost towns, the Long Porch makes clear you have arrived. But where you have arrived is not so clear, and that invites deeper exploration.
A Straightforward Structure in a Rural Landscape

Collaboratively designed by the architecture practices Big-Marks and DRAWINGS, the Long Porch is built in a straightforward manner fitting its rural context. “We both grew up in rural Oregon,” says Jonathan Heppner of Big-Marks. “There’s a matter of fact, resourceful way of building we intuitively channeled with these structures.”

The Long Porch is assembled from a repeating, self-supported cantilever of stick-frame wood. In the hot expanse of the open summer fields, the roof provides necessary shade over a raised deck, a place to drop off and gather belongings, people, and the necessaries of a long festival weekend. Just as straightforward to assemble, the structure is meant to be taken apart. Like the ephemeral experience of a festival, the pavilion is present, until it is not.

“Rural Oregon is full of these structures that provide meaning to us beyond their initial use,” says William Smith of DRAWINGS. “A barn might sit empty or be missing a wall, yet still serve as an orienting memory on our horizon.”
At Pickathon, the Long Porch orients its travelers. Preparing to come and go, everyone gathers at the Long Porch: the entry to a place built to disappear.

True to the Creative Neighborhoods mission, the Long Porch is built to live on. After the festival, its lumber begins a new journey. A portion will be repurposed as a garden greenhouse for a retired nurse in Milwaukie living on a fixed income. Another portion will travel to North Portland to frame a gallery installation for a community-planning project, where the material will support neighborhood conversations about the future of the district.

Big-Marks is an architecture practice based in Portland, Oregon, founded by Jonathan Heppner, AIA. At the forefront of timber innovation, Jonathan has contributed to first-of-their-kind wood projects across the U.S. The studio strengthens the connection between natural landscapes, material systems, and the built environment to create projects with enduring value, making thoughtful, well-loved buildings by clearing the barriers to participation and creativity.

DRAWINGS is an architecture practice based in Brooklyn, New York, and Portland, Oregon, led by Daniel Garcia and William Smith. The studio creates buildings and civic structures that feel at once unexpected and inevitable: clear in form, yet layered in experience. Seeking an architecture that invites discovery rather than revealing itself all at once, their work uses simple forms that contain hidden complexities and, in turn, activate and support the landscapes they inhabit.

Schommer & Sons, Inc has set the standard since 1937. Based in Portland, Oregon, the family-owned team is a trusted building partner for quality craftsmanship and exceptional care, helping clients tackle complex projects with tight timelines while setting the highest standards for safety and craftsmanship across the Pacific Northwest and beyond.

One of Oregon’s most beloved names, Bend’s own Deschutes Brewery returns with beer on tap all weekend, and this year they are joining us as a food vendor too. Be sure to catch their PARTYBOMB activation while you are at it.

Portland-roasted, farm-direct, and family-rooted, Nossa Familia Coffee keeps the whole festival fueled from sunrise to late night. Love what is in your cup? Take it home. The Nossa Coffee Club Subscription is simple and convenient: set it once and change anytime, save 20 percent on every order, enjoy $5 flat-rate shipping (free over $45), and unlock subscriber-only offers and perks. Fresh coffee, your way, delivered all year long. Visit nossacoffee.com to join.

PARTYBOMB is a 5% ABV, flavor-first beverage made with real fruit, full flavor, and low fizz. Look for nostalgic, fruit-forward flavors like Hard Peach, Hard Pineapple Whip, Hard Strawberry Lemonade, and Hard Punch. Every party looks different, whether you are by the pool, at a backyard BBQ, camping, or celebrating in the middle of the woods, and PARTYBOMB is all about the fun. Stop by the PARTYBOMB booth from 12pm to 7pm, Thursday through Sunday, with a sampling table at the Market Bar, to taste all four flavors.

Portland Cider Company pours crisp, Oregon-made cider from right in our backyard. Kachka Spirits brings small-batch spirits from Portland’s beloved Kachka, including their famous horseradish vodka. Holladay Bourbon offers handcrafted bourbon from one of America’s oldest distilleries. Biotic Ferments serves up Nira fermented sodas that are gut-friendly and low in sugar. Lolo keeps things light and easy for a long festival day. From Eugene, Drink Weird Yerba Mate delivers clean energy made with organic cane sugar and organic fruit juice, with no artificial sweeteners, colors, or preservatives, and about one gram of sugar per fluid ounce, which is less organic cane sugar than the natural sugar you would find in a typical apple. Freight Beer keeps it simple with real good American lager at a great price, and through The Foundry by Freight a portion of every sale goes back to the trades. And Ruse Brewing, a local favorite, is an artisanal brewery inspired by Portland’s creative community and culture.

Every Curation gathering is made richer by the drinks in hand. We are grateful to the beverage partners pouring alongside our chefs and artists this year: 360 Vodka, Autora Mezcal, Brokers Gin, Division Winemaking Co., Dominio IV Wines, Estelbrook Farms & Vineyard, Five Farms Irish Cream, Holladay Bourbon, Maloof Wines, Nira Fermented Soda by Biotic Ferments, Rubato Wines, and Wandering Goat Coffee. A heartfelt thank you for helping us fill every table with something worth savoring.

The Curation Experience pairs Portland’s top chefs with festival artists for an intimate multi-course meal in a hidden woodland oasis, and they always sell out. Only two seatings remain: Saturday Brunch on August 1 at 11am with Chef Cathy of Nostrana and Family Company, and Sunday Brunch on August 2 at 11am with Culinary Director Dominic Finzo of Screen Door and The Travelin’ McCourys. Grab the last seats at pickathon.com/tickets.
For more Pacific Northwest flavors, discover the restaurants, food trucks, and culinary creators in the Market and throughout the festival at the blog here.
See all of our beverage partners at pickathon.com/partners.

stories.t: Massage in the Refuge: Bookings now open!
stories.x: Treat yourself to a private 45-minute massage under the trees with one of our specially trained therapists.
stories.b: 🌿 Massage bookings are now OPEN in The Refuge at Pickathon! 🌿 Treat yourself to a private 45-minute massage under the trees with one of our specially trained therapists. It's the perfect way to bring your dancing body back to life before another night of music. Bonus: every massage includes a free p
f: 🌿 Massage bookings are now OPEN in The Refuge at Pickathon! 🌿
Treat yourself to a private 45-minute massage under the trees with one of our specially trained therapists. It’s the perfect way to bring your dancing body back to life before another night of music.
Bonus: every massage includes a free pre-massage shower. 🚿
Your body carries you through the woods and across the dance floor — give it a little love. Spots are limited, so book yours before they’re gone.

Alicia Markee — Alicia brings nearly six years of experience, much of it in injury-recovery work at a chiropractic office. She offers Swedish, deep tissue, trigger point therapy, and myofascial release.

Aspen Johnson — Aspen offers Swedish massage and craniosacral therapy with gentle to medium-firm techniques that guide the body into a dreamlike state. Her work is especially good for nervous-system tension and neck, shoulder, back, or jaw pain.

Bryan Warren — A graduate of East West College with four years in a chiropractic setting, Bryan specializes in deep tissue, myofascial release, cupping, and prenatal massage, blending anatomical knowledge with intuitive, restorative touch.

Carol “Caz” Duncan — Caz pairs clinical knowledge with trauma-informed care, drawing on deep tissue, sports massage, myofascial techniques, cupping, and Thai-style bodywork. They work with everyday clients and athletes alike to ease movement and recovery.

Connie Landers — Owner of Soul Glow Massage & Bodywork in Portland, Connie tailors each session using Swedish, deep tissue, myofascial release, trigger point, and neuromuscular techniques, specializing in reducing tension and easing chronic discomfort.

Dez Pebenito — A Portland LMT at Living Altar Wellness with a doctorate in Chinese Medicine, Dez works through shiatsu, tui na, craniosacral, and visceral manipulation to release tension and settle the nervous system. Sessions can be done fully clothed.

Dodie Davey — Dodie (they/them) has practiced biodynamic massage, craniosacral therapy, reiki, and acupressure for seven years, working from a trauma-informed perspective that lets the body guide each session.

Em Fensterman — Em blends focused deep work with breath and movement, using myofascial release, neuromuscular and trigger point therapy, and craniosacral therapy. Their collaborative sessions target pain while engaging the nervous system in healing.

Gretchen Hogue — For over 20 years Gretchen has offered intuitive bodywork at her SE Portland studio, Akasa Thai Healing Arts, integrating Thai massage and biodynamic cranial work to unwind stuck patterns and restore mobility.

Joseph “Winnie” LaDu — Winnie offers a calm, grounded presence, drawing on myofascial release, Swedish massage, craniosacral, and biodynamic massage. He pairs therapeutic touch with deep listening to help you rest and reconnect.

Nika Short — Based in Bend, Nika came to massage in 2017 after a decade as a wilderness educator. She specializes in injury assessment using deep tissue, trigger point, and neuromuscular techniques, alongside craniosacral therapy and reiki. Nika is offering free chair massage in the Refuge!

River Forbes — Practicing since 2022 with a focus on accident recovery and chronic conditions, River offers full-body Swedish relaxation, targeted deep tissue, myofascial release, and their specialty, craniosacral therapy. This is their first year in the Refuge!

Ryan Beam — A proud East West College graduate, Ryan works with presence, specificity, and consent, flowing between myofascial release, deep tissue, postural analysis, Muscle Energy Techniques, and cupping. His goal is for you to feel empowered in your body.

Savanna Wonderwheel — Savanna has spent over 12 years exploring listening through touch, offering biodynamic massage and craniosacral therapy. Her work is a sanctuary for deep rest, presence, and ease.
Shea Lloyd — Learning the craft since 1999, Shea combines soothing relaxation with deep tissue, joint mobilization, and cupping in a safe, nurturing, judgment-free space tailored to your needs.

Tessa Waring — With eight years of experience, Tessa offers Swedish massage, deep tissue, and myofascial release. Whether you want to bliss out or work a problem area, each session is tailored to you.

stories.t: The Woods Neighborhood 2026: The Freakin’ Epicenter of Sound
stories.x: Step into the Woods this year — where sound ripples out like waves across a pond and swirls up from a guitar into the leaves above. For 2026, our beloved Woods Stage reaches the culmination of its 7-year lifespan: the big year of its full flower, built in joyf
stories.b: Like outward ripples of sound moving across the surface of a pond, like the fibrous weave of a freakin' spider's web holding space in the pulse of the wind, and just exactly like a maelstrom of feeling swirling up from a guitar into the leaves above… well, you should probably just venture into the W
f: Like outward ripples of sound moving across the surface of a pond, like the fibrous weave of a freakin’ spider’s web holding space in the pulse of the wind, and just exactly like a maelstrom of feeling swirling up from a guitar into the leaves above… well, you should probably just venture into the Woods this year, and find your seat.

The Woods Stage has always been a joyful collaboration. What began as a shared spark between Zale and our lead designer grew, year over year, into something bigger — more scale, more complexity, more beauty. It usually starts with a seed of inspiration, and from there we respond, riff, and build. Whatever ideas take shape are always brought back to Zale and the core team to consider together, because several healthy, joyful minds who love life always make something better. Always.
The Big Year of Its Full Flower

And we’ve grown right alongside the stage. As the Woods Stage has gotten wilder and more elemental, so have we. We’ve just been flying — and sometimes, mid-flight, we notice things that were there for us to realize all along. Like the fact that the Woods Stage is a living thing. It undergoes a lifespan of about 7 years of self-development before it’s brought down and reinvented. Since the very start of Pickathon at Pendarvis Farm, the Woods Stage has been reborn about four times. And 2026? We think this is the culmination year of the current cycle — the year it reaches its zenith form. This is the big year of its full flower, before it’s reborn again next year.
Of the Farm, Of the Forest

The Woods Stage is of Pendarvis Farm. It sits in its remarkable, uniquely shaped draw in the land, always in conversation with the trees that nestle around it. When you’re there to be part of that conversation, the sense of place is total — the entire arena is alive, and the stage becomes a year-to-year interpretation that evolves before your eyes.

And the forest itself contributes. The trees drop the branches they want to add to the effect. The Douglas Fir offer their mighty branches, both straight and curved. The Maples give their stout posts and forked limbs. The few Cedar lend their tapering, sinuous curves. And the Vine Maple always delivers the most magnanimous, gently arcing lines of all, covered in moss. All of them contribute.
The Pickathon Woods Stage is a summation of all that the forest and people can give to beauty, love, and music.
Come find your seat in the Woods.

stories.t: Windmill 2026: One Neighborhood, Many Hands
stories.x: Windmill 2026: a community-built plaza with Sabin CDC and Waechter Architecture’s forest rooms, gateway, and DJ stage—where art, beer, and music mix under the firs.
stories.b: Perched on the forest edge above the Paddock, this neighborhood is defined by towering Douglas Firs and the farm's iconic rustic windmill. It marks the gateway to the Lush campground and serves as one of our two intimate, smaller daytime stages. Here, you are in the center of the action, feeling eve
f: Perched on the forest edge above the Paddock, this neighborhood is defined by towering Douglas Firs and the farm’s iconic rustic windmill. It marks the gateway to the Lush campground and serves as one of our two intimate, smaller daytime stages. Here, you are in the center of the action, feeling every moment. The vibe ranges from chill literary readings and morning coffee to visceral punk rock and afternoon DJs. It is a hillside lounge where art, beer, and music mix under the canopy.

Windmill comes alive through the work of many hands — a collective of architects, builders, students, and community partners. Below, two parts of the story: the collaborators shaping a community-rooted plaza with Sabin CDC, and Waechter Architecture’s forest rooms, gateway, and DJ stage.
From Pendarvis Farm to Sabin CDC’s Table

From the Pendarvis Farm to Sabin CDC’s table, Windmill is partnering with the Portland affordable housing nonprofit, envisioning a community kit of parts that goes full circle to build Windmill’s vendor booths, bar, seating, and stage. The downstream components support Sabin’s mission in placemaking, gardening, and community building at 17 properties they manage. Their kit of parts includes picnic tables, community share libraries, modular furniture for gatherings, block parties and flexible use, a greenhouse, and planter boxes. Using these elements in repetitive and creative ways at Pickathon they showcase Sabin’s mission to promote social equity by enhancing the livability of culturally diverse neighborhoods in Portland.

Sabin’s centers supporting African American and Afro-Indigenous households adversely affected by gentrification, systemic oppression, and inequalities. Painted furniture modules are designed to complement a street plaza scheme based on artist Isaka Shamsud-Din, revered by the local community and the namesake of a recent affordable housing development.

Planter boxes and a greenhouse give access to food production on various urban sites, as well as help Sabin grow native plants for naturescaping and habitat creation on their greenspaces. Furniture and free libraries bring neighbors together in outdoor spaces and foster community interaction and sharing.

Collaborations from many groups have made this possible and a highlight for Windmill is providing mentorship and workforce development opportunities with students at Tigard High School for a vendor booth design-build competition (that they won!), and with AmeriCorps members to build planter boxes.
The Windmill design-build is brought to life by a dream team of collaborators, including:
Tigard High School with CIEF & JHC Construction
This diverse group brings together creative minds across architecture, art, and community work to build something truly unforgettable.
Waechter Architecture — Gateway, DJ Stage & Forest Seating

There is a particular kind of relief that comes from stepping out of the crowd. At a music festival, it arrives in small doses: a seat in the shade, a quiet conversation, a moment when the body remembers it needs rest as much as it needs sound. This part of the Windmill site has always offered that. This year, Waechter Architecture took that quality of reprieve and made it the foundation for design.

The program was clear enough. Create seating in the forest, a DJ stage, a gateway into the site. But beneath those functional pieces was something more resonant. During the day people come to the Windmill to decompress. To grab food and a drink, to sit with friends, to let the festival wash over them from a comfortable distance. These moments are harder to find than they should be. A large music festival is an extraordinarily demanding sensory environment, beautiful and relentless in equal measure, and the chance to simply be still inside of it is rare and genuinely precious. Waechter took that observation seriously. We wanted the design to do more than provide benches.

The forest rooms are comprised of four walls with seating running around the perimeter. The exterior seating provides space to socialize, watch the DJ set, and continue to engage with the festival. If you’re seeking a quieter experience, a small passageway leads to an unexpected surprise. A cozy interior space allows a group to enjoy a moment of reprieve from the hustle and bustle of the festival. Four semi-screened walls surround the space, and above, nothing but canopy and sky. It is an invitation to lie down and look up, to trade the immense visual stimulation and horizontal sprawl of the festival for a single, quiet vertical view. In a place where almost every experience is designed to pull your attention outward and forward, this one asks you to stop and look up.

That same module used to create the forest room repeats itself as the gateway into the forest and wraps around the DJ stage. The same form that holds a resting body also marks the threshold of arrival and contains the energy of the dance floor. One idea, doing many things at once, felt right for a site where the line between rest and revelry was blurry to begin with.
Waechter Architecture is a Portland-based design practice. This part of the Windmill site was designed in collaboration with Pete Rust of the Port Townsend Shipwrights for the 2026 festival.
Windmill is more than a destination—it’s a celebration of culture, a statement of values, and a call to action. We can’t wait for you to experience it.
You can follow Windmill Design team’s process and design photos on Instagram at @pickathonwindmill.

stories.t: Laughs in the Lucky Barn: The 2026 Pickathon Comedy Showcase Lineup
stories.x: Pickathon’s late-night comedy club is back. For her tenth year, Amy Miller hosts Laughs in the Lucky Barn — a stacked 2026 lineup headlined by rising Tonight Show star Laura Peek, plus Portland favorites Shain Brendan, Julia Corral, and Sean Jordan. Ninety min
stories.b: Catch the Pickathon Comedy Showcase — LAUGH with Amy Miller — Friday, July 31st and Saturday, August 1st, 7:30–9:00 PM in the Lucky Barn. Did you know Pickathon has its very own late-night comedy club? For a decade, the Lucky Barn has transformed into a hub of hilarity on Friday and Saturday nights,
f: Catch the Pickathon Comedy Showcase — LAUGH with Amy Miller — Friday, July 31st and Saturday, August 1st, 7:30–9:00 PM in the Lucky Barn.

Did you know Pickathon has its very own late-night comedy club? For a decade, the Lucky Barn has transformed into a hub of hilarity on Friday and Saturday nights, hosting nationally touring comedians in one of the most intimate venues on the farm.
Amy Miller returns to host this year’s showcase, and she couldn’t be more excited:

“Pickathon 2026 officially marks my tenth year booking and hosting standup comedy in the Lucky Barn! This is not only one of my favorite lineups yet, but our superstar headliner Laura Peek is a dear friend and I find myself excited for her to experience Pickathon. It’s hands down my favorite festival as both a performer and a fan. The folks that cram into the Lucky Barn every year for those 90 minutes always show up with a fun spirit, ready to laugh, and open to being made fun of. We always have so much fun.”

Curated and hosted by the incomparable Amy Miller — seen on Comedy Central, After Midnight on CBS, Viceland, NBC, and more — Laughs in the Lucky Barn is a Pickathon tradition and fan favorite. These stand-up showcases feature some of the funniest people you’ve seen on Netflix, HBO, Amazon, and Hulu, along with the top comedy stages of Portland and Seattle. Past years have brought names like Kyle Kinane, Ian Karmel, and stars from Willamette Week’sFunniest Comedians in Portland list to the Lucky Barn stage.
The 2026 lineup is stacked with comedic firepower and features some first-timers who are sure to leave festival-goers in stitches. Here’s who’s taking the stage, in running order:

Amy Miller — HostAmy Miller was one of Comedy Central’s “Up Next” comics and has a half-hour special, Ham Mouth, on Comedy Central. She’s a paid regular at both the World Famous Comedy Store and The Comedy Cellar in New York, and she has two Don’t Tell Comedy sets on YouTube. Recently she was a guest on Comics Unleashed and CBS’s After Midnight, and hosted The Basement Tapes Podcast with the Osbourne family — yep, those Osbournes (the Ozzy ones). As a brand-new comic she was a breakout favorite in the final season of Last Comic Standing. She has a half-hour comedy special on Epix’s Unprotected Sets, and she regularly opens for Tom Segura, Wanda Sykes, Nicole Byer, and several more of her comedy idols. She was also a featured comic on Viceland’s Flophouse. You may have seen Amy on Viceland or heard her on Sirius XM, NPR, Doug Loves Movies, Jameela Jamil’s Bad Dates, The Bennington Show, All Fantasy Everything, So True with Caleb Hearon, Stavvy’s World with Stavros Halkias, or her own podcast Who’s Your God?

Laura PeekLaura Peek is one of the most promising young Los Angeles–based stand-up comics to come out of Nashville’s bustling comedy scene. She made her Tonight Show debut in 2025 and was named one of Deadline’s “20 Stand-Ups to Keep an Eye on in 2026.” In 2022, she was selected as a “New Face” at the prestigious Just For Laughs Festival in Montreal and named one of Vulture‘s Comics You Should and Will Know. Laura has appeared on After Midnight and Comedy Central’s Stand-Up Featuring series. She’s been featured twice in Don’t Tell Comedy’s popular Secret Sets series and is a paid regular and favorite at the Comedy Store in Hollywood. Her storytelling and sharp wit delight audiences across the country and internationally. She’s had the pleasure of working with comics like Taylor Tomlinson, Iliza Shlesinger, Fortune Feimster, Andrew Santino, Mark Normand, Marc Maron, and many more.

Sean JordanSean Jordan is a touring stand-up comedian and podcaster who has appeared on Comedy Central and The Late Late Show with James Corden, and whom Paste Magazine calls “both genuine and genuinely hilarious.” He co-hosts the wildly popular podcast All Fantasy Everything, the show where funny people and experts come together to fantasy draft pop culture — from music to movies to sandwiches. His latest stand-up album, Girl Dad, out on A Special Thing Records, is a raw, honest, and hilarious special documenting the birth of his daughter, the IVF that preceded it, the vasectomy that followed, and all points between. His newest podcast, It’s Nice to Be Nice, explores how someone “being nice” made a difference in the lives of his guests. You may also have heard Sean on podcasts like The Honeydew, Doug Loves Movies, Professor Blastoff, The Crabfeast, View from the Cheap Seats, Put Your Hands Together, and Alison Rosen Is Your Best Friend. His young daughter recently lauded Sean’s ability to “be tall” and “carry me upside down so I can walk on the ceiling.”

Julia CorralJulia Corral is a Latina comic from Portland, OR, who’s been described as the friendliest-caustic person you’ll ever meet. The alt-weeklies have named her one of the Funniest 5 comics (Willamette Week) and an Undisputed Genius of Comedy (Portland Mercury). She has performed at High Plains, Limestone, All Jane, Treefort, and Bumbershoot. She’s a paid regular and host at Helium’s Cooch Street (an all-women show), Kickstand’s Comedy in the Park, and many more shows around town. She has also been featured on NPR.

Shain BrendanA former winner of Portland’s Funniest Person, you’ve probably seen Shain in projects for NBA 2K, Nike, Google, Lowe’s, and Navy Federal Credit Union — and if not, he still got paid pretty well for all of them. He was a longtime co-host of NBA pre/post-game shows for the Portland Trail Blazers on NBC Sports, and he’s currently trying to break 80 on the golf course. Shain also has a special on Don’t Tell Comedy’s social channels. He co-hosts a weekly podcast with fellow comedian Seth Allen called The Washedmen, where they talk mostly about how old and “washed” they’ve become. If you also feel old, you’ll love hearing them complain about it. Shain can be seen performing at comedy clubs and venues around the country, and one time in college he threw a half-eaten corn dog that got stuck in Eli Manning’s helmet — and that’s… that’s just cool.

Ninety minutes, one barn, and some of the funniest people working today. Whether you’re a die-hard comedy fan or just looking for the best late-night hang on the farm, the Lucky Barn is where you want to be. Show up with a fun spirit, ready to laugh.
Laughs in the Lucky Barn — Friday, July 31st & Saturday, August 1st, 7:30–9:00 PM.

stories.t: Come to the Table: Inside Pickathon’s 2026 Curation Series
stories.x: Pickathon’s most intimate tradition returns for 2026: five gatherings pairing chefs and performing artists in unexpected combinations, each limited to just 100 guests. From Cafe Olli and The Brothers Comatose to Screen Door and The Travelin’ McCourys, here’s t
stories.b: Beneath the trees and beside the steady soundtrack of the creek, Pickathon's Curation experience unfolds as one of the festival's most beloved traditions. Chefs and Pickathon performing artists are brought together in unexpected combinations, each shaping the experience in their own way. Over a shar
f: Beneath the trees and beside the steady soundtrack of the creek, Pickathon’s Curation experience unfolds as one of the festival’s most beloved traditions. Chefs and Pickathon performing artists are brought together in unexpected combinations, each shaping the experience in their own way. Over a shared meal and intimate performances, guests are invited into the stories, inspirations, and creative connections that make Pickathon feel a little like stepping into another world.

Rooted in the same spirit of discovery that has defined Pickathon for more than two decades, Curation brings guests closer to the artists honoring musical traditions, reshaping genres, and charting new directions for what comes next. Each of the five gatherings is limited to just 100 guests.
Step into a hidden corner of the farm and settle into an experience that unfolds at its own pace. As guests arrive, a Pickathon DJ sets the mood while drinks are poured and conversations begin.

Each Curation gathering is intentionally crafted by Pickathon, pairing chefs and performing artists who inspire one another in surprising ways. The meal’s featured chef presents a menu influenced by the artists and music at its center, creating a shared experience where food, sound, and storytelling come together around the table.

Throughout the event, guests are invited into a rare behind-the-scenes experience, one that blurs the line between performance and gathering, creating space for connection, discovery, and the unexpected moments that make Pickathon unforgettable.
Access requires a Weekend Pickathon Pass or the corresponding Day Pass for the event date, plus a separate Curation ticket for each gathering you’d like to attend.
Cafe Olli x The Brothers ComatoseDJ: Country Co-op Friday, July 31 · 6:30 PM – 8:00 PM

Cafe Olli and The Brothers Comatose come together to celebrate craftsmanship, community, and the traditions that bring people together. Nearly a decade after their first Pickathon appearance, The Brothers Comatose will be joining us again at Pendarvis Farm. They return with a richer catalog, seasoned musicianship, and the infectious harmonies that have made them one of modern bluegrass’s most enduring acts. Known for seasonally driven cooking, house-made breads and pastries, and thoughtful sourcing from local farms and producers, Cafe Olli creates food meant to be shared. Paired with The Brothers Comatose’s harmony-rich blend of bluegrass, folk, and Americana, this gathering celebrates the simple pleasures of good food, good music, and good company.

The Chefs Taylor Manning and Siobhan O’Malley are the owners of Cafe Olli and Olliní, a cafe and bakery in Northeast Portland known for its seasonal menus, naturally leavened breads, and deep relationships with local farmers and producers. Taylor began cooking alongside his uncle in North Carolina before working in Italy, New York, and Portland, while Siobhan discovered her love of cooking through a culinary arts program in her hometown of Austin, Texas, and later worked in Scotland and New York, where the pair met. Together, they have built Cafe Olli into a beloved neighborhood gathering place where thoughtful food, warm hospitality, and a commitment to employee ownership and sustainability go hand in hand.

The Artist The Brothers Comatose are a San Francisco-based bluegrass band known for their infectious harmonies, virtuosic string work, and high-energy performances. Blending traditional bluegrass, Americana, and folk influences, their music is rich with storytelling, spirited musicianship, and the kind of communal energy that turns a crowd into a family.

The DJ Formed in 2017, Country Co-op is a Portland DJ collective known for spinning a lovingly curated mix of outlaw country, honky-tonk, loner folk, and cosmic country. Longtime fixtures of the local music scene and frequent Pickathon collaborators, their vinyl-forward set brings warmth, deep cuts, and a back-porch spirit to the evening.
Nostrana x Family CompanyDJ: Greasy Saturday, August 1 · 11:00 AM – 12:30 PM

Chef Cathy Whims and Family Company come together for a leisurely late-morning gathering rooted in tradition, connection, and the pleasures of slowing down. This is Nostrana’s second year at Pickathon, and Chef Cathy’s countryside-inspired Italian brunch and Family Company’s warm, harmony-rich folk sound create an atmosphere designed for sharing, lingering, and easing into the day together.

Guests will be welcomed with a table of seasonal dishes kissed with a brunch flair. Soft sformato (an Italian savory custard), poached eggs layered over summer vegetables alongside lighter fare like pastries and fresh fruits. The accompanying breads, baked straight from the Nostrana oven, will anchor the meal, meant to be torn, shared, and passed around. It’s an unhurried, countryside-style approach to brunch rooted in tradition, built for community, and in rhythm with the ease of the morning.

The Chefs Cathy Whims is the James Beard Award-winning chef and founder of Nostrana, one of Portland’s most beloved Italian restaurants. She is joined by Nostrana’s Executive Chef Bryan Donaldson, her collaborator of 15 years and a whisperer of her love for Italy. Inspired by the traditions of Italian hospitality, together they offer a seasonal brunch spread featuring dishes kissed with a brunch flair, house-baked breads fresh from the Nostrana oven, and a menu designed for gathering, grazing, and passing plates around the table.

The Artist Family Company blends folk, Americana, and rich vocal harmonies into music that feels both intimate and expansive. Their collaborative spirit and easygoing sound evoke the comfort of a front-porch gathering, creating the perfect soundtrack for a relaxed morning centered on community, conversation, and connection.

The DJ DJ Greasy has spent decades collecting and sharing overlooked treasures from the worlds of soul, funk, R&B, reggae, gospel, and beyond. His vinyl selections provide the perfect backdrop for a slow morning, inviting guests to settle in, stay awhile, and savor the rhythms of good food, good company, and a day just getting underway.
Sunday Sauce x The Womack Sisters DJ: VNPRT Saturday, August 1 · 4:00–5:30 PM

Chef Isaiah Brown and The Womack Sisters come together for a happy hour rooted in family traditions, soulful expression, and the enduring power of stories passed from one generation to the next. Sunday Sauce’s Italian-American comfort food meets The Womack Sisters’ generational soul for an afternoon that celebrates the people, places, and traditions that shape us.

The Chef Isaiah Brown is the executive chef of Sunday Sauce, a Northeast Portland restaurant inspired by co-owner Amanda Winquist’s New Jersey upbringing and the long-simmered Italian-American recipes that bring families together around the table. Drawing on experience at acclaimed restaurants including Canlis, Normandie, and Hale Pele, Isaiah brings care and craft to comfort food classics, transforming beloved family traditions into vibrant, shareable meals.

The Artist The Womack Sisters carry one of soul music’s most celebrated legacies into a new generation. Granddaughters of Sam Cooke and daughters of songwriting duo Womack & Womack, the sisters blend rich harmonies, heartfelt storytelling, and timeless soul into performances that honor their roots while forging a sound all their own.

The DJ VNPRT is a Portland DJ and curator whose dynamic sets weave together house, techno, baile funk, amapiano, and other global dance sounds. A fixture of the city’s DIY and community music scenes, VNPRT brings an adventurous spirit and an infectious energy that invites people to gather, move, and celebrate together.
República x Mexican Institute of Sound DJ: disco diablo Saturday, August 1 · 7:30 PM – 9:00 PM

Chef Angel Medina of República brings his Mexico-forward lens to Pickathon, where every plate begins somewhere specific, and the point of view does not flinch. Chef Angel’s cooking treats food as a living thing, rooted in region and carried by intent. Every plate holds the weight of where it came from; from the Olmec, the Zapotec, the Toltec, and everyone after, down to everything that made modern Mexican food the greatest cuisine of all. That evolution continues here. Pacific Northwest ingredients, met with technique and history. Joined by Mexican Institute of Sound and disco diablo, this Saturday dinner celebrates the traditions, histories, and creative energy that continue to shape contemporary Mexican culture.

The Chef Angel Medina is the Founder of República & Co. and TODOS Media. Born in Southern California and raised between Guadalajara and Tijuana, Medina came to Portland in 2010 and built a path from Mexican-grown coffee to a small group of restaurants. His work treats Mexican cuisine as history and reclamation, separating what is ancestral from what colonization introduced. República has earned national recognition from the James Beard Foundation and Bon Appétit.

Established in November of 2020, República began as a humble space offering beloved classics such as Pozole, Menudo, and Cochinita Pibil, and within weeks gained popularity as one of the best Mexican restaurants in the city. By only its sixth month, the restaurant began offering an evening Chef’s Tasting Dinner that quickly caught the attention of local press and the L.A. Times. In February of 2023, República settled into its new home on the corner of NW 10th and NW Couch in the Pearl District, not only a larger space but the right space, curating an experience that mirrored something in Paris, New York, London, or the restaurants of Mexico City.

The Artist Mexican Institute of Sound is the acclaimed musical project of Mexico City producer and DJ Camilo Lara. Drawing from cumbia, mariachi, norteño, mambo, hip-hop, electronic music, and global dance sounds, Lara creates exuberant, genre-defying performances that celebrate Mexico’s musical heritage while pushing it boldly into the present.

The DJ Vinyl devotee and host of Manteca on KMHD, disco diablo spins genre-blurring sets full of thoughtful energy and unexpected gems, all guided by a love of filling space with sound. Their vibrant, dancefloor-driven selections move effortlessly across disco, house, Latin rhythms, and global club sounds, keeping the energy flowing long after the last course is served.
Screen Door x The Travelin’ McCourysDJ: DJ Dentside Sunday, August 2 · 11:00 AM – 12:30 PM

This Sunday brunch is a celebration of two enduring American traditions, Southern cooking and bluegrass music, gathered around a shared table. Screen Door brings the soul of its Southern kitchen to Pickathon, with Culinary Director Dominic Finzo showcasing dishes that span brunch to dinner and honor Southern cuisine’s past, present, and future. The Travelin’ McCourys carry one of bluegrass’s most respected legacies into the present with virtuosity, spontaneity, and joy, while Portland’s DJ Dentside opens the morning with an easygoing soundtrack that bridges eras and genres. Together, it’s an invitation to settle in, pass the plate, and experience how food and music become traditions worth returning to.

The Restaurant Nicole and David Mouton, longtime Portland residents originally from South Louisiana, opened Screen Door Eastside in 2006 with the help of friends, family, and early employees. Their vision was to blend the rich traditions of Southern food with the fresh, local, and sustainable values of the Pacific Northwest. This blend, a meeting place of “fried and fresh,” celebrates both Southern comfort food and the region’s agricultural bounty, reflecting their deep passion for quality ingredients and thoughtful cooking. At the heart of Screen Door is a commitment to hospitality and the joy of sharing food and culture, a mission to bring people together over meals that honor both heritage and community.

The Chef Born and raised in Tennessee, Culinary Director Dominic Finzo represents a new generation of Southern chefs, one rooted in tradition while constantly looking ahead. Blending classical technique with a modern Pacific Northwest sensibility, he is passionate about preserving the soul of Southern cuisine while continuing to push it forward. His cooking is guided by a deep respect for heirloom ingredients and the stories they carry, believing that every dish is an opportunity to honor the people, places, and traditions that have shaped Southern food. Working closely with regional farmers and producers, he creates menus that celebrate the seasons, showcase exceptional local ingredients, and reflect the rich diversity of Southern culinary heritage.

The Artist The Travelin’ McCourys carry one of bluegrass music’s most respected legacies into the present. Led by brothers Ronnie and Rob McCoury, whose roots run deep in the Del McCoury Band, the group honors bluegrass traditions while embracing new musical pathways with virtuosity, spontaneity, and joy. Their performances celebrate a living tradition, growing stronger each time it’s shared.

The DJ Opening the morning, Portland DJ Dentside sets the tone with a thoughtfully curated selection that bridges eras and genres, creating an easygoing soundtrack for conversation, coffee, and the first meal of the day.
Every Curation gathering is made richer by the drinks in hand. We’re grateful to the beverage partners pouring alongside our chefs and artists this year:

Wandering Goat Coffee (Eugene, OR) · Autora Mezcal · Holladay Bourbon · 360 Vodka · Brokers Gin · Five Farms Irish Cream · Maloof Wines · Rubato Wines · Division Winemaking Co. · Dominio IV Wines · Estelbrook Farms & Vineyard · Nira Fermented Soda by Biotic Ferments
And a special shout out to Tre-Fin Foods, providing high quality, locally caught sustainable seafood in the Pacific Northwest.
A heartfelt thank you for helping us fill every table with something worth savoring.
Only 100 seats per gathering. Access requires a Weekend Pickathon Pass or the corresponding Day Pass for the event date, plus a separate Curation ticket.

stories.t: Wednesday Hootenanny: Early Entry Kicks Off with a Barn Dance
stories.x: This year, Early Entry lands on Wednesday. Gates open to the public at 5PM on Wednesday, July 29, giving you a full evening to settle in before the music begins Thursday.
stories.b: This year, Early Entry lands on Wednesday. Gates open to the public at 5:00 PM on Wednesday, July 29, giving you a full evening to settle in before the music begins Thursday. Wednesday Early Arrival Ticket: Arrive a day early to claim your favorite forest campsite and enjoy a "test the magic" previe
f: This year, Early Entry lands on Wednesday. Gates open to the public at 5:00 PM on Wednesday, July 29, giving you a full evening to settle in before the music begins Thursday.
Wednesday Early Arrival Ticket: Arrive a day early to claim your favorite forest campsite and enjoy a “test the magic” preview of the farm’s lights and soundscapes. Requires a 4-Day Pass.

Here’s what to expect: most folks will head straight to set up camp, then start wandering. The site will still be coming together around you. Crews will be building, sound testing will be happening, and the farm will be in motion. That’s part of the charm of arriving early. You get to watch Pickathon wake up, a true behind the scenes experience.

And you won’t be roughing it. Parking and the gear shuttle will be open, along with the Galaxy Bar, and the Galaxy Courtyard food trucks will be serving, and the Dish program will be up and running. Market and merch operations open Thursday.
But it wouldn’t be Pickathon if we didn’t plan something special for night one.
The Galaxy Barn Opens with a Barn Dance

On Wednesday night, the Galaxy Barn hosts our first-ever early entry Barn Dance. The evening starts with Two-Step lessons from 7pm to 8pm, led by the Showdown Saloon’s own BootScootPDX and Honkytonkbasement. Then William Surly & the Barroom Gospel Band take over until 10pm. The bar will be open, and the music stays inside the barn, so campers turning in early can rest easy while the dance floor does its thing.
No dance experience required. That’s the whole point of the lessons.
Meet Your Instructors: BootScootPDX and Honkytonkbasement

New to Two-Step? Been to a few drop-in lessons at the Showdown Saloon and looking for more? Welcome to BootScootPDX and Honkytonkbasement, a team of experienced Two-Step instructors based in Portland, Oregon.

Robbie Veltman proves you don’t have to grow up dancing to be part of the community. An avid live music fan and show attendee, she got sick of watching the dancers have all the fun and gave it a shot. She was quickly hooked, taking East Coast Swing, Lindy, and Balboa lessons. Two-Step has always been her favorite style, and frustrated by the lack of class options, she started her own class to help grow the local dance and live music scene. Her favorite part of teaching is building confidence in new dancers and assuring them it’s always more fun to be dancing than not. Find her at @bootscootpdx and @corndog_cowgirl.

James Jones is the owner/creator of Honkytonkbasement, a weekly guide to country music and dance events in PDX. A Mexican-American artist and social dancer, he brings over four years of experience in Two-Step, West Coast Swing, Lindy Hop, Salsa, Balboa, and Slow Balboa. He discovered dancing after attending countless country shows and deciding he didn’t want to just watch. He wanted to be part of the dancing community. For James, dance is a connection, both to the music and to the friends he’s made along the way. As a teacher, there’s nothing better than seeing a student have a breakthrough moment, when they finally get a move they’ve been trying to learn and start to truly enjoy themselves on the dance floor. Find him at @honkytonkbasement.
The Band: William Surly & The Barroom Gospel Band

William Surly is a singer/songwriter who saddles his horse (metaphorically speaking) in Portland, Oregon. Within his music he mixes classic country with outlaw, honky tonk, a dash of folk, some rock, and soul.

Inspired by storytellers of the Outlaw and Folk movements of the ’60s and ’70s and rejuvenated by the modern sounds of Sturgill Simpson, Margo Price, Mike and The Moonpies, Nikki Lane and more, Surly pays homage to the ones who came before him, singing songs best suited for a long running bar tab.

Best known for his role in the Lonesome Billies, who have shared the stage with nationally touring acts like Pokey LaFarge, Hurray for the Riff Raff, Blitzen Trapper and Nikki Lane, Surly has been in the Portland music scene for many years. His newest endeavor, William Surly & The Barroom Gospel Band, brings together a mighty fine mix of talented musicians currently working on their next album release.
Galaxy Bar, Galaxy Courtyard food trucks, and Dish program: open Wednesday evening
Two-Step lessons with BootScootPDX: 7-8pm, Galaxy Barn
William Surly & The Barroom Gospel Band: 8-10pm, Galaxy Barn
Market and merch operations open Thursday
Wednesday Early Arrival Ticket requires a 4-Day Pass
The music officially begins Thursday, but the dancing starts Wednesday. Grab your Wednesday Early Arrival ticket and be there when the farm comes to life.

stories.t: From Sea to Stage: Cherry Hill Surfaces With a Net-Woven World for 2026
stories.x: Woven from disused fishing nets by the PSU School of Architecture, Cherry Hill’s 2026 stage translates ocean waves into musical waves before shipping on to Ukraine to save lives.
stories.b: The Cherry Hill Neighborhood at Pickathon 2026 If The Woods is our daytime cathedral, Cherry Hill is its dark, mysterious sister. This neighborhood sleeps during the day, waking up after sundown to become a glowing, avant-garde wonderland on the ridge. Led by the PSU School of Architecture, Cherry H
f: The Cherry Hill Neighborhood at Pickathon 2026

If The Woods is our daytime cathedral, Cherry Hill is its dark, mysterious sister. This neighborhood sleeps during the day, waking up after sundown to become a glowing, avant-garde wonderland on the ridge. Led by the PSU School of Architecture, Cherry Hill features massive, student-built structures that guide you through the festival’s most radical visual experiments. Today, we’re thrilled to reveal what’s rising on the ridge in 2026.

Continuing an enduring tradition that marries radical environmental responsibility with inspirational visual form, the Cherry Hill neighborhood will once again burst with evocative design and wildly innovative materials, courtesy of the creative minds at PSU School of Architecture.

This year’s Cherry Hill theme is inspired by the power and rhythms of the ocean, and the nets that are at the heart of the fishing industry. In the ocean, fishing nets respond to the pulsing waves and currents deep under the water, taking on megalithic forms far below the surface. As the primary material for the 2026 Cherry Hill stage, disused fishing nets form cylindrical shapes on land, stretched and draped from a series of elevated towers reminiscent of carrelet fishing huts, intermingling with the tall trees behind the stage. The undulating fishing net surfaces, with their knotty textures, will catch and reflect light behind the performers, while strategically placed uplights showcase the large implied volumes. In the context of the festival, the ocean waves that once moved these weighty nets beneath the water symbolically translate into musical waves.

As light passes through the nets, the material catches reflections, shadows, and fleeting glimpses of movement. In the same way that water moves through a fishing net and eventually reaches the shore, sound waves move through the installation, pass through its layers, and reach the human body and consciousness.
The nets do not simply enclose space. They filter light, sound, views, and movement. They create moments of opacity and transparency, separation and connection, enclosure and openness.

The 2026 Cherry Hill structure embodies the Diversion Design-Build concept, a design practice invented by professors and students at Portland State’s Architecture school, where the materials for the venue are temporarily diverted from their usual purpose in order to construct a breathtaking stage at the festival and then either moved on for recycling or put back into use. The goal: to create an ephemeral performance venue that leaves no trace on the land and creates as little waste as possible, but makes a lasting imprint in our memories.

The first instance of a Diversion Design-Build venue was the 2014 Treeline Stage, created solely from hundreds of shipping pallets, which went back to their usual purpose of transporting appliances and the like after the stage was dismantled. Subsequent iterations of the Treeline Stage, and later the Cherry Hill neighborhood, included giant cardboard tubes used for wrapping sheet steel, apple harvesting crates, large cable reels, dimensional lumber, and wooden trusses that ultimately became sleeping pods for veterans transitioning out of homelessness in Clackamas County.

This year’s Diversion Design-Build takes the concept of reuse in a new and dramatic direction. Thanks to the innovative maritime recycling nonprofit Net Your Problem, once the nets have served their purpose at Cherry Hill, they will be shipped to Ukraine to protect villages from drone attacks. The nets will go from a life of catching fish and providing a way of life for Oregon fishermen to catching drones, saving lives in a war zone. And in between, they will form a performance venue where the people of Pickathon will gather to experience a weekend of joy, beauty, music and togetherness.

A net is made through connection. Each individual strand depends on the others, creating a larger system of support, interdependence, and collective strength. In this way, the material reflects the values of community and gathering at the heart of the festival.
Professor Travis BellTimothy BoscacciCourtney FrederickRuss GolubevIsabelle JonesJake MuldoonAnthony Westwolf
About the PSU School of Architecture

The Portland State University School of Architecture’s academic programs, which include a four-year bachelor’s degree, two-year professionally accredited Master of Architecture and three-year track of the Master of Architecture, emphasize focused study in architectural design, the humanities, tectonics and the profession. The rich, design-based curriculum prepares students for a career as a licensed architect while emphasizing the critical role of architects to make a positive impact on the built environment and communities in general. The Master of Architecture program concludes with the completion of a major design thesis study of individually inspired questions concerning architecture, culture and technology. PSU’s Graduate Certificate in Public Interest Design, the first of its kind in the United States, is also offered through the School of Architecture’s Center for Public Interest Design.
