b: Pickathon offers everything you need for an incredible weekend, but there are a few key things you’ll want to bring to make the most of your experience. Here’s your ultimate packing list, categorized for easy reference:
Footwear: Comfortable walking/hiking shoes are a must, as the festival grounds can get dusty.
Climate Control: Pack layers for both hot days and cool nights.
Financial Essentials: Bring a credit card or cash for vendor purchases. Your ID is also needed to pick up tickets and purchase alcohol.
Sun Protection: Pack sunscreen, a hat, and sunglasses to shield yourself from the sun.
Hydration: Bring a reusable water bottle to stay hydrated throughout the festival. Water is readily available for free on-site.
Pickathon Cup: While a stainless steel cup can be purchased at the festival, consider bringing your own with a carrying method.

Cell service is spotty in the woods; bring a battery pack, but note that public phones are unavailable. Bring your portable battery chargers or charge your devices for a fee at the solar-powered vendor.
Seating: A low-back lawn chair or blanket can provide a comfortable spot to relax and enjoy the music.
Portable Charger: Cell service might be limited, so a portable charger can keep your phone powered up (on-site charging is available for a fee).
Yoga Mat: Morning classes are available to awaken the body and refocus the mind.
Pack light as most everything you need is onsite.

Pack your camping gear in a way that allows for easy transportation to and from your campsite to the nearest Gear Drop location (which could be located within a range of 10 yards to a 1/3 of a mile up or down trails).
For more details refer to our Camping Guide.
There’s no need to pack coolers! Pickathon offers a wide variety of delicious and affordable food and drink vendors to keep you satiated all weekend.
Leave your furry friends at home: Pets are strictly prohibited.
No outside alcohol: Security checks vehicles upon entry. Outside alcohol will be confiscated.
Respectful Seating: Chairs and blankets left unattended become communal seating. Be neighborly upon your return.
Leave No Trace: Open fires, fireworks, firearms, and portable shade structures are not permitted. Camp stove usage requires extreme caution.
By packing smart and following these guidelines, you’re all set for a smooth and enjoyable Pickathon experience!
Pickathon is renowned as a pioneering leader in festival sustainability. To get there, we started with a dream.
What if Pickathon eliminated all plastic?
In 2010, Pickathon became the first major American music festival to make it happen.
Plastic beer cups were replaced with stainless steel cups that every attendee reused all weekend and took home as a collectible.
Plastic water bottles were replaced with reusable water bottles.
Water was made free and abundant.
The result of eliminating plastic was our waste volume went down by over 40%.
We were excited but not 100% satisfied, as we knew the huge volume of compostable dishware at most music festivals ends up in the landfill. This inspired a new dream!
What if Pickathon eliminated all single-use dishware/utensils?
In 2011, Pickathon became the first major American music festival to eliminate all single-use food dishes & utensils, replacing them with reusable bamboo-based dishes + utensils that we wash on-site.
Eliminating single use dishware reduced our waste by an additional 30%.
Covid shut the festival down for two years, but during this time, a new dream was born.
What if we minimized our carbon footprint by using time and natural terrain?
In 2022, Pickathon redesigned the entire festival experience to better fit within the environmental footprint of Pendarvis Farm.
During the day when the sun is burning hot, performances take place in thickly wooded locations to provide a cool shaded experience to the performers and audience.
As the sun goes down and the crowds swell, we move to huge open meadows to finish the day under the stars.
This made Pickathon’s festival experience better in every way, and led to us enshrining one of our three core design principles – Nature is the Best Vibe.
Here’s what else we do every year to keep Pickathon environmentally sustainable:Recycling & Compost
Pickathon’s recycling and compost team is made up of volunteers who spend most of the festival rounding up everything that can be either recycled or composted.

Pendarvis Farm hosts a permanent solar array on the roof of the Galaxy Barn. The energy generated during the year offsets 100% of the energy used during the festival in the Galaxy Barn plus a portion of the electricity used by the food and craft vendors.
Pickathon financially incentivizes our audience to ride bikes and take mass transportation to Pickathon to minimize the total carbon footprint of Pickathon.
Work traders help build and run Pickathon and earn their pass. You must be 18 or older.

Creative Neighborhoods, our nonprofit design-build partner, is the team behind Pickathon’s neighborhoods. Every stage, bar, patio and gathering place you see on the farm is designed with leading architects and builders, stands at Pickathon for one weekend, and then goes to work somewhere else for years.
If you need a stage, a patio, a pavilion, a classroom or a play space, we can design it with you and build it. It debuts at Pickathon in front of thousands of people, then we deliver it to your site.
Businesses and private owners: you bring the budget. We aim to come in at least 10% under the open-market price, with a structure designed by top architects.
Nonprofits and community groups with a budget: it works the same way.
Nonprofits still raising money: we can help you find partners to fund the build.

Recent builds went to Parrott Creek Child & Family Services (outdoor classrooms), Sabin CDC (gardens and gathering spaces at 17 properties), Dream Plaza 2.0 in Portland’s Central Eastside, Girls Build, and Alliance Charter Academy.
We push what a building can be

The festival is a testing ground. Each year our design teams try new structures, materials and ways of putting a building together and taking it apart, so it can be reused instead of thrown away. That work has earned AIA design awards.
Students and apprentices build alongside working architects and carpenters, from Portland State architecture students to youth shop programs. They leave with real projects and real skills.

Pickathon has built its neighborhoods by hand for two decades. The idea of Creative Neighborhoods took shape in 2023, and in 2024 we launched it as a nonprofit so the building work could stand on its own and serve the community year-round.
Ready to talk about a project? Use the Build with Pickathon form, or email info@pickathon.com.

You think you know music festivals? Pickathon will make you rethink everything. Leave your expectations at the gate. This isn’t your typical festival, it’s a portal to a different world of music. Imagine stumbling upon your new favorite band while wandering through a sun-dappled forest.

We don’t just book headliners; we cultivate a community of groundbreaking artists. You’ll leave with a playlist full of hidden gems and stories of ‘I saw them before they were big.’ The smaller size of the fest and the multiple performances give you a much higher chance of actually meeting some of the artists.

Imagine stages nestled among towering trees, where the music blends seamlessly with the sounds of nature. Feel the cool forest air, hear the music resonate through the trees, and taste the locally sourced flavors – Pickathon is a feast for the senses. This isn’t just a backdrop; it’s an integral part of the experience, providing shade and comfort.

More than just a festival, Pickathon is a gathering of like-minded souls. We prioritize sustainability with our reusable dish program and creating a space where you can connect with nature and each other guilt-free. Enjoy the significant savings that come with free camping.

Pickathon has a reputation for being something special, an experience that those who’ve been understand on a deeper level. Join the ‘IYKYK’ (if you know, you know) crowd and discover why. Pickathon is a “word of mouth” festival. Once you experience the magic, you’ll never look at festivals the same way again.
Follow us on Instagram at @pickathon for real-time updates and more!

There’s a common saying among those who return to Pendarvis Farm year after year: “You won’t understand unless you come.” It’s an understatement. How do you describe a place that feels less like a music festival and more like a summer camp for the soul? It’s a world built for wandering, for connection, and for the kind of joyous discovery that sticks with you long after the weekend is over.

The secret is that Pickathon is an experience where everything is intertwined. The world-class music, the stunning architecture, and the beautiful natural landscape don’t just coexist—they enrich each other to create something truly different.

We don’t just set up stages in a field; we build a temporary city within a lush, 80-acre forest. Winding paths lead you through groves of trees to a series of distinct “neighborhoods.” To see how it all connects, you can view the festival map and learn more in our guide to Getting Around Pickathon.
Each neighborhood is a functional work of art, featuring large-scale, ephemeral structures created by world-class architects and designers.
These aren’t just decorations; they are the stages, bars, and gathering spots, all built in harmony with the natural surroundings. This is the stunning world you get to live in for four days.

This unique environment is the driving force behind everything else. It’s what makes the discovery of music here so profound. We are a legendary launching pad for future icons, and our stages are designed to be the most memorable settings to see them for the first time. The universe of artists who played here just before they broke out is vast, including a select few like Sturgill Simpson, Billy Strings, Tyler Childers, Future Islands, Lake Street Dive, Shakey Graves, Khruangbin, and Black Pumas.

This design also creates a feeling of freedom. With most artists playing twice, the frantic pressure of other festivals disappears. You have the time to follow your curiosity, stumble upon a mind-blowing meal from an award-winning chef, or relax in a hidden oasis. The experience is yours to create.

It all rests on a foundation of respect for the land and for each other. Our commitment to sustainability and community is what fosters the famously relaxed, safe, and friendly atmosphere that makes this “summer camp for the soul” possible. It’s a world built to be explored, and we invite you to come, get lost, and find something new.

Comedy · Already a name. Portland-born comic, co-head writer of The Late Late Show with James Corden, and a 2019 Emmy winner for the Carpool Karaoke McCartney special.
Literary · Already a name. Novelist whose books The Motel Life, Lean on Pete and The Night Always Comes became feature films. He also founded Richmond Fontaine and The Delines.
Literary · Already a name. Novelist and Kelly Reichardt's screenwriter on Old Joy, Wendy and Lucy, Meek's Cutoff and First Cow. He was Emmy-nominated for HBO's Mildred Pierce.
Literary · Already a name. Science writer whose Becoming Earth is a New York Times bestseller and won the Rachel Carson Environment Book Award.

Literary · Here early. Filmed for Pickathon's Spoken Series at the farm in 2016. She later wrote the essay collection This Is Major, a National Book Critics Circle Award finalist, and the memoir How to Live Free in a Dangerous World (2024).
Literary · Here early. Read at Pickathon in 2018, before being named Oregon's 10th Poet Laureate in April 2020. He now curates Pickathon's poetry lineup.
Literary · Here early. Her later novel Madwoman (2025) became a national bestseller and an Oprah's Best Book of the Year.

Literary · Here early. First read at Pickathon as a debut novelist. The Edge of Water then won the Westport Prize and the Ploughshares Zacharis First Book Award and was named a TIME Best Book of the Year.
Comedy · Here early. Named one of Netflix's 'Introducing' comics in 2022. She has done a Comedy Central Stand-Up Featuring set and opened for Taylor Tomlinson.
Comedy · Here early. Libyan-born Portland comic who did a stand-up set on Conan about three weeks after Pickathon 2019. He now tours nationally and has Comedy Central credits.
Comedy · Here early. Recorded his first Comedy Central stand-up special in 2019. He is also on NBC's AP Bio and co-hosts the All Fantasy Everything podcast.
Comedy · Here early. Portland's Funniest Person of 2015 who started Pickathon comedy in 2016. She went on to a Comedy Central half-hour special, Last Comic Standing and CBS's After Midnight.
Literary · Here early. Read from her debut Wolfish the year it came out. The book went on to win the 2024 Oregon Book Award.
Literary · Already a name. Her debut novel Deep Cuts (2025) is a national bestseller published in 14 languages and is being adapted for film by A24.
Film · Already a name. Emmy-nominated film director and author of Dogwalker and Turtleface.
Literary · Already a name. Journalist and host of the Bundyville podcast. Her book Blazing Eye Sees All won the 2026 Oregon Book Award for General Nonfiction.

Founded in 1993 by Lori S., the San Francisco doom band is named in The Encyclopedia of Heavy Metal and the A to Z of Doom, Gothic & Stoner Metal (both 2003), with eight releases through Beyond Vision.
Won a W.C. Handy Award for Best New Artist in 1997 and Down Beat's Best Blues Album in 1999, and took a Grammy in 2005 after a nomination in 2003.
You Forgot It in People won the 2003 Juno for Alternative Album of the Year. Forgiveness Rock Record made the Polaris shortlist, and Hug of Thunder (2017) ended a seven-year gap.
Daptone's Screaming Eagle of Soul, who found his audience in his sixties - three albums and a documentary behind him. He died seven weeks later.

deep.n: CJ Chenier & the Red Hot Louisiana Band
deep.l: Won the 1997 Living Blues Critics' Poll Award for The Big Squeeze. He has led his father Clifton's band since 1987, toured with Paul Simon, and played to a huge crowd at the 2001 Chicago Blues Festival.

Joined The Gladiators in 1969 as bassist, singer and songwriter through their 1970s and 80s roots-reggae run, then moved to Seattle in 1987 and has led the Boogie Brown Band through about ten solo albums.
A Franklin County, Virginia kid, signed but still playing regional rooms. A year on, his own small-theatre dates across the country and a tour of England.
A Swedish home-recordist unknown in America. He had played Brussels' AB Club that spring; that October he sold out its main hall.
A founding member of the David Grisman Quintet in 1977 and of the Turtle Island String Quartet in 1985, which won Grammys in the classical crossover category. Decades of teaching and session work.
Formed in 1984, they made You're Living All Over Me (1987) and Bug (1988) for SST, then reunited the original lineup, J Mascis and Lou Barlow included, in 2005.
Four albums in on Park the Van, a working small club act. An ANTI- deal and Shame Shame (2010) took them to the Crystal Ballroom and comparable ballrooms.
Twenty years and a dozen albums deep, from Southern Rock Opera to American Band, Jason Isbell among the alumni, and a New Year's run at Athens' 40 Watt as an institution.
Founded in 1973 by Kahil El'Zabar, with a discography stretching back to 1981 and more than fifty years of standing.
Howe Gelb's Tucson band, active since 1980 with roughly twenty albums and steady Uncut, MOJO and Pitchfork coverage. The root of the Tucson sound and of Calexico.
Griff Washburn was self-releasing EPs from a van with no studio album. Then the debut Lola (2024), amphitheater headlines and the Hollywood Bowl on October 4, 2025.
Won the Telluride band competition in 2006 and hit #1 on the US bluegrass chart with If Sorrows Swim (2014) and All for Money (2019).
Iowa folk songwriter recording since 1974, with two Grammy nominations, NAIRD Indie Awards for One Big Town and The Poet Game, and a long run as a Prairie Home Companion regular.
Four EPs, no album, and small clubs when she came. Her debut arrived in 2020; by 2022 she was headlining Le National in Montreal.
A Brooklyn folk songwriter playing small clubs in 2025, then opening Mumford & Sons arena dates in Australia, with headline runs through Britain, Europe and New York.
Founded in 1992 and the best-known Tuvan ensemble in the West, with roughly twenty releases and work alongside Frank Zappa, the Chieftains and Kronos Quartet.

Signed to Daptone in 2022 and released a debut album in 2023, then headlined US and UK theaters and played Glastonbury's West Holts stage. Before that: self-released singles, no label, small UK rooms.
Co-founded X in 1977. Los Angeles, Wild Gift and Under the Big Black Sun have sat on critics' best-of-the-eighties lists for decades. Solo since 1990 and a working actor.
Three sisters playing living rooms off one self-released record. Fifteen months later they were opening James Bay's sold-out arena tour and headed to Coachella.
Won the Americana New and Emerging Artist award in 2009, the year he played the Beacon Theatre and Bonnaroo. He had one EP, Yuma, and a stint in his father Steve Earle's band behind him.
All-Ireland Fleadh winner in 1966, then The Bothy Band, Patrick Street (co-founded 1985) and the Celtic Fiddle Festival. He later received an NEA National Heritage Fellowship.
Signed to Dead Oceans after two Woodsist albums, he sold out Bowery Ballroom, then Town Hall and Brooklyn Steel in New York. Before that: small clubs.

Verve signed the Los Angeles League of Musicians out of a weekly Highland Park bar residency. They recorded a live album at Chicago's Thalia Hall and play outdoor dates at farm and amphitheater scale.
Moved from small clubs and low bill slots to headlining theaters within about five years, with The Way We Move (2012) and heavy sync placement behind it.

deep.n: Laurie Lewis, Tom Rozum, and Tom Sauber
deep.l: Two-time IBMA Female Vocalist of the Year (1992, 1994), a 1995 Grammy nominee with Tom Rozum, and a performer on True Life Blues, the 1997 Grammy winner for Best Bluegrass Album.
Recording soul since 1969 and nicknamed Little JB. My World (2009) helped set off the retro-soul revival.
Co-founded Solesides, later Quannum Projects, with DJ Shadow, Blackalicious and Lateef, and made Latyrx: The Album (1997) with Lateef. Solo since Later That Day (2003); rapping for thirty-plus years.
Came up in small rooms and support slots with the Spillage Village collective. Her debut, The Jungle Is the Only Way Out, was followed by headline dates at The Showbox in Seattle.
Four Birmingham, Alabama musicians who started as teenagers, independent and barely touring. Now signed with Red Light Management, they headline the 9:30 Club in DC and tour Australia.
A platinum single in 2015 and multiple sold-out nights a year at Red Rocks since 2016, already an amphitheater headliner.
Both of them still had day jobs. Two years on, an album, a label, and their first headline tour of clubs in the States and England.
A streaming-built Victoria, B.C. folk duo that went from small rooms to headlining Sydney’s City Recital Hall within a year.
Went from busking and solo bar dates with two self-released records to the Grand Ole Opry and theater headlines within about five years.
"Feel It Still" reached the top five of the Hot 100 and No. 1 on the Alternative chart in 2017, and won the Grammy for Best Pop Duo/Group Performance in January 2018.
Sam Coomes and Janet Weiss have made ten studio albums since a 1993 cassette, most recently Breaking the Balls of History on Sub Pop, and toured as Elliott Smith's band in 1998-99.
His song "Tuyo" became the Narcos theme seven months after booking, reaching No. 6 on Latin Pop Digital Songs and earning a Primetime Emmy nomination for Outstanding Main Title Theme Music.
Alec Duckart, a self-releasing Portland artist, sold out the Mercury Lounge on his first headline tour, then played Vicar Street in Dublin and KOKO in London.
A New York band two years in, with a debut that had come out that January. They went from Boston's Paradise to the House of Blues in a year.
Active since the early 1990s: Big Easy Awards in 1999, 2008 and 2010, Best of the Beat 2012, the Rounder album Unlock Your Mind, and spots with Jools Holland, Conan and NFL Honors.
Granddaughters of Sam Cooke, signed to Daptone with one EP and no album. They opened for Al Green at the Hollywood Bowl and supported Thee Sacred Souls on an amphitheater tour.
The 2013 White Lighter tour took the eleven-piece band from Schubas in Chicago to the 9:30 Club and Webster Hall, then a Crystal Ballroom headline and a live album.
Zambia's defining 1970s zamrock band, led by Emmanuel "Jagari" Chanda and named for We Intend To Cause Havoc. Reformed and touring behind the album Zango.
First recorded for Folkways in the 1960s with First Songs, and later lived in northwest Oregon and played Portland often.
Started recording in his seventies; Fat Possum released five of his albums between 1997 and 2008.
A Tokyo psych band self-releasing on Guruguru Brain to small clubs. Four years later their farewell tour sold out Brooklyn Steel and took two Portland nights.
Cardinal made them a critics' band in small clubs. They headlined Brooklyn Steel in 2019, then sold out two Brooklyn Bowl nights and played Thalia Hall in 2022.
Played small clubs outside New Zealand, then released Live at Auckland Town Hall by January 2019. A Melbourne homecoming drew thousands.
Pitchfork called Natural Brown Prom Queen the year's second best album. Sudan Archives came with two EPs and small rooms, then headlined Webster Hall.
An Auckland band in small clubs and support slots when they came. Four years later they headlined Brooklyn Steel, Webster Hall and the Fonda.
Britain took to Ezra Furman: from small rooms they grew to Shepherd's Bush Empire and O2 Forum Kentish Town.
My Gospel put him on Rolling Stone's 2016 country list. He was playing small rooms when he came, and later headlined the Ryman.
Bandleader James Hunter's People Gonna Talk earned a Grammy nomination for Best Traditional Blues Album.
A new club act newly signed to Blue Note in 2006; they grew into Red Rocks and Ryman headliners with a Grammy nomination thirteen years on.
Dan Bejar's Destroyer was shortlisted for the Polaris Prize for Kaputt in 2011 and Labyrinthitis in 2022.
A Tuareg guitarist from Niger whose Afrique Victime drew near-universal praise and made The Guardian's ten best albums of 2021.
Uncut called Nixon the best album of 2000.
Chris Thile's young quintet, two albums in, when they played the farm in 2010. They went on to Ryman-tier halls and a Grammy for best folk album in 2019.
Their self-titled album won the Grammy for Best Bluegrass Album in 2019.
Grammy-nominated for Best Regional Roots Music Album in 2014 for The Life & Times of... The Hot 8 Brass Band.
Sara Watkins (Nickel Creek's platinum run) and Sarah Jarosz (already a Grammy winner) skipped the clubs and opened at theater level. A 2020 Grammy for Best American Roots Song followed.
A Vermont folk songwriter touring a small-label album called Hadestown in 2010. Nine years later it was on Broadway, won eight Tonys including Best Musical, and took a Grammy.
One small-label record and small rooms at the start. By 2017 she sold out Seattle's Neptune Theatre and played Brooklyn Steel.
A Tuareg guitar hero in small clubs when he came. Nonesuch and Dan Auerbach followed, then a No. 1 Billboard World debut, Bonnaroo, Newport Folk and Outside Lands, and in 2019 a Grammy nomination.
A cult favorite in tiny rooms when he came. Muchacho and “Song for Zula” took him to big rooms, the Billboard 200, a tour with Robert Plant and The Amazing Spider-Man 2.

John Dwyer's garage band was on the edge of a hiatus when they came. Under several names, a record almost every year and a near-universal rave for Floating Coffin, they went on to sell out far bigger rooms than the clubs of 2012.
A self-released Portland band until Sub Pop signed them. Furr made Rolling Stone's best of 2008, and within a year they were on Conan and at Coachella, in rooms far past the clubs they started in.
Light Up Gold ranked in Rolling Stone's top 15 albums of the year. Parquet Courts were playing Brooklyn basements, then headlined Webster Hall 22 months later.
Queens of the Breakers made the Polaris Prize long list. From Montreal clubs, they reached the Metropolis by November 2014 and headlined it outright in November 2017.
Fox Confessor Brings the Flood made her a critics' favorite and Middle Cyclone reached the Billboard top three. She was already a theatre headliner when she arrived.
A multi-platinum album in The Reminder, the '1234' iPod ad, four Grammy nominations and a Juno sweep. The Metals tour played big theaters and festival main stages.
Nearly twenty years of looped violin and whistling, from the Squirrel Nut Zippers' platinum record to Break It Yourself reaching No. 10, in theatres and concert halls worldwide.
Four Grammys including one for producing Mavis Staples, after 25 years fronting Uncle Tupelo and Wilco. Wilco headlines amphitheatres and runs its own festival, Solid Sound.
His Dinosaur Jr. record You're Living All Over Me ranks among Pitchfork's best albums of the 1980s.
LA punk band X put its debut on Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums, and its second came second only to The Clash with critics in 1981.
Austin's banjo-and-tuba band, unofficially split in 2000, back together for a few shows in 2008.
Songwriter Todd Snider was inducted into the Oregon Music Hall of Fame in 2021.
A bluegrass pioneer who recorded with Hazel Dickens from the 1960s; inducted into the Bluegrass Hall of Fame two years after playing Pickathon.
Drag City's songwriter for twenty years, from Smog to his own name; Apocalypse topped the year-end lists at Pitchfork, Mojo and Uncut, and Dream River was Mojo's album of 2013.
A platinum debut, a gold This Side, Grammys and two sold-out Ryman nights before their 2007 hiatus; they won another Grammy after the 2014 reunion.

In 2011 he was on the road most of the year, grinding it out in small bars and clubs. By 2018 Hard Times and White Lines hit No. 2 on Billboard's Heatseekers chart and he played the Ryman Auditorium in Nashville for the first time.
A Best Americana Album Grammy nomination for Shine On Rainy Day, with clubs as his own rooms. Opening arenas and amphitheatres for Chris Stapleton put him in front of far bigger crowds.
A Grammy-nominated mandolin prodigy playing theaters and small halls when she came. A No. 1 bluegrass album in 2020 and far bigger stages followed.
Teen Dream was Pitchfork's No. 5 album of 2010 and Bloom reached No. 7 on the Billboard 200; they had closed Pitchfork Music Festival and played London's Roundhouse before they came.
A Sub Pop band and 2006 Polaris nominee who had played the Wiltern and Osheaga before this reunion year.
Berkeley bluegrass fiddler and singer, twice IBMA Female Vocalist of the Year (1992, 1994) with a Grammy win in 1997 on True Life Blues.
Irish fiddler from London, a member of The Bothy Band and co-founder of Patrick Street, awarded an NEA National Heritage Fellowship in 2002.
Berkeley-area bluegrass mandolinist and singer, Laurie Lewis's duo partner since 1986 and Grammy-nominated with her for The Oak and the Laurel.
Fiddler and co-founder of the David Grisman Quintet era new-acoustic movement, Turtle Island String Quartet and Psychograss.
Everyone's Crushed was Pitchfork Best New Music and made Pitchfork's and Rolling Stone's best albums of 2023.
Nate Amos had just released Box for Buddy, Box for Star on Double Double Whammy. He then signed to Matador, announced Holo Boy and a global tour, and played rooms like Vancouver's Hollywood Theatre.
Vincent Neil Emerson released Blue Stars in April 2026, an album Saving Country Music praised. He first played Pickathon in 2024, the summer he opened for Whiskey Myers at Red Rocks.
A Vermont songwriter whose Burnover made Paste's best albums of 2025 the year after he played.
Colorado band formed in 2006 that calls its style transcendental folk; it went on hiatus in 2018 and is back on the road.
In 2025 the City of Los Angeles named Rogê one of eleven master-artist fellows, a $10,000 grant, a year after NPR's Morning Edition reviewed his album Curyman II. He first played Pickathon in 2024.

A Seattle bartender who released his first album on his 50th birthday in 2023. The Seattle Times called him one of the city's best kept secrets, and Pickathon named him a 2024 Rising Star Spotlight artist. He signed to Saddle Creek in 2025, and Paste scored his second album an 8.4.

Rhododendron signed to The Flenser in March 2026, released Ascent Effort in May, and headlined Portland's Aladdin Theater on May 30. The trio formed in 2019 as School of Rock students and drew a Willamette Week feature the spring before their Pickathon 2024 sets.

The Chicago band played clubs at Pickathon 2024 after The Window topped Treble's and Under the Radar's lists. Singin' to an Empty Chair (Feb. 2026) then won strong reviews from Pitchfork and led to their own headline rooms.

In 2026 Bella White released her third album, A Sign in the Weather, and Saving Country Music gave it a strong review. She first played Pickathon in 2022 and returned in 2024, a year after her song “Burn Me Once” appeared on The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes soundtrack.
Vulture ranked Diaspora Problems the fifth best album of the year. The Philadelphia hardcore band has since played a Tiny Desk and a Coachella side stage, and co-headlines small clubs.
Tamara Lindeman's Ignorance was Uncut's album of the year, praised by nearly every critic who reviewed it, and shortlisted for Canada's biggest album prize.
Critics on both sides of the Atlantic put On Your Own Love Again among the year's best. Over three albums she went from small rooms to theaters and churches.
Legacy! Legacy! was among the records indie critics singled out in 2019. She toured it headlining small clubs and opening for Common and Raphael Saadiq.
Won the 2018 Grammy for Best Regional Roots Music Album for Kalenda, after a 2009 nomination. The Cajun band contributed to the Beasts of the Southern Wild score.
Relatives in Descent was one Rolling Stone writer's favorite record of 2017, from a Detroit band almost every critic praised. Protomartyr played small clubs before and after.
Critics put three records running among the year's best, from The Navigator to The Past Is Still Alive. Rooms grew from small to mid-size clubs and festival side stages.
Her debut landed on Paste's and PopMatters' best-of-2018 lists. Five years on she was still playing Mississippi Studios in Portland.
Spin ranked his two 2011 albums among the year's fifty best.
'Call Me a Fool,' with Carla Thomas, earned a 2022 Grammy nomination for Best American Roots Song. She began in clubs and played small theaters at most by 2017.
The year MC Taylor signed to Merge. A Grammy nomination followed for Terms of Surrender; seven years on he was still headlining clubs like DC's 9:30.

In January 2026 Saving Country Music called Ellis Bullard a “honky tonk hardliner” at Mile 0 Fest in Key West, after Rolling Stone ran a feature on him in 2025. He first played Pickathon in 2024 with two strong Saving Country Music reviews behind him and was invited back in 2025.
The Party was shortlisted for the Polaris Prize and nominated for a Juno. Andy Shauf went from small clubs to Revolution Hall and Union Transfer.
Formed in 1994 and the go-to backing band for Neko Case, Jon Langford and Andre Williams, The Sadies won a 2023 Juno for Colder Streams, also Polaris-shortlisted. They remain a club band.
SPIN named Civilian its album of the year. Wye Oak's headline slots moved from small to mid-size clubs.
Grammy-nominated for Best Folk Album in 2019 for Black Cowboys and again in 2024 for Traveling Wildfire.
Grammy-nominated for Best Bluegrass Album in 2014 for This World Oft Can Be.
The banjo innovator, a Pickathon regular since its early years, was Grammy-nominated for Best Bluegrass Album in 2021 for Man on Fire.
Reissued by Awesome Tapes From Africa after decades driving a DC cab, Hailu Mergia saw Lala Belu top critics' lists at Mojo and The Wire. He plays small rooms.
Her album Designer won over nearly every critic who reviewed it in 2019.
Crushing drew near-universal praise and six ARIA nominations. Julia Jacklin played Sydney's Metro Theatre before and after it, and New York's Bowery Ballroom.
Cheap Silver and Solid Country Gold was Saving Country Music's Album of the Year for 2019.
Old Flowers earned a Grammy nomination for Best Americana Album in 2021. Courtney Marie Andrews plays listening rooms, clubs and small UK chapels.
Won Emerging Artist of the Year at the 2023 Americana Honors & Awards.
Paste named Everybody Works its album of the year, and Pitchfork and Rolling Stone ranked it too. Melina Duterte went from small to mid-size clubs.
Big Ugly landed near the top of both Time's and Paste's best albums of 2025, from a band still playing bars.

Florry's 2025 album Sounds Like... landed on year-end lists including No. 3 at Uproxx, and in 2026 the Philadelphia band opened Ratboys' theater shows in Toronto, Washington and Atlanta. They first played Pickathon in 2024.
Stereogum put Pohorylle among the best country records of 2021. The Enterprise, Oregon songwriter plays small clubs and listening rooms and tours European clubs.
Hard-core traditional bluegrass: Danny Paisley was named IBMA Male Vocalist of the Year in 2016.
This Kyiv 'ethno-chaos' quartet won the Shevchenko National Prize, Ukraine's highest award for the arts.
The Cajun fiddler and singer shared three straight Grammy nominations with the Pine Leaf Boys.
The old-time fiddle master was Grammy-nominated for Best Traditional Folk Album with Fiddlers 4.
Americana Song of the Year for She Left Me for Jesus, then a charting KMAG YOYO.
Their debut earned four ARIA nominations and an Australian Music Prize nod.
Veracruz son jarocho band with two Grammy nominations for Best Regional Mexican Music Album.
New Orleans juke-blues elder who received OffBeat's Lifetime Achievement Award in Music in 2022.
Guitarist Yasmin Williams' Urban Driftwood made NPR Music's 50 Best Albums of 2021.
Spin, NME and The Times praised The Pirate's Gospel, and she went on to Rough Trade for To Be Still.
Forced Witness arrived that September to strong reviews from Pitchfork and Uncut, and never came near a chart.
Her 2021 album was premiered by Glide and reviewed by Saving Country Music, with later notice from Nashville Scene and The Bluegrass Situation. Rooms stay clubs like Knuckleheads in Kansas City.
He ran old-time banjo through punk with the Bad Livers, and won Steve Martin's banjo prize in 2015.
Bad Livers founder who won the Steve Martin Prize for Excellence in Banjo and Bluegrass in 2015. His ATO albums and sessions with Bill Frisell round out the record.
Powell made the music for Cold Mountain (2003) and produced Rhiannon Giddens; Granger, from the Balfa family line, joined the Pine Leaf Boys. Both stayed in dance halls and folk clubs.
Formed in 1989 and routinely credited in the roots press as founders of the alt-country sound, with strong national reviews in the 1990s. Scheherazade followed on Bloodshot in 2016.
Three Rounder albums between 1998 and 2004, including Heart of a Singer with Hazel Dickens; deep standing among Appalachian peers and no commercial profile.
Four albums for Bella Union across thirteen years, admired by Pitchfork and the British press, and the venues never grew past the club circuit.
Rykodisc recorded him from 1995, and Sky Like a Broken Clock (2001) was widely listed among the year's best roots records. A slide guitarist who stayed in folk clubs and listening rooms.
Pachy Garcia's one-man dub studio, out of Puerto Rico by way of Los Angeles and signed to ATO, built its following on dub nights, support slots and small clubs.
Native American Music Awards recognition and steady national press; she has opened for First Aid Kit and Langhorne Slim and played CMJ bills, Johnny Brenda's and Warehouse XI.
Five Los Angeles improvisers who recorded two albums of acclaim in two years.
Winner of Portland's Muddy Award for Best Acoustic Guitar every year since 1992 and a Cascade Blues Association Hall of Fame inductee in 1998; Stop This World topped the Living Blues Radio Chart.
Blue Horse (2000) and Chinatown (2003) brought the Vancouver trio Juno roots-and-traditional recognition and strong UK press and radio.
David Lynch put the Minneapolis brothers in the Twin Peaks revival in 2017, and Easy Way topped the indie-retail chart in 2019; Red House signed them in 2016.
Won the Steve Martin Prize for Excellence in Banjo and Bluegrass in 2015, after a decade with the Bad Livers on Quarterstick and Sugar Hill.
Eight or nine albums on Munich, Sugar Hill and Yep Roc since 1994; their bluegrass 'Gin and Juice' was so often credited to Phish that the mix-up became their best-known fact.
Texas state fiddle titles by 2001, the Opry by 2003, the Kennedy Center by 2006 - fifteen years of honors and the same size halls throughout.
40 Days won the 2005 Juno for roots and traditional album of the year (group), and by 2006 they were recurring guests on A Prairie Home Companion.
National Bluegrass Banjo champion at Winfield in 1987 and 1991, with six Rounder albums from 1990 to 2000 and appearances at Telluride and Kerrville.
Pianist who came up in New York's experimental jazz scene after Berklee, now based near Woodstock; his records include TigerFace (2012).
Los Angeles duo Thes One and Double K, fully independent for 17 years; their 2002 album O.S.T. is long treated as an independent hip-hop classic.
A Rounder artist since the mid-1990s and member of Balfa Toujours, he played on the Cold Mountain soundtrack and was Joan Baez's musical director.
Afro-Peruvian music mixed with electronica, from Lima, formed in 2001 and released worldwide on Cumbancha.
Carrying his grandfather R.L.'s hill-country tradition; he won a Grammy in 2022.
Anais Mitchell, Eric D. Johnson and Josh Kaufman already drew theater and folk-hall crowds when the project was unannounced. Two Grammy nominations followed in 2021.
Played the Apollo and shared bills with Otis Redding and James Brown in the 1960s. His band, three months old, later headlined Revolution Hall for his 85th birthday and toured Europe.
Watchhouse's songwriter, formerly of Mandolin Orange, with three solo instrumental albums, Buried in a Cape and the pair Witching Hour and Fable & Fire.
California rockabilly and western swing band, together since 1988, with albums on HighTone and Yep Roc.
A Dallas soul artist and producer who also worked A&R for several labels. I Got More Soul, on Omnivore, was his return after a long break from recording.
Replaced Morrissey's opening act at the last minute in 1991, signed to Atlantic, then started her own label, Right On Records, in 2000.
A Santa Cruz string band formed in 2001. I'm a Stranger Here, their first record on New West, came out that October.
Folk rock from Palenville in the Catskills, who toured with Bright Eyes in 2007 and opened for Dave Matthews Band in 2010.
Austin-based singer who mixes western swing, country and rockabilly, recording since his 1995 debut Thunderstorms and Neon Signs and on Bloodshot since 2001.
A free EP, no album, playing bars when he came. A year later he was opening theaters for Steve Earle and selling out Lincoln Hall in Chicago.

press.q: Pickathon showed why it’s the best indie festival in the country.
…where the best artists look as if they’d been whittled from the surrounding woods.
Imagine a music festival without any of the worst parts of a music festival.
Play Pickathon well, the story goes, and you just might make it big.
Pickathon has become known for getting an early jump on acts about to break big.
Welcome to Pickathon, perhaps America’s most unique and highly-curated music festival.
Pickathon doesn’t attract the same kind of attention as its peers — and that’s by design.
It remains the best festival I’ve ever been to, by a fairly wide margin, and I’ve been to a bunch.
With a zero-waste ethos, the Pickathon festival combines art, architecture, food and music.
The greenest festival in North America.

x: Pickathon began on September 25, 1999, as a one-day benefit for KBOO community radio at Horning’s Hideout, near North Plains, Oregon. Volunteers ran it, and the money went to the station.
By 2003 it was a two-day roots music festival in August with a Friday night square dance, and in 2005 it spent one year at Pudding River.
In 2006 Pickathon moved to Pendarvis Farm, and in 2007 it grew to three days.

Over the next years the farm took shape: Portland State students designed and built the Treeline Stage starting in 2014, with a new design each year through 2019, and the festival filmed its sets and shared them online.
COVID-19 canceled the 2020 festival, and there was no Pickathon at the farm in 2021.
The festival returned in 2022 laid out as neighborhoods, each area designed and built by its own team, such as Portland State students at Cherry Hill and the Branch Crew in the Woods.
In 2024 Happy Valley approved a 10-year permit for the festival at Pendarvis Farm, and Creative Neighborhoods started as its own nonprofit.
It designs and builds the neighborhoods with architects, schools and makers, and works to give them a second life after the festival.

2010.t: Became the first major American music festival to drop plastic cups and bottles for reusable steel ones.

2011.t: Became the first major American festival to eliminate all single-use dishes and utensils.
Drew over 3,300 people, up almost a thousand from 2010, with 44 artists.
Booked synth-pop band Future Islands, moving past a purely roots lineup.
Founder laid out a 10-year plan to make Pickathon a year-round video event.

2012.t: Introduced year-specific wooden dish tokens and let people wash their own reusable dishware.

2013.t: Booked Feist, its biggest headliner up to that point, alongside Andrew Bird.
Debuted the Windmill Hill kids area, a new Cafe stage and a shade sculpture over the main bowl.
PSU architecture students built their first Pickathon piece: a bamboo entry portal.
Tickets capped at 3,500, and every band played at least twice on different stages.

2014.t: First Treeline Stage, built by PSU architecture students from about 600 shipping pallets.

2015.t: Treeline Stage rebuilt from 435 giant cardboard tubes, seating up to 1,000.
The 2015 Treeline Stage won the Jury Award at the AIA Portland Architecture Awards.

2016.t: Premiered the Starlight Series, live videos shot at the 2015 festival.

2017.t: Treeline Stage won a Citation Award in the AIA Portland Architecture Awards.
Treeline Stage trusses were reused as sleeping pods at the Clackamas County Veterans Village.

2018.t: Celebrated its 20th festival, still capped at 3,500 attendees.
Filmed 64 acts with more than 80 cameras and a 500-person production team.
Treeline Stage lumber went on to build parts of Kenton Women's Village.

2019.t: Ran seven stages, from the Mainstage and Woods to the Galaxy Barn and Lucky Barn.
Phil Lesh played the Woods Stage's first three-hour double set.

2020.t: The canceled lineup included John Prine, (Sandy) Alex G, Joan Shelley and Chad VanGaalen.
Streamed 60 past sets, one a day, to raise money for MusiCares COVID relief.
A new Grove Stage had been planned to debut.

2021.t: Canceled for a second year; there wasn't enough time to plan a safe event.

2022.t: Returned after two years and reorganized the farm into 'neighborhoods,' with daytime sets in shaded woods.
Introduced LIT Sunday author readings with Literary Arts.

2023.t: Became the first festival to power stages with a hydrogen fuel cell generator.
Paste called it 'the best indie festival in the country.'
About 7,500 people on site, including about 2,500 volunteers and staff.

2024.t: Creative Neighborhoods launched, with four programs at the festival in its first year.
Happy Valley renewed the festival's permit at Pendarvis Farm for 10 years.
Hoffman Construction and ZGF built the Paddock mainstage, 'Antlers & Sunset.'
All 15 neighborhoods were redesigned; nine held stages.

2025.t: Hoffman, ZGF and Exactonaut built the Timbre stage as the Paddock's centerpiece; its timber was donated afterward.

2026.t: PSU built the Cherry Hill stage from worn-out Oregon coast fishing nets, one of 10 venues.
Cherry Hill lumber went to Creative Neighborhoods for reuse after the festival.
The Galaxy Courtyard was built by Blackbird Public Arts; its lumber went to the Guild of Oregon Woodworkers.

1999.t: Started in 1999 as a KBOO radio fundraiser at Horning's Hideout in North Plains, with about 90 people.
Attendance more than doubled to about 220 in year two, then stayed in the low 200s for several years.

2005.t: Moved to a hay field by the Pudding River in Woodburn in 2005, after losing Horning's Hideout on two months' notice.
2005 was the first year with both running water and electricity on site.

2006.t: Moved to 80-acre Pendarvis Farm in Happy Valley in 2006; the Avett Brothers played that year.

Pitchfork reviewed both Pile and Toy after the Austin punk band signed to Merge, following eight years of club work.
"Habib Galbi" was the first Arabic-language song to top the Israeli pop chart. The three Yemenite-Israeli sisters were little known in the US before an NPR Tiny Desk in 2019.
Verbena's frontman reborn as a hushed solo writer. Spin praised 2011's Believers, then he vanished for eight years.
Willamette Week named them Portland's best new band. An NPR Tiny Desk and Newport Folk followed.
Their 2015 self-titled album, on Free Dirt, was named one of Folk Alley's 10 favorites of the year and reviewed by Songlines, Country Standard Time and Sing Out!. An old-time duo.
An Adelaide bassist whose 2024 record drew universal acclaim and almost no sales.
Outsiders was NPR's Best Roots Music of 2022 and Ann Powers' top album of the year. Living Thing was Folk Alley's No. 1 album of the year.
A Los Angeles post-punk trio on Stones Throw. They opened for Bauhaus at the Greek, but their first headline tour ran through small rooms.
A Brooklyn post-punk trio whose second album came out the same week they played.
Azniv Korkejian's Spacebomb debut drew raves from NPR and the Guardian and almost no sales.
Nominated for BBC Sound of 2016, she had four UK-charting albums by 25. She told The Independent she never recouped her two Sony albums.
A Detroit rapper and producer whose 2010 album won critics over completely and barely registered on the charts.
Their Sugar Hill debut peaked at No. 4 on the US bluegrass chart and drew an NPR First Listen. A Decemberists side project, the band itself was only three years old.
An Astoria band that put a top-twenty album on the Billboard chart, still headlining the same Portland theatres an hour from where they started.
A Raleigh punk kid turned funk bandleader: a Captured Tracks debut, then well-reviewed records through Normaltown on New West.
Three albums drew attention from Pitchfork and The Guardian, the latest, The Clearing, on Dead Oceans. The North Carolina folk trio played clubs and small halls throughout.

deepcuts.n: Bradford Lee Folk & The Bluegrass Playboys
deepcuts.line: The Fader featured him, Sing Out! reviewed him and he showcased at IBMA's Bluegrass Ramble. Open Road's former frontman, back from farming, stayed in listening rooms and on festival side stages.
"Class Historian" made public-radio year-end lists at KOSU and Louisville Public Media and has turned up on Cartoon Network and Reservation Dogs. The Oklahoma band plays clubs like Elsewhere.
Richmond jazz-funk on Concord, working small clubs and a heavy festival schedule, with no theatre headline dates known.
Free Dirt Records, NPR features and UK folk club tours followed a single self-released record. They stayed in house concerts and small folk rooms like Seattle's Tractor Tavern.

Jesse Lege is a Cajun Music Hall of Fame inductee. The Right Combination, with fiddler Joel Savoy, drew reviews from Songlines, OffBeat and No Depression. Dance halls and folk festivals before and after.
The New York Times called Roots & Crowns "enthralling." Tim Rutili's art-folk band had thirteen years of critically respected records, on Thrill Jockey and then Dead Oceans.
Won the Academy of American Poets' Walt Whitman Award for Curses and Wishes. Saint Friend followed from McSweeney's, along with a Lannan Foundation residency.
A self-releasing Ontario songwriter with a devoted audience and no label pushing her. Three years on she's still co-billing small theaters.
Nine albums of Duluth country blues on tiny labels; Red House and Smithsonian Folkways came later.
Every record charted on Billboard's bluegrass list, and Autumn, Sharing the Covers, Winter Stories and Strange Fascination reached No. 1. Yep Roc's Raleigh four-piece stayed in clubs and theatres.

Kelly Joe Phelps made a run of praised Rykodisc records from 1994 to 2001, with consistently high marks in the acoustic-blues press. Magnetic Skyline paired him with Corinne West; both kept to small halls.
Corinne West was a Kerrville Folk Festival New Folk finalist. Magnetic Skyline paired her with Kelly Joe Phelps, who brought a 1990s Rykodisc run of his own.
Wand's frontman, whose solo albums the critics love and the charts ignore.
Paranoid Cocoon and Tall Hours made them a Suicide Squeeze favorite. The band wound down two years later, still playing small rooms.
His debut had arrived three months earlier to almost uniformly good reviews, and never touched a chart.

Recording honky-tonk since Cheatin' Heart Attack (HighTone), a traditionalist holdout against Nashville, he founded the Ameripolitan Music Awards in 2014. His rooms remain dance halls and Austin bars.
The Moth named her co-host of its national podcast in May 2019. A Detroit storyteller who performed with The Moth while working a day job in soap marketing.
FolkWorks reviewed King's Lament, on Old-Time Tiki Parlour, as the first record of exclusively old-time fiddle duets. David Bragger teaches at UCLA.
An Omaha lo-fi lifer. Pitchfork and Magnet both championed Staunch Honey, on records that sold in the hundreds.
Three albums by 2010, including Sweet Heart Rodeo on Cooking Vinyl, drew steady NPR Music and UK broadsheet coverage. Row (2020, Yep Roc) later became a stage musical.
Two Fire Talk albums reviewed by Pitchfork, Paste and the Chicago Tribune led to a Sub Pop deal in April 2023 and a 2024 European run supporting Depeche Mode.
Two Fire Talk albums nearly every critic liked, then Fat Possum signed them. The hometown room is still Thalia Hall, same as before.
Anatolian psych-folk on the bağlama: Kar Yagar (Bongo Joe, 2019) ran in Songlines' 'Top of the World' banner, and she moved to Big Crown for Yarin Yoksa.
St. Croix roots reggae singer named Atlanta's Best New Female Reggae Artist in 2001, with six albums on I Grade Records since.
Pitchfork singled out Oshin in 2012 and Is the Is Are in 2016, and the halls stayed the same size for most of a decade before they caught up.
Constant Companion (No Quarter, 2010) was reviewed by The New Yorker, Spin and PopMatters, with Garth Hudson and Feist on it; Pitchfork covered him again in 2023.
The Rainbow Wheel of Death (Wharf Cat, 2023) placed on PopMatters' Best Country Albums of 2023. Cosmic country out of Brooklyn, billed solo as Dougie Poole.
Pitchfork and Stereogum both singled out their record, from a band almost nobody has heard of.
His solo debut drew universal acclaim; he is still better known as a band's frontman.
Her fifth album, Queen of the Minor Key (Signature Sounds), debuted on the Billboard folk chart; NPR World Cafe had featured her in 2007.
Drive & Cry (2024), SXSW 2025 and a UK and European tour widened her map.
A Rolling Stone top-100 album of 2022 that never translated into sales.
Memphis punk band on Goner, their Ty Segall-produced records reviewed in PopMatters and premiered by Pitchfork; no chart, no sales.
Found playing on the street in Los Angeles, he released an old-time fiddle and banjo debut on Tompkins Square, made two more albums by 2013, then largely stopped touring.
Fairfield was found busking, released on Tompkins Square, drew an NPR feature in 2010 and was picked by Fleet Foxes as support; Axelrod has recorded with Jim Kweskin.
Eric D. Johnson had seven years on Sub Pop and a turn in The Shins behind him.
Boston traditionalists whose Hound Dog Taylor tribute climbed the blues chart.
Nashville-born country songwriter whose third album drew strong reviews from Saving Country Music and No Depression, with no radio to match.
Two 2020 year-end placements on a micro-label: Nightcap at Wits' End at No. 65 on Uncut's Top 75 and Peoples Motel Band at No. 61 on MOJO's Top 75.
Their debut was four months old and made them the most written-about hardcore band of the year.
Sub Pop signed them after a decade on Feeding Tube, NNA, Tzadik and DFA; Famously Alive was reviewed by Pitchfork, NPR and PopMatters.
Dan Penn, the Muscle Shoals songwriter, produced all three of their albums. After Chris Gaffney died in 2008, Dave Alvin's tribute drew Springsteen, Los Lobos and Alejandro Escovedo.
Stereogum named them a Band to Watch in 2014 on the strength of Weird Little Birthday. The London trio never outgrew the clubs.
A Portland band whose quiet string-and-voice records drew national reviews and a Kill Rock Stars deal the next year. They have been a club act ever since.
A duo reworking Appalachian hymns for Thrill Jockey, praised by nearly every critic who reviewed it and bought by almost nobody.
Minnesota folk with an NPR Mountain Stage session; Right On (2024) placed on KGNU's Top 10 Albums of 2024, a community-radio list.
A Dublin string band with good notices at home and a Nashville label deal the next year. The folk clubs and festival tents stayed the same size.
An LA band with a huge young following who were already selling the El Rey twice over.
The Euro Americana Charts named Barn Doors album of 2011, and Uncut, Mojo and Q praised Silver Season that October. He kept playing the same clubs.
Berklee-trained Austin blues guitarist, named her city's musician of the year with an Austin City Limits taping behind her.
Solo debut Wintres Woma (Paradise of Bachelors, 2017) was an NPR First Listen; he has long been a sideman to Jeff Tweedy, Richard Thompson and Steve Gunn.
A former high-school English teacher from Oregon whose 2023 record won universal acclaim and sold almost nothing.
A national career built from no records or label at 21; a 2025 Blues Music Award nominee for Acoustic Album, with a Smithsonian Folkways debut in Things Done Changed.
A songwriter who draws their own album art, and whose 2023 record was the one indie critics singled out that year.
A comic's comic with six charting albums and a 2017 Comedy Central special, best known as Better Call Saul's Dr. Caldera.
Tom Waits publicly championed her, and Anti- released Catalpa (2003) and Escondida (2004) to heavy critical attention.
Won a 2024 Grammy for Best Alternative Jazz Album as producer and player on Meshell Ndegeocello's The Omnichord Real Book; Unusual Object (2024) made multiple year-end jazz lists.
Robert's Western World's house fiddler, whose Third Man debut Mr. Jukebox drew a strong Saving Country Music review that April.
Twenty-one albums deep by 2016, the Anacortes musician's Introducing Karl Blau (Bella Union) was widely reviewed and named a WXPN Artist to Watch.
No Depression and the British roots press championed her dusty country-psych.
One Sub Pop album and years behind him in Witch with J Mascis. Two more records and good notices.
Smoking in Heaven (2011) drew coverage from Paste, American Songwriter and NPR and reached No. 145 in the UK. The London siblings had already played arenas as Coldplay's support.
Four albums on Signature Sounds from 1998 to 2006 and a member of the trio Redbird with Jeffrey Foucault and Peter Mulvey; well reviewed in the folk press and a folk-radio staple.
She gave an early NPR Tiny Desk concert and made albums for Barsuk.
There's a Light reached No. 6 on Billboard's Top Gospel chart and No. 13 on R&B after an NPR Songs We Love pick and a Ramseur reissue. She stayed a club and church-hall singer.
A nine-piece Portland chamber-pop band NPR championed, with a Decemberists tour weeks later. Seven years on they were still playing Mississippi Studios and the Doug Fir.
Pitchfork singled out her album Hannah as one of the year's best new records; the rooms never grew past small clubs.
Brian Corum's Raleigh band has a devoted North Carolina following: Lincoln Theatre in 2011, Cat's Cradle in Carrboro now, nothing bigger in between.
Adam Weiner's Philadelphia band - a Rolling Stone favorite on Obama's playlist, and still selling only clubs.
His self-titled 2016 album topped Saving Country Music's most-essential list for the year; signed to Thirty Tigers, never a chart act.
Colombian-American band in New York whose Mezcla earned a strong Songlines review in 2016 on Glitterbeat, with no commercial profile.
The a cappella singer has drawn attention from DownBeat, KCRW and KXCI, with bookings at the MFA Boston and MOCA, but her headline clubs stay small, like Belly Up Solana Beach.
Multiple Blues Music Award nominations for Acoustic Artist of the Year and Cascade Blues Association Muddy Awards.
Three solo albums after Page France and Cotton Jones, a name other songwriters trade.
A Canadian power-pop revivalist on Daptone's rock imprint, well reviewed in 2018 and selling like the cult record it was.
One album on Terrible Records and a second that critics loved. She opened for Mitski in big halls.
Dan Auerbach's Easy Eye label released the debut of the Korean-American country blues singer and poet; since then he has opened for Parker Millsap and played small clubs.
Nansemond (Paradise of Bachelors, 2014) was reviewed by Aquarium Drunkard and streamed by NPR; the banjo player also works in Pelt and Steve Gunn's band, in lofts and small halls.
Crack named him one of the artists who defined 2023, DJ Mag ran a Recognise feature, Resident Advisor gave him a podcast. Still club nights.
Sergio Mendoza's Tucson mambo orchestra drew a strong Songlines review for Vamos a Guarachar (2016, Glitterbeat) and was a WOMEX showcase artist.
Their debut YOUNG (Arts & Crafts) was an NPR First Listen, and NPR named it one of the best albums of 2017.
A debut that drew near-universal critical praise and a Boston music award, followed by a spot on a Rolling Stone guitarists list.
A Joshua Tree country-disco singer whose Magic Mirror was warmly reviewed by the handful of critics who found it, and never charted.
Four-time Juno winners for Traditional Roots Album of the Year, Canada's top honor for old-time music.
Megafaun co-founder and Hiss Golden Messenger sideman whose own People Are My Drug (2018, Psychic Hotline/Thirty Tigers) drew press.
Stereogum tagged them a band to watch off a single EP; they went on playing small rooms, Mississippi Studios among them.
Illinois State Fiddle Champion at 17, whose Shame (2017, Free Dirt), produced by Andrew Marlin, drew NPR and Paste coverage.
A Dallas holiness minister playing cigar-box slide blues. The Austin Chronicle praised 2010's When I Rise.
Fabi Reyna's Afro-Latin guitar project: Malegria (2024, Psychic Hotline) made The Bitter Southerner's Best Southern Albums of 2024, with repeated NPR features.
Touring drummer for The Shins and The Black Keys and producer for Foxygen, Damien Jurado, Nathaniel Rateliff and Kevin Morby.
The Deslondes' deep-voiced singer, whose New West solo debut earned praise from Holler and the quiet audience that goes with it.
Leah Song and Chloe Smith built a following through grassroots touring, headlining theaters and playing a Red Rocks bill with Trevor Hall and Citizen Cope.
A Houston writer whose Photographs made American Songwriter's fifty best albums of 2011. Four acclaimed records later, he still headlines clubs.
Philadelphia-to-North Carolina songwriter; No Medium made her a critics' album, and 2024's Bite Down took Stereogum's Album of the Week on Merge.
Ripley Johnson's country-leaning project after Wooden Shjips: five Thrill Jockey albums since 2019, reviewed by Uncut, Mojo and Relix.
The New York Times put his I See the Sign among 2010's ten best and Nonesuch signed him in 2013.
A 2017 Kresge Literary Arts Fellow who sang as a Bride of Funkenstein with Parliament-Funkadelic and founded Detroit's Secret Society of Twisted Storytellers in 2012.
Signed to Sub Pop in 2007; From Where I Started (2017) was an NPR First Listen. Former Carissa's Wierd drummer and early Band of Horses player.
Kevin Russell's project began as a side to The Gourds, who recorded for Sugar Hill and Yep Roc from 1996, and became his full-time band after the Gourds' 2013 hiatus.
Musical director of the all-star Atomic Bomb! Band, which played William Onyeabor with David Byrne and Damon Albarn; Mean Love (2014, DFA) was widely reviewed.
Co-founded Sun City Girls in 1979 and has released solo records on Drag City since 2007, earning cult reverence in rooms like Cafe OTO.

In March 2026 Sluice released its third album, Companion, and Paste gave it a B+. The Durham, North Carolina band first played Pickathon in 2024, a year after its album Radial Gate made The Guardian's list of the best albums of 2023 so far.
One EP, then a Grammy for his work with Mavis Staples. He opened theaters for Leon Bridges.
Athens, Ohio folk-rock that the critics nearly all loved in 2009 — then the band broke up without ever outgrowing the bars.
Critics had already made him a guitarist's guitarist on Time Off, and Matador signed him next.
A Brooklyn trio critics took to straight away, whose follow-up scraped the British top forty. Nearly ten years on they still headline small clubs.
Charleston band whose & I'm Fine Today was named South Carolina's album of the year by SceneSC - regional acclaim, no sales.
Lo-fi post-punk duo who recorded in a disused lab. NME praised the debut, BrooklynVegan named it indie album of the week, and the clubs stayed small.
Austin band whose St. Mojo landed on three Austin Chronicle critics' 2017 lists and an NPR World Cafe session, without charting.
A teenage brother-and-sister act out of Edmonton with one EP and a devoted online following. A year later they were playing small theaters, and stopped there.
Ryan Gustafson's North Carolina project: Unsung Passage (2018) was listed second on The Bluegrass Situation's top albums of 2018, with features from WUNC and Indy Week.
The string trio made a 2012 Smithsonian Folkways record with John Cohen, and otherwise played Brooklyn's Jalopy Theatre, house parties and old-time festivals.
Look Out! reached No. 6 on the Americana chart, and the band backed Charlie Louvin on a 2003 national tour and appeared on NPR's Weekend Edition in 2005.
'Far From Any Road' became the theme to True Detective's first season in 2014, bringing a UK chart entry; Mojo and Uncut had championed them since the 1990s.
Featured on Anderson .Paak's Oxnard (2018) and Mark Ronson's Late Night Feelings with Alicia Keys (2019); Portland rapper signed to local label EYRST in 2015.
Laura Burhenn's band. Generals arrived two months before the farm to strong reviews and sales that never followed.
Dear Wormwood (October 2015) brushed the national chart, and the Texas siblings have kept filling theaters since.
Pacific Northwest old-time quartet who started as kids; Saving Country Music praised their 2020 album and called them the form's most respected young group.
Ought's frontman, whose solo debut Saturday Night (Jagjaguwar) was an NPR Songs We Love pick and widely reviewed.
Chicago honky-tonk band whose debut took an A-minus from The Vinyl District and an NPR feature, on a small independent label.
With Dave Carter she was among the most-played artists on the FOLKDJ-L radio charts in 2001-02, and Joan Baez took them on tour; her solo Flower of Avalon followed Carter's death in 2002.
A London post-punk band signed to Sub Pop after a single gig. Decent reviews, and very little else.
Los Angeles band whose debut Supergiant drew reviews from Rolling Stone and PopMatters.
Ganglion Reef (2014) came out on Ty Segall's God? Records and led to a first tour supporting Segall; Laughing Matter (2019) was well reviewed by Pitchfork and Stereogum.
Coachella alumni from 2011 whose self-titled second album reached the UK top 20; they have headlined theaters since.
Austin power trio, Best New Band at the 2008 Austin Music Awards and a Rolling Stone breaking artist.
Luz Elena Mendoza's Portland band: Ojos del Sol made NPR's 50 best albums of 2016, and Mujeres reached No. 7 on the Latin Pop chart in 2019.
Portland poet and Octopus Books co-founder, an Oregon Book Award finalist for Fjords Vol. 1 and again for The Book of Joshua.
His debut This Highway was a nominee for Saving Country Music's 2017 Album of the Year, alongside records by Tyler Childers and Jason Isbell.
Banjo and fiddle duo on Free Dirt; de Groot plays clawhammer banjo with Molsky's Mountain Drifters, and Hargreaves has played fiddle with Gillian Welch and Laurie Lewis.
Austin funk band, an offshoot of Grupo Fantasma, with Brownout albums on Six Degrees since 2008; Brown Sabbath (Ubiquity), their funk take on Black Sabbath, was widely covered.
Two albums on Signature Sounds, and a new lineup: cellist Tristan Clarridge and fiddler Brittany Haas joined in January 2008.
Four guitarists, Nashville, and a 2013 album, I'm Rich Beyond Your Wildest Dreams, recorded in eight days, mostly live.
London afro-funk band fronted by Eno Williams, with three albums by 2019, two of them on Merge.
Co-founder of the everybodyfields, a Ramseur Records band that split in 2009; she went solo with a self-titled EP.
A Boston string band that won the Podunk Bluegrass band contest in 2007; bassist Bridget Kearney also plays in Lake Street Dive.
Shana Cleveland's surf-noir quartet, two Hardly Art records, one produced by Ty Segall.
Two members of Black Mountain, Amber Webber and Joshua Wells, with two Jagjaguwar albums: Lightning Dust (2007) and Infinite Light (2009).
Sam Jayne's band, formed in 1994 after his band Lync ended, with records on K Records and Sub Pop.
Percussionist and vibraphonist who has played with Les Claypool, Ani DiFranco and Rickie Lee Jones, and leads Punkadelick.
Band whose second album, Miracle Temple (2013), was its first for Merge; How to Dance followed in 2016.
A North Carolina-linked quartet playing old-time and bluegrass; banjo player Riley Baugus sang on the Cold Mountain soundtrack and appears on Raising Sand.
Baton Rouge Cajun and western swing band on Sugar Hill since 2007, whose rhythm section backed Linda Ronstadt and Ann Savoy on Adieu False Heart.
Co-founder of the everybodyfields with Jill Andrews; the Ramseur Records band split in 2009 so both could pursue solo careers.
New Orleans roots band, formerly the Tumbleweeds; their self-titled debut came out on New West in 2015.
Nashville band with three albums on its own Oh Wow Dang label; Robert Christgau praised Screws Get Loose and SPIN praised Blur the Line.
A metal band with members of YOB, Agalloch and Hammers of Misfortune, with two albums on Profound Lore, VHÖL (2013) and Deeper Than the Sky (2015).
Old Crow Medicine Show's founding member gone solo, with a Rawlings-produced debut that May.
Indie rock band with two albums on Saddle Creek, the second released in 2018.
Cahalen Morrison's honky-tonk band, whose debut album The Flower of Muscle Shoals came out on Free Dirt. The same group later became Western Centuries.
Omaha rock guitarist David Nance, whose records came out on Trouble in Mind; he later put out an album on Third Man.
Mount Moriah's former frontwoman. Her solo debut Lionheart came out on Merge in 2018, with help from Kathleen Hanna.
A Red Lake Ojibwe pow wow singer from Minneapolis. His 2022 album Niineta came out on 37d03d, the label run by Justin Vernon and the Dessner brothers.
Jupiter Bokondji's Kinshasa band. Damon Albarn and Warren Ellis play on their 2017 album Kin Sonic.
Nicole Wray and Terri Walker's retro-soul debut, out in March 2013 on Truth & Soul. Wray's earlier solo single 'Make It Hot' reached the Hot 100 top five.
Kyle Field's indie folk project, with albums on K Records. Field is also an acclaimed visual artist.
A North Carolina songwriter whose debut for Geffen was shelved. Steve Earle called him the best songwriter he ever threw out of his recording studio.
Three of the four men who were DeYarmond Edison; the fourth left and made Bon Iver.
A harpist and songwriter from Rochester, New York, who has released records on Rounder and Kill Rock Stars and has played with Bob Weir.
The last bassist Prince hired before his death in 2016, known for microtonal funk bass.
Dan Boeckner's new synth band, one EP old — but Wolf Parade and Handsome Furs came first.
A young Nashville country-rock band whose 2013 self-titled debut came out on Paradise of Bachelors.
A Nashville experimental musician whose 2022 album I Survived, Now It's Over came out on Third Man Records.
A Portland rock 'n' roll band on Partisan Records. They announced their breakup in December 2013.
Eva Moolchan's post-punk project, on Merge Records. Highway Hypnosis came out in 2019.
A Boston-area roots band formed in 1994, playing early blues, gospel and Appalachian music. Two albums on Rounder.
A Brooklyn ragtime and blues band, invited to tour with Bob Dylan in 2009.
Two Londoners, Jack Cooper of Mazes and James Hoare of Veronica Falls. They formed in 2014 and split in 2018.
A Manchester duo, Alice Merida Richards and Sam Pillay, on Fire Records. Ecstatic Arrow came out in 2018.
Cahalen Morrison, Ethan Lawton and Jim Miller, a Donna the Buffalo co-founder, formed the band. Their debut Weight of the World came out on Free Dirt in 2016.
Jeremy Earl's Brooklyn band, eight albums in by 2014, released on his Woodsist label.
A Michigan trio of guitar and banjo, cello and percussion, making atmospheric acoustic folk.
East Nashville cosmic country on ATO, produced by one of the Milk Carton Kids, with NPR behind it.
A Grammy-nominated storyteller, raised in Oakland, telling African American stories on the kids' stage.
Eric D. Johnson of Fruit Bats under his own initials, years before Bonny Light Horseman.
Seattle's gothic country-rock, three Barsuk albums and a turn singing for Sunn O))).
A Mississippi bluesman born in 1928, featured in the 2008 documentary M for Mississippi.
Venezuelan Llanera musician Larry Bellorin, an asylum seeker in North Carolina, paired with Joe Troop of Che Apalache in a Venezuelan-Appalachian duo.
Signed to Rounder in 2018, with a debut album produced by T Bone Burnett.
Mike Merenda and Ruth Ungar of The Mammals, touring as a duo since 2008; she is the daughter of fiddler Jay Ungar.
Daniel Johnston taught him to write songs; Beck was his roommate in New York, and PolyGram and Sire both signed him in the 1990s.
A Boston psych-folk band on Mexican Summer, with three albums between 2011 and 2016.
Willy Vlautin's Portland band, together from 1994 to 2016, with a following in the UK and Europe.
Two Saddle Creek albums, and an engineer and producer on records by Cass McCombs, Big Thief and others.
Sonny Smith's San Francisco band, with two Fat Possum albums, Tomorrow Is Alright and Hit After Hit.
Emmett Kelly's own band; he also plays with Will Oldham and, from 2016, in Ty Segall's band.
A Tampa rap duo whose 2022 album Finally, New was acclaimed by DJ Mag and made its year-end list.
A folk band whose Sub Pop album Tight Knit came out in February 2009.
An old-time duo; Leva's 2018 solo album Time Is Everything featured Calcagno, and their own album followed on Free Dirt.
Tim Presley's White Fence put out several records from 2010 to 2013, including Hair with Ty Segall.
Sam Cohen's Brooklyn band; he went on to produce Kevin Morby's Singing Saw and later albums.
Psychedelic duo Ripley Johnson and Sanae Yamada, formed in San Francisco in 2009. Pitchfork reviewed Circles, and NPR called Shadow of the Sun “the best Moon Duo record to date.”
Eighteen, with a hundred CDs she had pressed herself. Nonesuch signed her and she opened theaters for the Black Keys.
XXL called Below the Heavens (2007) one of the year's most celebrated hip-hop releases. The duo never left the underground.

Old-time band formed in 1992 with two Rounder albums that reached Billboard's Americana Top 20, and a 1996 second-place finish on A Prairie Home Companion's talent contest. Bluegrass Today called them the most popular modern old-time string band in the world.
Ten months old when they came, with Invitation Songs on Matador. They headlined small rooms in London.
Shortlisted twice for the Polaris Prize, in 2008 and 2016.
Her album with Neko Case and k.d. lang landed on critics' year-end lists all over the world.
Records for Sub Pop and Secretly Canadian, including a Richard Swift-produced trilogy critics loved, and listening rooms throughout a 25-year career.
Adrian Quesada's Austin funk band, an offshoot of Grupo Fantasma, on Six Degrees since 2008. They went from Austin clubs and SXSW showcases to Bonnaroo in 2012.
On Fat Possum since Patrick Carney of the Black Keys vouched for them. Arrow reached No. 78 on the Billboard 200 in 2012, and their headline rooms grew from small clubs into halls.
Vancouver-based Celtic-bluegrass band formed in 1993 that toured North America extensively and released two albums on Nettwerk.
Portland folk-punk and rock songwriter, leader of Casey Neill & the Norway Rats, with albums on Appleseed Recordings from 1998.
The Packway Handle Band is an Athens, Georgia bluegrass-rooted band formed in 2001 that released two albums before its first Pickathon.
Drunken Prayer is the Portland and Asheville alt-country project of Morgan Geer, who released records on Fluff and Gravy.
Erin McKeown is a Connecticut-born singer-songwriter who released her fifth album Sing You Sinners in the US in January 2007.
The Flat Mountain Girls are a Portland old-time string band with three albums by 2007.
Seattle old-time and country duo with Eli West, working the folk-club and festival circuit.
Louisiana zydeco accordionist and bandleader who fronts the Zydeco Roadrunners.
Indianapolis indie rock trio on Secretly Canadian and later Joyful Noise since 1995.
Seattle funk-jazz organ quartet led by organist Joe Doria and featuring saxophonist Skerik.
Family-music performer Andy Furgeson, who tours festivals and libraries with a puppet-and-band show.
Portland family and reggae musician and educator who founded 1 World Chorus.
Forest Grove High School mariachi ensemble that played Pickathon 2022 and opened for George Lopez at the Schnitz.

Two Runner released Porchlight on Gar Hole Records on August 28, 2026, and a review called it a “fully assured sophomore release.” They first played Pickathon in 2024, a year after touring hard behind their debut, Modern Cowboy.

Headlined La Cigale in Paris in April 2024, after North Sea Jazz and Nice Jazz Fest in 2023. The Portland Mercury named her one of nine Pickathon picks, and her album Lotus Glow (2023) drew a good review from The Line of Best Fit.

This fall Pahua, the Mexico City project of percussionist-producer Paulina Sotomayor, plays Flushing Town Hall in Queens and the Star Theater in Portland, a year after her album Cerca del Lugar. KEXP and Rolling Stone en Español profiled her before Pickathon 2024.

True Loves, the Seattle instrumental funk and soul band, played Portland's Waterfront Blues Festival in July 2026 and headlined a five-night run at Dimitriou's Jazz Alley that April. Their 2018 KEXP session has passed two million YouTube views.

This summer Panama-born drummer Daniel Villarreal took his Philadelphia trio to San Francisco's SFJAZZ Joe Henderson Lab for two nights and headlined Chicago's Judson & Moore. His 2022 debut Panamá 77 landed at No. 20 on Treble's list of the year's 50 best albums.
Leads Brass Empire, a San Diego band that mixes Afrobeat, cumbia and soul. His second album, A Way In, came out in April 2026, and he headlined the Quartyard in San Diego for the release show.

In 2025 Sami Braman played fiddle in Willie Watson's band on the Alison Krauss & Union Station tour, and her string band The Onlies earned a strong Songlines review for You Climb the Mountain. She first played Pickathon in 2024, a year after her solo debut of original fiddle tunes, Riveter.

In 2025 J.D. Simo was asked to coach Jeremy Allen White on guitar for the Bruce Springsteen film Deliver Me from Nowhere, according to Guitar World. He came to Pickathon in 2024 touring with Luther Dickinson behind their album Do The Rump!.
A Kentucky old-time banjo player from Whitesburg, and the banjo on Tyler Childers's Long Violent History.

PACKS' album Melt the Honey drew good reviews, including Pitchfork's and Paste's. The Toronto band, led by Madeline Link, first played Pickathon in 2024 and shared the single “before i was bleeding” in February 2025.

2010.t: Lineup included Bonnie "Prince" Billy, Dr. Dog, Punch Brothers and Heartless Bastards; early tickets with camping cost $115.
The Portland Mercury said Bonnie "Prince" Billy's forest set was "about as amazing as you could have hoped for."
Pendarvis Farm's owner rode a horse to the front of the stage during a Black Prairie and Blue Giant supergroup set.
Decemberists guitarist Chris Funk played his first Pickathon, with Black Prairie.
Klean Kanteen made the $5 steel pint cups that replaced 25,000-plus plastic beer cups; no bottled water was sold.
A solar array went on the Galaxy Barn, called the first permanent one at a major U.S. festival site.
The Woods Stage ran on solar power.
Peacock Radio broadcast the Mountain View and Fir Meadow stages live on 90.1 FM.
Pickathon/Pendarvis Farm-labeled wines were sold to the public for the first time; Widmer poured the beer.
Kids programs included Circus Cascadia, Music Together, yoga, square dances and a Cardboard Songsters cartoon show.

2011.t: Sturgill Simpson, then fronting Sunday Valley, fell into the crowd when a monitor gave way, and kept playing.
Saving Country Music named Sunday Valley its set of the weekend, calling Simpson a "singular talent."
Weekend passes sold out by Friday afternoon.
Mavis Staples' onstage KEXP interview drew a crowd so big that part of the Workshop Barn patio collapsed.
82-year-old Mississippi bluesman L.C. Ulmer played guitar behind his head in the Workshop Barn.
Saving Country Music declared "Pickathon has no peer" for fostering creativity in the U.S.
Bambooware dishes and GO Box clamshells replaced disposables, via a $10 dish token traded back at a washing station.
KEXP carried an HD webcast of up to five stages, built with more than 130 professionals and Stumptown Bliss.
Live & Breathing filmed a series of 33 Pumphouse Sessions, released on the Pickathon blog starting January 2012.
Pickathon added still-photo and film-professional volunteer crews for the first time.
Pickathon and Stumptown Bliss produced a live broadcast of Benefest, a benefit for Buckman Arts Elementary.
About 20 Portland food carts served the crowd; kids did circus training, wand-making and foam-arrow archery.
Schoenborn said the 2010 festival had produced 50,000 water bottles to recycle, a reason for the changes.

2012.t: Neko Case told the crowd, "This is the most amazing place I have ever played."
Saving Country Music said Lake Street Dive's Workshop Barn set got the biggest ovation he had ever seen.
