KEXP carried a live webcast: over 40 hours of music from six stages, plus interviews and private sessions.
Thee Oh Sees tore through a Friday-night Galaxy Barn set of "physically impossible" energy, per Saving Country Music.
Heartless Bastards' Galaxy Barn set ran so late it was shut down.
Portland Playhouse staged a music-based Twelfth Night in the Workshop Barn with Laura Gibson, Bruce Molsky and Casey MacGill.
Trackers Earth ran survival-skill workshops and fire-by-friction demos; Circus Cascadia ran weekend circus camps.
Green Hammer and Urban Timberworks built the beer, wine and cider garden bars from locally harvested lumber.
Food came from Bunk Sandwiches, Pine State Biscuits, Lauretta Jean's and others; Hopworks joined Widmer pouring beer.
Pickathon reported landfill garbage down close to 50% since 2009 and phased out compostable cups and straws.
Fan Greg Abernathy built a beta mobile festival map on Esri's ArcGIS; printed schedules were dropped.

2013.t: Feist's main-stage set was the first Pickathon show with a full lighting and stage production.
An estimated 28,000 fans streamed Marco Benevento's six-camera set, while several hundred watched in person.
A 183-person crew, mostly volunteers, shot 600 hours of footage; filmmaker Ondi Timoner (Dig!) documented the festival.
Shakey Graves packed both of the smallest venues; Saving Country Music said Pickathon underestimated his draw.
Shabazz Palaces' Ishmael Butler likened the Galaxy Barn sound to a blown-speaker cassette in a 1989 Corolla.
Pickathon projected under 1.5 gallons of garbage per person, 60%-plus recoverable, all fitting one 40-yard dumpster.
Four mobile solar generators ran a 350-plus device charging station; 3.5-plus miles of LED trail lights were solar-planned.
Greywater was filtered in on-site bioswales; about a quarter of people came by bus or bike.
Kids partners included Trackers Earth's four guilds, Circus Cascadia, Mother Earth School and a Cedarwood Waldorf kindergarten camp.
New Bunny Glade Sessions with KEXP filmed Andrew Bird, Sharon Van Etten and Ty Segall, beside the Pumphouse Sessions.
A new hand-pump water station went in under the windmill, and new gates joined the main-bowl beer garden to the Galaxy Barn.

2014.t: Pickathon filmed the making of the first Treeline Stage with PSU's Clive Knights, Travis Bell and their students.
Diarrhea Planet's late set had a guitarist on the amps and two crowdsurfing; WWeek said it entered Pickathon's late-night "pantheon."
The War on Drugs' Adam Granduciel told the crowd, "this is the one we'd actually attend."
Courtney Barnett, Angel Olsen, Valerie June, Mandolin Orange and Hiss Golden Messenger played their first Pickathon shows.
Angel Olsen answered a Lucky Barn heckler: "You're not wearing a shirt."
Added extra-cost Thursday "undercover" shows for early ticketholders, with Ural Thomas & the Pain and Lonnie Holley.
The Workshop Barn was renamed the Lucky Barn.
Took no corporate sponsors; Schoenborn said, "We've limited attendance and made the choice not to exploit the festival with sponsorship."
Worked with Portland nonprofit CASH Music on an automated system to pay bands royalties from festival video.
PSU students rented about 600 pallets for the first Treeline Stage and sold them back after the festival.
Few trash cans: $6 reusable aluminum cups, $10 dish tokens, compost bins, and hundreds of bikes at the entrance.
Published a full schedule of kids and family activities for the weekend.

2015.t: Leon Bridges, backed by White Denim, drew the weekend's biggest crowds; the barn line stretched into the beer garden.
Kamasi Washington, touring behind The Epic, played a Friday barn set with his father on soprano sax.
Ty Segall played with Wand as "The Roling Stons"; the Mercury called it possibly the festival's most intense hour.
Wolf People missed their slot in Seattle traffic, then played an impromptu 1 a.m. pumphouse set.
Glide called Pickathon "one of the most modern and intelligent music festivals in the country."
Launched six stage-named video channels with media partners Aquarium Drunkard, NPR Music and OPB, Grist, Bluegrass Situation, Wondering Sound and Inhabitat.
REI sponsored the NPR/OPB Woods Stage video channel and Tanner Goods the Galaxy Barn channel, Pickathon's first season sponsors.
REI ran an on-site pop-up shop.
KEXP webcast more than 40 hours from seven stages and over 50 bands.
Treeline Stage's cardboard tubes and 1,800 bolts went back to construction sites for reuse after the festival.

2016.t: Portlandia opened its sixth season with an episode called 'Pickathon,' with the Flaming Lips headlining the festival.
Jeff Tweedy played two sets of nearly 20 songs each without repeating a single song.
Spectrum Culture named Cory Henry's gospel-funk Hammond organ set on the Woods Stage 'my favorite set of the weekend.'
King Sunny Adé's 13-piece band 'stretched the foundation of the small Woods stage,' wrote the Portland Mercury.
Launched the Curation Series with Ned Ludd's Jason French: six chef-and-artist meals, 55 guests each.
Curation paired Ava Gene's chef Joshua McFadden with the Deslondes, and Ned Ludd's Mike Delaney with Cory Henry.
Opened the Wild Horse Stage for kids; under-12s free, teens half price, nearly 1,000 attendees under 12.
Kids programs ran with Trackers Earth, Circus Cascadia, Cedarwood Waldorf School, City Repair and Mother Earth School.
Treeline Stage used about 1,280 2x4s from Lease Crutcher Lewis, which reused them on Oregon job sites.
Backstage caterer sourced most protein from farms within 30 miles; all vendor contracts carried sustainability requirements.
Poured from 30 Oregon beverage makers, including Fort George, Deschutes and Reverend Nat's, into Klean Kanteen pint cups.
NPR Music premiered Pickathon videos such as Ty Segall's "Feel" and Alvvays' "Next of Kin."

2017.t: Filmed Curation Series season one, pairing chefs with Billy Strings, Tank and the Bangas and others; it premiered February 2018.
Glide Magazine said Billy Strings 'may be the next big thing in bluegrass' after his Mt. Hood Stage set.
Charles Bradley turned the Woods Stage into a funk-and-soul dance party.
Dungen played a live score to the 1926 animated film The Adventures of Prince Achmed under the stars.
Treeline Stage was built from 690 wooden trusses, designed by PSU's Center for Public Interest Design.
Treeline trusses went to Clackamas County's veterans village, with Catholic Charities, Communitecture and the Village Coalition as partners.
Schoenborn said Pickathon videos drew about 5 million viewers in 2017, more than double the year before.
The Stranger ran the Starlight Series, reaching episode nine by July 2017.
Thirty beverage partners poured, including Lagunitas, Deschutes and Hopworks; no headline sponsor was named.

2018.t: The Ringer: 'You can think of Pickathon as a content company with a live event.'
NPR Music streamed sets from all six main stages, the festival's eighth straight year of broadcasts.
Black Pumas played an intimate Curation dinner for 75 guests in the Old Farmhouse.
Built to Spill played their first-ever Pickathon, on the Woods Stage, then the Mt. Hood Stage the next night.
Ukraine's DakhaBrakha closed their Mt. Hood set by unfurling a Ukrainian flag and anti-Kremlin posters.
Rolling Stone named Charley Crockett, Colter Wall and I'm With Her among its 10 best things at Pickathon.
Treeline Stage's 113 pinwheel columns were moved to Kenton Women's Village, to shelter 24 women.
Released about 20 original series and more than 250 videos a year, almost daily from October to July.
Sixteen food partners, including Pok Pok, Pine State Biscuits and Podnah's; Elysian and Lagunitas headlined the beer stages.
Solar panels offset 100 percent of the weekend's energy; Portland Monthly called it the country's most sustainable music fest.
Ran organized 20-mile bike rides from Portland, with gear hauled for riders.
Cited USA Today 10Best, The New Yorker and Willamette Week readers' Best Music Festival among 2018 honors.

2019.t: Tyler Childers played two headlining sets the same weekend his album Country Squire came out.
Khruangbin played the Mt. Hood Stage Friday night; a Portland Mercury writer called them her new favorite band.
Sold an All-Access Streaming Pass for $19.99, with HD streams from four stages.
About 700 people, including staff, worked on Pickathon's video production.
Curation was produced as a packaged TV show: top chefs and discovery artists, about 100 guests per meal.
Treeline Stage stacked 160 borrowed apple bins into seven towers; the bins went back for the apple harvest.
Treeline reused 70 columns from 2018 and screws in use since 2014, aiming for zero waste.
Curation season two premiered with support from Travel Portland, co-hosted by PBS Original Fare creator Kelly Cox.
Eight Curation meals paired chefs like Kachka's Bonnie Morales with artists like Mandolin Orange, 80 seats each.
UK site Gigwise ran a series of Pickathon Pumphouse Sessions filmed in a 6x9-foot shack.
Brand partners included Snow Peak, Riff Cold Brewed, Sisters Coffee and Oatly.

2020.t: Canceled in May after Oregon's governor banned large gatherings through September; it had been set for July 30 to August 2.
The canceled lineup also included Jaimie Branch's Fly or Die, Vanishing Twin, Michael Nau and Tatiana Hargreaves.
Sierra Ferrell was booked for the canceled 2020 lineup.
Ticket holders could roll passes forward or gift them to the festival instead of taking refunds.
Worked with the Recording Academy and supported NIVA and Save Our Stages during the shutdown.
A Concert A Day began April 8 on YouTube's Stay Home #WithMe, Amazon Music's Twitch and the Recording Academy's Facebook.
Amazon Music gave direct support; Bandcamp and Bandsintown were also named partners.
Planned for 60 days, the series ran 17 weeks and over 100 days.
Schoenborn estimated the streams had raised about $50,000 for MusiCares by mid-May.
Had raised $200,000 for MusiCares by late July, including Spotify's matching gifts.
Pickathon At Home, July 31 to August 2, streamed past sets by Khruangbin and Drive-By Truckers, aiming for $60,000 more.
On April 10, Pickathon posted a tribute to John Prine, who was set to play that year.

2021.t: Called off June 18: Oregon lifted restrictions too late to do the year of work the festival needs.
Unlike 2020, offered full refunds to ticket holders who needed them.
Founder Zale Schoenborn's new company, Frequency, built ticketed live streams where fans could interact with artists in real time.
Promised 'a triumphant Pickathon return' at Pendarvis Farm in 2022.
FRQNCY's Qsound technology let performers hear remote viewers' cheers and applause.
FRQNCY's first public event, in Brooklyn in June, featured Zola Jesus, Downtown Boys and Chapo Trap House.
FRQNCY's first venue test was Vieux Farka Touré at Portland's Star Theater on September 12.
Asked fans to tell local and state governments how important the arts are.

2022.t: Sons of Kemet played their final U.S. shows before splitting; Esperanza Spalding joined them Sunday night.
Wet Leg headlined the Paddock Stage on Friday, and GZA played both Friday and Saturday.
TV Priest played a secret 1 a.m. Galaxy Barn set, bumping Emma-Jean Thackray to a buzzed-about 9 p.m. slot.
Golf-course parking filled by 11 a.m. Friday; Schoenborn marked out a new lot himself and ran emergency shuttles.
Saving Country Music called Mike and the Moonpies "the greatest live band in country music."
A Curation brunch in a ravine paired Chef Luna Contreras of Chelo with the band Rosali.
PSU students built the first Cherry Hill stage from 175-plus cable reels borrowed from Portland General Electric work yards.
The reels went back into utility service after the festival, under PSU's "diversion design-build" approach.
Skylab Architecture, McFadin Design, EMA Architecture and Green Anchors helped design the new neighborhoods.
The festival was livestreamed in full for the first time, with $14.99 to $29.99 stream tickets.
New Refuge neighborhood offered wellness programming; Coyote Corner ran kids' workshops, and kids under 13 got in free.

2023.t: Zale Schoenborn launched the Pickathon Podcast in April, talking with artists like Lee Fields, W.I.T.C.H. and Wednesday; 44 episodes followed.
Paste called Wednesday's Paddock set "maybe the best rock 'n' roll performance I'd seen this year."
They Hate Change tore up the Galaxy Barn, rapping "like their lives depended on it," per Paste.
MJ Lenderman played the Woods Stage, freshly signed to ANTI-, leaning on his album Boat Songs.
Krautrockers Møtrik played in white coveralls; their fog machine set off the Galaxy Barn smoke alarm.
Cherry Hill rose on arching Western hemlock beams, a "forest-within-a-forest," per Oregon ArtsWatch.
Curation ran five meals of 80 seats at $95, pairing Say She She with Chef Carlo Lamagna of Magna.
Began the PSU urban planning (MURP) study on a long-term future for Pendarvis Farm.
Hoffman Construction, Precision Construction and Clackamas Academy of Industrial Sciences students built "Mt. Pickathon" at the Farmhouse.
Hampton Lumber donated the dimensional lumber for the Mt. Pickathon entrance landmark.
Cherry Hill's hemlock arches were slated to become an outdoor classroom at PSU's Oak Savanna, supporting Indigenous ecological knowledge.
The 50 kW hydrogen generator came from Toyota Racing Development, with Pacific Northwest Toyota Dealers Association support.
Earthwell made the festival's new 2023 reusable cups.
LIT Sunday, curated with Literary Arts, featured Poet Laureate Anis Mojgani and a live Archive Project podcast taping.
After the festival, the team dreamed up Creative Neighborhoods, a nonprofit to keep building stages and giving them to the community.

2024.t: Courtney Barnett returned a decade after her first Pickathon to close Sunday night at the Paddock.
La Lom drew a massive Sunday crowd at the Woods; Dean Johnson owned the Paddock's magic hour.
Glide Magazine said the festival "landed on its feet," leaning on discovery over big headliners.
PSU's Cherry Hill stage wound 80 gates, up to 27 feet tall, around the trees; its wood went to school woodshops.
Schoenborn told Axios: "This is fantasy island, you don't get it until you come."
Creative Neighborhoods ran a first-job barista mentor program with Proud Mary, Coava and Guilder coffee.
Benson High School video students made a short documentary at a Creative Neighborhoods film camp.
Mark Lakeman and Samantha Rayvin's Branch Crew wove the Woods Stage backdrop from trees and branches.
Sponsors included Toyota, Bulleit Bourbon, Earthwell, Travel Oregon and Travel Portland; OPB was media partner.
Brew Dr. Kombucha returned as a beverage sponsor, a Pickathon backer since 2011.
Literary Arts and OPB co-curated author readings; novelist Willy Vlautin was interviewed on the Windmill Stage.
Comedy director Amy Miller hosted stand-up in the Lucky Barn with Tom Thakkar, Imani Denae and others.

2025.t: Spectrum Culture named Jimetta Rose & the Voices of Creation's Woods set "the top set of the weekend."
Taj Mahal's two sets drew the biggest crowds of the 25th-anniversary weekend.
Artists including Fruit Bats and Alela Diane paid tribute to Michael Hurley, who died in April while billed.
Kahil El'Zabar's Ethnic Heritage Ensemble played Coltrane's A Love Supreme at Cherry Hill.
PSU's 32-foot 'Water Serpent' Cherry Hill stage wore 400-plus burlap coffee-sack flags.
In Paste, Fruit Bats' Eric Johnson called Pickathon "the dog park for bands too."
GBD Architects, Andersen Construction and McFadin Design-Build made the Farmhouse; its parts became raised beds for food banks.
Fractal Forest and Lucky Bramble materials were slated to become covered bike corrals for shelters and age-in-place housing.
AfroVillage Oasis vendor booths were slated to become a greenhouse for a Portland-area community garden.
Friends of Noise trained teen sound engineers on a festival stage.
Cascade Sound's new Martin Audio Paddock system cut sound about 35 dB at the site boundary, toward nearby homes.
Curation ran five 100-seat meals, including Kachka's Bonnie Morales with Surprise Chef and Nostrana's Cathy Whims with Fruit Bats.

2026.t: The Womack Sisters, Sam Cooke's granddaughters, left the Woods crowd "in collective gape-eyed awe," per Portland Monthly.
Steve Earle and Shakey Graves headlined the 26th festival.
Hogslop String Band's Sunday Grove set ended with the crowd circling them, then a chaotic square dance.
Folk-punks Big Tractor stole the unamplified late-night talent show at the Woods Stage.
Curation hosted five gatherings of 100 guests, pairing the Womack Sisters with Sunday Sauce.
Scott Edwards Architecture and Bremik Construction built the Paddock "Synthesis" stage, bound for Old Town's Q-Side Skatepark.
Home Building Foundation youth helped build the Paddock with mentorship from P:EAR.
Bora Architecture and Andersen Construction built Farmhouse and Orchard pieces for Dream Big City's Dream Plaza 2.0.
Waechter Architecture led Windmill; its kit of parts went to Sabin CDC for gardening and placemaking at 17 properties.
Cherry Hill's fishing nets, from Net Your Problem, were slated to ship to Ukraine as drone protection.
LIT Sunday readings, curated by Frayn Masters, featured Leah Sottile, Olufunke Grace Bankole and Kevin Maloney.
Amy Miller hosted Lucky Barn comedy nights headlined by Laura Peek.

1999.t: 1999: Zale Schoenborn started Pickathon as a party where his own band could play, a couple of years after moving to Portland.
1999: Zale on the first year's 90 people: "It was pretty sparse, but we had a great time."
1999–2004: Zale's parents, Carol and Ted Schoenborn of Bend, set up, took tickets and filled in wherever needed.
1999–2004: Zale's younger brother Eric handled Pickathon's early web presence; Zale called it "all hands on deck."
Local acts Little Sue and Lynn Conover headlined the 1999 debut at Horning's Hideout.
At Horning's, Dirk Powell, Otis Taylor and the Holy Modal Rounders played a custom wood stage beside a lake.
Happy Valley granted a five-year conditional-use permit after Schoenborn met with the neighborhood association.

2000.t: 2000: The Mercury wrote that a dozen artists, all volunteering their time, would play a makeshift stage "from dusk until midnight."
Kelly Joe Phelps topped the 2000 bill, a high-water mark of the first five years.

2001.t: 2001: Willamette Week called Zale a "mandolin wizard" and quoted him: "We're covering more ground than your traditional bluegrass festival."
2001: Zale's goal: to "unite bands that don't get much Top-20 radio play but who have a face on KBOO."
2001: Willamette Week on Pickathon: "It's not Telluride and it's not Boulder, but it is ours."

2002.t: 2002: The Mercury called Horning's, with its pond and peacocks, "probably the best outdoor venue this side of the Gorge."
2002: Seattle's Circus Contraption brought vaudeville to Pickathon, with accordions, fiddles and face paint.

2003.t: 2003: Pickathon moved from late September to August, opening Friday, Aug. 22 at Horning's Hideout.
2003: The Mercury said the Horning family donated the land for the KBOO Pickathon.

2004.t: 2004: Po' Girl, co-founded by Allison Russell, played; Russell later won a 2024 Grammy for "Eve Was Black."

2005.t: 2005: Pickathon announced the Pudding River move on July 12, saying Horning's Hideout had lost its festival license.
2005: The Pudding River site was about 100 acres with a natural amphitheater, roughly 20 miles south of Portland off I-5.
2005 Saturday from 11 a.m.: Be Good Tanyas, Freakwater, Jolie Holland, Crooked Jades, Foghorn Stringband, Shiftless Rounders, Danny Barnes Collective.
2005: GuildWorks' Mar Ricketts supplied the shade cloth at Pudding River.
2005: Zale, looking back: "The biggest thing is we never thought about the experience, at all, at Horning's."
In the 2005 Pudding River hayfield, volunteers built shade from sewer poles and shade cloth bought off a train car.
The 2005 bill, its biggest yet, had the Be Good Tanyas, Freakwater and the Hacienda Brothers; it broke even.
After 2005, sponsor KBOO cut the festival loose over its growing liability, and the landowner evicted it.
Mar Ricketts of GuildWorks, the "Architect of the Air," has built Pickathon's floating fabric shade structures since 2005.

2006.t: 2006: Willamette Week placed Pickathon's Aug. 4–5 debut at Pendarvis Farm "between PDX and Boring."
The first Pendarvis year, 2006, ran three stages with Iris DeMent, Greg Brown and the Wailin' Jennys.
The Avett Brothers' 2006 debut set was in the Galaxy Barn.
The 2006 Pendarvis build used about 10,500 sq ft of shade cloth, 26,000 sq ft of fabric and a 20-foot entrance.
In 2006 Pickathon pledged recycling, composting, alternative transportation and renewable energy offset credits at its new farm site.
The 2006 festival offered kids activities all weekend and a dedicated family camp.
Pendarvis owners Scott and Sherry Pendarvis agreed to host on the condition it be run cleanly and sustainably.

2007.t: Added a full third day in 2007 and earned a Festie nomination for Most Scenic Festival Setting.
The 2007 lineup brought back the Avett Brothers, with Trampled by Turtles, Langhorne Slim and Alela Diane.
Elwood Johncox arrived by motorcycle in 2007 and went on to build the LED-lit forest trails.
A double CD of the 2007 festival was the eighth in Pickathon's yearly CD series.

2009.t: Fleet Foxes and The Tallest Man on Earth played in 2009.
In 2009, partner hotels ran free shuttles to the farm, and the festival urged a low-carbon trip.
A 34-track compilation of the 2009 festival went on sale on iTunes in January 2011.

2008.t: 2008 added the first Pickathon Cafe, run by Al Forno Ferruzza, plus new beer gardens, trails and camping.
In 2008 the Galaxy Barn's late-night shows went all-ages, with beer moved outside to a second garden.
2008 kids offerings included a toddler camp, Circus Cascadia and a kids' square dance.
2008 food came from local farms, including Gaining Ground Farm and Canby Asparagus Farm; EcoShuttle ran free bio-fueled shuttles.
2008 merch was made with Red Canary, and Fur Turtle Show Prints printed limited-run posters.
A 33-track live compilation of the 2008 festival came out in October 2009.

eras.h: A benefit that outgrew its home
eras.t: Pickathon started as a KBOO Community Radio benefit at Horning’s Hideout, run by volunteers, friends and family. As the weekend grew, so did the risk, until the station’s mission could no longer carry it. After one summer on a hayfield by the Pudding River, the festival went looking for a farm.

At Pendarvis Farm, the goal was to scale something special without ruining it. The farm stayed small: stages in the woods, every band playing twice, a first rough version of neighborhoods, and Treeline stages built with PSU architecture’s Clive Knights and Travis Bell. The growth went online instead, with cameras on every stage and sponsors paying for videos that reached millions. It was an idealistic tech idea, and it worked for a long time.

COVID canceled two festivals, so Pickathon put its film library to work: A Concert A Day streamed with the Recording Academy and Amazon Music and raised money for MusiCares. By the time the farm reopened in 2022, ad tech had replaced the sponsorships that paid for the videos. Pickathon came back anyway, rebuilt as neighborhoods.

eras.h: Splitting the mission from the moment
eras.t: After 2023, Pickathon separated the mission from the festival. Creative Neighborhoods, a nonprofit, now builds the neighborhoods with architects, builders and students. Pickathon uses them for one weekend, and then each structure moves on to a permanent home in the community.

2010.th: The crowd grew by half; the plastic went
2010.ln: With a crowd about half again as big as 2009's on the way, the team did the math in May and didn't like it: 20,000 to 30,000 plastic cups in the beer gardens alone. They asked readers whether to sell a steel cup and stop selling bottled water, and by August both were real, with Klean Kanteen pints and refill stations across the farm. The music brought its own surprises, from Bonnie "Prince" Billy in the forest to the farm's owner riding a horse up to the stage during a Black Prairie and Blue Giant set. Three days after, the team said their heads were still "in a fuzz."

f.t: The May post on the coming pile of plastic cups: "We are not happy with this thought."
Per person, total waste fell 22% from 2009; the steel cups did the most good, ending bottled water close behind.
The Portland Mercury on Bonnie "Prince" Billy's forest set: "about as amazing as you could have hoped for."
The team, afterward: "The bar was raised and we (you + us) lived up to the expectation."
Became the first major American music festival to drop plastic cups and bottles for reusable steel ones.
A solar array went on the Galaxy Barn, called the first permanent one at a major U.S. festival site.
The Portland Mercury said Bonnie "Prince" Billy's forest set was "about as amazing as you could have hoped for."
Pendarvis Farm's owner rode a horse to the front of the stage during a Black Prairie and Blue Giant supergroup set.

2010.lu: Indie names now lead the bill, but the roots side gets stronger too, with Chris Thile's Punch Brothers and returning old-time pillars.

lf.t: Punch Brothers, Chris Thile's band, played 2010; Thile returned with the reunited Nickel Creek in 2014.
Anaïs Mitchell sang Hadestown's "Why We Built the Wall" in 2010; the musical won her the 2019 Tony for Best Original Score.
Michael Hurley, a Holy Modal Rounders collaborator, played 2010 with Delta bluesman T Model Ford, linking back to Horning's.

2011.th: The farm overflowed, so they set a cap
2011.ln: This was the summer the farm ran out of room. Weekend passes were gone by Friday afternoon, and when Mavis Staples sat for an onstage interview, so many people pressed into the Workshop Barn that part of its patio gave way. Sturgill Simpson, then fronting Sunday Valley, kept playing after a monitor gave out and pitched him into the crowd, and 82-year-old L.C. Ulmer played guitar behind his head. Afterward the team wrote down a promise: grow about 30% over two years, then hold the cap there, and never charge for water or camping.

f.t: Mavis Staples' onstage interview drew a crowd so big that part of the Workshop Barn patio collapsed.
Mississippi bluesman L.C. Ulmer, 82, played guitar behind his head in the Workshop Barn.
Saving Country Music named Sunday Valley its set of the weekend, calling Sturgill Simpson a "singular talent."
Waste report: attendance up about 20%, total waste flat, and 60% of it kept out of the landfill.
Founder laid out a 10-year plan to make Pickathon a year-round video event.
KEXP carried an HD webcast of up to five stages, built with more than 130 professionals and Stumptown Bliss.
Became the first major American festival to eliminate all single-use dishes and utensils.
Sturgill Simpson, then fronting Sunday Valley, fell into the crowd when a monitor gave way, and kept playing.

2011.lu: A soul legend tops the bill for the first time, and the lineup reaches past roots into synth-pop and deep soul.

lf.t: Lee Fields & The Expressions played 2011 and returned in 2023, when Paste listed him among the lineup's recognizable names.
Bill Callahan and Damien Jurado led a deep 2011 bench of indie songwriters; Jurado returned in 2019.
Danny Barnes was still on the 2011 bill, nine years after his first Pickathon at Horning's.

2012.th: Fewer cars, camp hosts, goodbye to "Indie Roots"
2012.ln: After a crowded, testy 2011 in the car-camping lots, the team split the passes into camp-in-your-car and camp-near-your-car, and found "far less cars" and far less arguing. A new Camp Host Crew worked like a front desk at the edge of the woods, walking people to sites and lending out shovels and rakes. Neko Case told the crowd it was the most amazing place she had ever played, and Heartless Bastards ran so late in the Galaxy Barn that their set was shut down. In the wrap-up the team retired the "Indie Roots" label as no longer fitting, and that fall it thanked the portable-toilet crews, "those that arrive first."

f.t: Neko Case, onstage: "This is the most amazing place I have ever played."
Campers could check out a shovel or rake from the new Camp Host Crew to fix up their site.
October post: "Portable toilet service men and women of the world. Thank you very much."
Zale on reusable cups and free water: "It seems so radical, something like reusing a cup."
Neko Case told the crowd, "This is the most amazing place I have ever played."
Saving Country Music said Lake Street Dive's Workshop Barn set got the biggest ovation he had ever seen.
Thee Oh Sees tore through a Friday-night Galaxy Barn set of "physically impossible" energy, per Saving Country Music.
Pickathon reported landfill garbage down close to 50% since 2009 and phased out compostable cups and straws.

2012.lu: The discovery engine starts producing: the War on Drugs and Shovels & Rope play early sets, and global acts like Hot 8 Brass Band join.

lf.t: The War on Drugs and Shovels & Rope made their first Pickathon appearances in 2012; both came back.
Zale called Thee Oh Sees' Galaxy Barn set "one of my top five concerts"; garage bookings like Ty Segall and King Tuff followed.
New Orleans' Hot 8 Brass Band and Mali's Vieux Farka Touré widened the 2012 bill beyond American roots.

2013.th: Fifteen, and the fence moved closer
2013.ln: For its fifteenth year, the changes were small and physical. The audience fence came in from 15 feet to 4, a new shade sculpture over the main bowl threw twice the shade, a hand pump went in under the windmill, a "bathroom swat team" stood by, and PSU architecture students built an entry portal, their first piece on the farm. Feist brought the first full lighting rig the festival had hosted, while Shakey Graves, booked into the two smallest rooms, packed both. Shabazz Palaces' Ishmael Butler compared the Galaxy Barn's sound to a blown-speaker cassette in a 1989 Corolla.

f.t: The 2013 map: fence moved from 15 feet to 4, and "over twice as much shade as last year."
Ishmael Butler likened the Galaxy Barn's sound to a blown-speaker cassette playing in a 1989 Corolla.
New Windmill Hill kids area promised "a whole summer worth of kids activities in one weekend."
Shakey Graves packed both of the smallest venues; Saving Country Music said Pickathon underestimated his draw.
Booked Feist, its biggest headliner up to that point, alongside Andrew Bird.
Tickets capped at 3,500, and every band played at least twice on different stages.
PSU architecture students built their first Pickathon piece: a bamboo entry portal.
An estimated 28,000 fans streamed Marco Benevento's six-camera set, while several hundred watched in person.

2013.lu: The biggest bill to date puts arena-level indie names next to the founding old-time players, all under the same 3,500-ticket cap.

lf.t: Zale on the Feist year: "We went a little bigger than we could handle," a gamble he says nearly sank the festival.
Dirk Powell, Foghorn Stringband and the Caleb Klauder Country Band shared the 2013 bill with Feist and Andrew Bird.
Sturgill Simpson returned in 2013 under his own name, two years after playing with Sunday Valley.
Shakey Graves and Parquet Courts both made their first Pickathon appearances in 2013.

2014.th: Pallets in the trees, and Thursday goes public
2014.ln: PSU students rented about 600 pallets, stacked them into the first Treeline Stage at the edge of the woods, and sold them back when it was over. For the first time the low-key Thursday shows for early arrivals went on the printed schedule, with Lonnie Holley at Treeline and Ural Thomas & the Pain in the Galaxy Barn, and the old Workshop Barn got a new name, the Lucky Barn. Riders could pedal 14.5 miles from Velo Cult in Portland while a shuttle hauled their tents. The War on Drugs' Adam Granduciel told the crowd this was the festival they'd actually attend, and Angel Olsen shut down a heckler with five words.

f.t: Adam Granduciel of The War on Drugs, to the crowd: "this is the one we'd actually attend."
Angel Olsen answered a Lucky Barn heckler: "You're not wearing a shirt."
The bike ride was "a mellow, 14.5 miles with one good climb," with chaperones and a gear shuttle.
Three weeks later, the team was still "digging out, cleaning up, tucking away" and "soaking it all in."
First Treeline Stage, built by PSU architecture students from about 600 shipping pallets.
Courtney Barnett, Angel Olsen, Valerie June, Mandolin Orange and Hiss Golden Messenger played their first Pickathon shows.
The War on Drugs' Adam Granduciel told the crowd, "this is the one we'd actually attend."
Took no corporate sponsors; Schoenborn said, "We've limited attendance and made the choice not to exploit the festival with sponsorship."

2014.lu: Reunions and punk history join the discovery class: Nickel Creek's comeback, X, and a crop of future stars in their first sets.

lf.t: Nickel Creek played 2014, the year it returned from a 2007 hiatus with A Dotted Line, its first album in nine years.
Los Angeles punk band X topped the 2014 bill with Nickel Creek and Warpaint.
Jolie Holland, on the 2005 Pudding River bill, returned in 2014 alongside Lonnie Holley and Valerie June.

2015.th: A heat wave under fabric diamonds
2015.ln: Afternoons pushed toward 100 degrees, and the crowd lived under the fabric diamonds that GuildWorks and its Sky Crew volunteers rigged day and night over the Mountain Stage. The Treeline Stage came back as 435 recycled cardboard tubes braced with Douglas fir, and left no trace on the farm. Portlandia filmed on Thursday with the Flaming Lips, Leon Bridges drew a barn line that ran into the beer garden, and Kamasi Washington played with his father on soprano sax. Wolf People, stuck in Seattle traffic, missed their slot and made it up with a 1 a.m. set at the Pumphouse.

f.t: The thank-you post credited the Sky Crew for "working day and night on the fabric diamonds" during the heatwave.
Leon Bridges drew the weekend's biggest crowds; the barn line stretched out into the beer garden.
Wolf People missed their slot in Seattle traffic, then played an impromptu 1 a.m. Pumphouse set.
The cardboard-tube Treeline Stage "left no trace on Pendarvis Farm afterward."
Leon Bridges, backed by White Denim, drew the weekend's biggest crowds; the barn line stretched into the beer garden.
Kamasi Washington, touring behind The Epic, played a Friday barn set with his father on soprano sax.
Treeline Stage rebuilt from 435 giant cardboard tubes, seating up to 1,000.
The 2015 Treeline Stage won the Jury Award at the AIA Portland Architecture Awards.

2015.lu: Jazz, soul and Saharan rock now share the bill with bluegrass elders, and Billy Strings makes his first appearance in a duo with Don Julin.

lf.t: Bluegrass Hall of Famer Alice Gerrard, of the duo Hazel & Alice, played 2015; she was inducted in 2017.
Tinariwen, the Malian Tuareg band, played 2015 and returned in 2018.
Kevin Morby and Rodrigo Amarante joined Leon Bridges and Kamasi Washington as 2015 first-timers.

2016.th: Seen on Portlandia, then pulling up a chair
2016.ln: The year opened with Portlandia's season premiere, an episode called "Pickathon," shot on the farm the summer before. The festival's own firsts were quieter than TV: late-night comedy in the Lucky Barn, a Wild Horse Stage for kids, and the first Curation dinners, where chefs like Ned Ludd's Jason French cooked for 55 guests with a band at the table. Jeff Tweedy played two sets of nearly 20 songs each without repeating one, and King Sunny Adé's 13-piece band crowded the little Woods Stage. When it was over, the team thanked Elwood, Ronnie, Biggs and J. Razz for putting the farm back in order for Scott and Sherry Pendarvis.

f.t: Jeff Tweedy played two sets of nearly 20 songs each without repeating a single song.
King Sunny Adé's 13-piece band "stretched the foundation of the small Woods stage."
The post-fest survey opened with a photo of "The Dan Deacon Dance Off."
The farm-restoration crew were "four of the most important people in the world right now."
Portlandia opened its sixth season with an episode called 'Pickathon,' with the Flaming Lips headlining the festival.
Premiered the Starlight Series, live videos shot at the 2015 festival.
Launched the Curation Series with Ned Ludd's Jason French: six chef-and-artist meals, 55 guests each.
King Sunny Adé's 13-piece band 'stretched the foundation of the small Woods stage,' wrote the Portland Mercury.

2016.lu: The peak indie headliner year: Beach House, Yo La Tengo and a reunited Wolf Parade, with Margo Price as the discovery.

lf.t: Wolf Parade, on hiatus since 2011, made Pickathon one of its first reunion dates in 2016.
Margo Price played her first Pickathon in 2016, and Daniel Norgren played his first U.S. show there.
WWeek called Jeff Tweedy "perhaps the platonic ideal of a Pickathon headliner" as the 2016 bill neared a first sellout.

2017.th: Sun-kissed, dusty, and a lost knife
2017.ln: The wrap-up began "Sun-kissed, exhausted, and thankful," with the crew still washing off sunscreen and dust. New small rituals appeared: a first all-ages two-mile fun run at 7 a.m. Saturday and a morning bake sale for the Rock 'N' Roll Camp for Girls. Charles Bradley turned the Woods into a funk-and-soul dance party, Dungen played a live score to a 1926 animated film under the stars, and Glide guessed Billy Strings might be bluegrass's next big thing. Afterward the blog put out a plea for Big Thief's Buck, whose knife went missing, while the Treeline's nearly 700 wooden trusses went on to become sleeping pods at a veterans village.

f.t: Lost and found: Buck of Big Thief's knife, engraved "Lonewolf," with two 2018 passes offered for its return.
Sunday's photo caption: "All Smiles With Sherry Pendarvis."
Saturday began with the first-ever all-ages two-mile fun run, gathering at 7 a.m. by the Medical Tent.
Dungen played a live score to the 1926 animated film The Adventures of Prince Achmed under the stars.
Treeline Stage trusses were reused as sleeping pods at the Clackamas County Veterans Village.
Treeline Stage was built from 690 wooden trusses, designed by PSU's Center for Public Interest Design.
Treeline Stage won a Citation Award in the AIA Portland Architecture Awards.
Schoenborn said Pickathon videos drew about 5 million viewers in 2017, more than double the year before.

2017.lu: The discovery side hits its stride with Big Thief and Tank and the Bangas, while a 2002 old-time veteran comes back.

lf.t: Big Thief, Tank and the Bangas, Brent Cobb and Sunflower Bean all played their first Pickathon in 2017.
Cajun fiddler Courtney Granger, who played with Dirk Powell in 2002, returned on his own in 2017.
Tuvan throat singers Huun-Huur-Tu and Thailand's Khun Narin pushed the 2017 bill further toward global music.

2018.th: At twenty, the founder went crowd surfing
2018.ln: Pickathon's twentieth weekend came in at a kind 83 degrees, and the staff's own list of favorite moments reads like a diary. Zale crowd surfed at the Treeline Stage during Bee Bee Sea; Hailu Mergia's drummer insisted the band never plays "Tizita" in concert, then played it; and a man at The War and Treaty's set asked a stranger for a hug because he'd missed hugging his neighbor. DakhaBrakha closed their Mt. Hood set by unfurling a Ukrainian flag, and Built to Spill played the farm for the first time. Behind the scenes, staff were proudest of new consent signs and a setup week where "Everyone Is Important."

f.t: Hailu Mergia's drummer: "We don't play Tizita in concerts." That night, they played it.
After The War and Treaty, a man asked a staffer for a hug; he'd missed his chance to hug his neighbor.
One staffer stayed awake about 22 hours to catch Wild Child at 1 a.m.: "100% worth it."
DakhaBrakha closed their Mt. Hood set by unfurling a Ukrainian flag and anti-Kremlin posters.
Celebrated its 20th festival, still capped at 3,500 attendees.
The Ringer: 'You can think of Pickathon as a content company with a live event.'
Filmed 64 acts with more than 80 cameras and a 500-person production team.
Black Pumas played an intimate Curation dinner for 75 guests in the Old Farmhouse.

2018.lu: The 20th festival spans eight decades of music, from the Blind Boys of Alabama to Black Pumas, with founding players still on the bill.

lf.t: Portland Monthly said the Blind Boys of Alabama, founded in 1939, were the 2018 festival's oldest band.
The Danny Barnes Trio and Caleb Klauder & Reeb Willms played the 20th festival, 16 and 17 years after their first.
Colter Wall, Charley Crockett and The War and Treaty were 2018 discoveries, with Portland's Haley Heynderickx.

2019.th: A full house, and apple bins due back
2019.ln: The 21st festival was full enough that Saturday day parking sold out, and the blog pointed people to the free EcoShuttle from Clackamas Town Center instead. PSU students stacked 160 borrowed apple bins into seven towers for the Treeline Stage, held together with screws in use since 2014, and sent the bins back in time for the apple harvest. Tyler Childers played two headlining sets the weekend Country Squire came out, Phil Lesh took the Woods Stage, and Khruangbin played Mt. Hood on Friday night. The thank-you post joked that "no one spilled beer all over the Polaroids."

f.t: Saturday morning post: "Day parking for Saturday is now SOLD OUT."
A Portland Mercury writer left Khruangbin's Friday Mt. Hood set calling them her new favorite band.
The photo roundup included a square dance, "a Pickathon tradition," and Mdou Moctar on the Starlight Stage.
Treeline's 160 apple bins went back to their owners for the harvest.
Khruangbin played the Mt. Hood Stage Friday night; a Portland Mercury writer called them her new favorite band.
Tyler Childers played two headlining sets the same weekend his album Country Squire came out.
Phil Lesh played the Woods Stage's first three-hour double set.
Curation was produced as a packaged TV show: top chefs and discovery artists, about 100 guests per meal.

2019.lu: The fullest lineup of the original era, mixing big draws like Nathaniel Rateliff with global and discovery acts on seven stages.

lf.t: Mdou Moctar, Jupiter & Okwess and Ibibio Sound Machine carried the 2019 bill's global side.
Zale calls 2019 the "Apex Discovery" lineup, citing Khruangbin, Tyler Childers, The Marías, Mereba and Viagra Boys.

2020–2021.th: Two summers off, and a concert a day
2020–2021.ln: With the farm closed in 2020, the team put one past concert online every afternoon at 1 p.m., planned it for 60 days, and kept it going for 17 weeks, raising $200,000 for MusiCares with Spotify's match. Two days in, they posted a goodbye to John Prine, who had been booked to play, remembering his songs as a reminder that "we don't have to go it alone," and many ticket holders rolled their passes forward or gave them to the festival. In June 2021 the team called off a second summer and asked everyone to "be good to each other this year." That fall, two nights of music at Topaz Farm on Sauvie Island, with Bill Callahan and Antibalas, were the first time the Pickathon crowd had gathered since 2019.

f.t: Pickathon At Home closed the series with archived sets from Khruangbin, Dan Deacon and Drive-By Truckers.
On John Prine: his songs were a reminder that "we don't have to go it alone."
A February 2021 livestream let Caleb Klauder and Reeb Willms hear their audience's applause from home.
The Topaz Farm harvest shows were "the first opportunity since 2019 for the Pickathon community to reunite."
The canceled lineup included John Prine, (Sandy) Alex G, Joan Shelley and Chad VanGaalen.
Streamed 60 past sets, one a day, to raise money for MusiCares COVID relief.
Had raised $200,000 for MusiCares by late July, including Spotify's matching gifts.
Worked with the Recording Academy and supported NIVA and Save Our Stages during the shutdown.

2020–2021.lu: The booked 2020 lineup, with John Prine and Sierra Ferrell, never played; the next bill would come in 2022.

lf.t: Sierra Ferrell, booked for the canceled 2020 festival, went on to win four Grammys in 2025.

2022.th: A redrawn farm, a parking scramble, then dancing
2022.ln: After two summers away, Pickathon came back with the farm redrawn into neighborhoods, a Cherry Hill stage built from more than 175 cable reels borrowed from Portland General Electric, and much of it no longer where regulars remembered. The first morning tested everyone: the golf-course parking was full by 11 a.m. Friday, and Zale was out marking a new lot in the grass by early afternoon. Then the weekend settled into joy. Sons of Kemet played their last U.S. shows with Esperanza Spalding sitting in, TV Priest slipped into a secret 1 a.m. barn set, a young fiddler busked on the quail trail, and Zale said he had "never danced so much in my whole life."

f.t: Zale, afterward: "euphoria on another level" and "never danced so much in my whole life!"
Cedric Burnside's golden-hour Paddock set: "Hill country blues at its finest!"
TV Priest played a secret 1 a.m. Galaxy Barn set, bumping Emma-Jean Thackray to a buzzed-about 9 p.m. slot.
Saving Country Music called Mike and the Moonpies "the greatest live band in country music."
Returned after two years and reorganized the farm into 'neighborhoods,' with daytime sets in shaded woods.
PSU students built the first Cherry Hill stage from 175-plus cable reels borrowed from Portland General Electric work yards.
Skylab Architecture, McFadin Design, EMA Architecture and Green Anchors helped design the new neighborhoods.
Sons of Kemet played their final U.S. shows before splitting; Esperanza Spalding joined them Sunday night.

2022.lu: The return lineup leans hard into discovery and new jazz, hip-hop and global sounds, with Built to Spill and GZA as anchors.

lf.t: Wet Leg played 2022, months after their debut album; it won two Grammys in 2023.
Cedric Burnside, R.L. Burnside's grandson, played 2022, the year his I Be Trying won the Grammy for traditional blues album.
Valerie June, a 2014 first-timer, returned to top the 2022 lineup announcement.

2023.th: The new layout's second year, and it fit
2023.ln: With a year of practice in the new layout, the farm felt lived-in rather than new, and the team described it as "a total immersion experience." Cherry Hill rose on arching hemlock beams that Oregon ArtsWatch called a forest within a forest, students from the Clackamas Academy of Industrial Sciences helped raise a lumber landmark called Mt. Pickathon, and a hydrogen generator from Toyota Racing Development ran stages. Wednesday played what Paste called maybe the best rock 'n' roll set it had seen all year, and MJ Lenderman, just signed to ANTI-, played the Woods. In the Galaxy Barn, Møtrik played in white coveralls until their fog machine set off the smoke alarm.

f.t: Paste on Wednesday's Paddock set: "maybe the best rock 'n' roll performance I'd seen this year."
Krautrockers Møtrik wore white coveralls; their fog machine set off the Galaxy Barn smoke alarm.
They Hate Change rapped in the Galaxy Barn "like their lives depended on it," per Paste.
Hampton Lumber donated the lumber for Mt. Pickathon, built with Hoffman and Precision Construction and high schoolers.
Paste called it 'the best indie festival in the country.'
MJ Lenderman played the Woods Stage, freshly signed to ANTI-, leaning on his album Boat Songs.
Cherry Hill's hemlock arches were slated to become an outdoor classroom at PSU's Oak Savanna, supporting Indigenous ecological knowledge.
Became the first festival to power stages with a hydrogen fuel cell generator.

2023.lu: Paste says the festival is returning to discovery over big headliners, with a lineup reaching Africa, Latin America, hip-hop and Portland.

lf.t: Paste wrote that 2023 marked a return to discovery rather than big headliners like Phil Lesh, Beach House and Nickel Creek.
W.I.T.C.H., Zambia's top 1970s band, played 2023, the year it released Zango, its first studio album in nearly 40 years.
Vieux Farka Touré, first booked in 2012, returned in 2023 alongside Wednesday and Dehd.

2024.th: A letter to neighbors, dogs in the barn
2024.ln: In late July Zale wrote an open letter to Happy Valley: a new permit had secured the next decade on the farm, neighbors within half a mile could ask for free day tickets, and a hotline number was printed for anyone bothered by the sound. Build week ran on lumber and good humor, with the Cherry Hill, Windmill and Grove teams hauling materials while the dogs napped in the Lucky Barn. Mark Lakeman's Branch Crew wove the Woods Stage backdrop from trees and branches, and PSU students wound 80 gates, some 27 feet tall, around the trees at Cherry Hill. Courtney Barnett came back a decade after her first Pickathon to close Sunday at the Paddock, and Dean Johnson owned its magic hour.

f.t: Build-week post: "Even the dogs are part of the fun, chilling in the barn and playing in the open fields."
The founder's letter, to campers: "happy campers are quiet campers!"
Zale to Axios: "This is fantasy island, you don't get it until you come."
Glide said the festival "landed on its feet," leaning on discovery over big headliners.
Creative Neighborhoods launched, with four programs at the festival in its first year.
Happy Valley renewed the festival's permit at Pendarvis Farm for 10 years.
Hoffman Construction and ZGF built the Paddock mainstage, 'Antlers & Sunset.'
Courtney Barnett returned a decade after her first Pickathon to close Sunday night at the Paddock.

2024.lu: Alumni return as headliners, Courtney Barnett and Bonnie "Prince" Billy, over a young class led by Geese and Water From Your Eyes.

lf.t: Bonnie "Prince" Billy returned as a 2024 headliner, 14 years after his 2010 set.
Kara Jackson, the 2019 U.S. National Youth Poet Laureate, played 2024 after her 2023 debut album.

2025.th: Twenty-five, and the crowd voted to stay put
2025.ln: Before the 25th, the team asked the audience what Pickathon should become, and more than 1,600 people answered nearly as one: keep the small stages, keep the farm, keep the free water. The weekend kept that promise in small ways, from blackberry brambles slowing the walk between the Galaxy Barn and the Woods to a red-breasted sapsucker working the firs over Rose City Band. Taj Mahal drew the biggest crowds of the weekend, and friends played Michael Hurley's songs after the Portland folk legend died in April while still on the bill. A new Paddock sound system cut the volume toward nearby homes by about 35 decibels, and photographer Kelsey Jean shot the weekend on expired Polaroid film.

f.t: The survey's answer, in the team's words: "You want Pickathon to stay Pickathon."
Fruit Bats' Eric Johnson in Paste: Pickathon is "the dog park for bands too."
Spectrum Culture named Jimetta Rose & the Voices of Creation's Woods set "the top set of the weekend."
Kelsey Jean's expired film chased "inside jokes scrawled on napkins" and "handwritten setlists."
Marked the 25th Pickathon.
Taj Mahal's two sets drew the biggest crowds of the 25th-anniversary weekend.
Hoffman, ZGF and Exactonaut built the Timbre stage as the Paddock's centerpiece; its timber was donated afterward.
GBD Architects, Andersen Construction and McFadin Design-Build made the Farmhouse; its parts became raised beds for food banks.

2025.lu: The 25th festival bills its own alumni as legends and frames the rest, about 50 acts, as the core discovery lineup.

lf.t: Pickathon billed Haley Heynderickx, a 2018 discovery, among its 2025 "legends" with Taj Mahal and Fruit Bats.
The 2025 announcement called the roughly 50 lesser-known acts, like Being Dead and Jake Blount, the heart of the festival.
Fruit Bats, first booked in 2010, played their fifth Pickathon in 2025.

2026.th: Woods Stage's last bloom, and a barn dance
2026.ln: For the first time the gates opened on a Wednesday evening, with two-step lessons and a barn dance in the Galaxy Barn before a single festival set. The Woods Stage, rebuilt about every seven years from fir, maple, cedar and vine-maple limbs off the property, reached what the team called its "full flower," with a rebirth planned for 2027. The Womack Sisters left the Woods crowd speechless on Sunday, and Hogslop String Band stepped off the Grove stage onto the woodchips until the crowd circled them in a stomping square dance. Many builds left with an address: the Long Porch's lumber was headed to a greenhouse for a retired nurse in Milwaukie, and Cherry Hill's fishing nets to Ukraine.

f.t: Orquestra Pacifico Tropical's drummer, opening night: "This is music that wants to give the world a hug."
The team on its forest stage: "the Woods Stage is a living thing."
Folk-punks Big Tractor stole the unamplified late-night talent show at the Woods Stage.
The Galaxy Courtyard's lumber water lilies move on to new art pieces, then to the Guild of Oregon Woodworkers.
Steve Earle and Shakey Graves headlined the 26th festival.
The Womack Sisters, Sam Cooke's granddaughters, left the Woods crowd "in collective gape-eyed awe," per Portland Monthly.
PSU built the Cherry Hill stage from worn-out Oregon coast fishing nets, one of 10 venues.
Scott Edwards Architecture and Bremik Construction built the Paddock "Synthesis" stage, bound for Old Town's Q-Side Skatepark.

2026.lu: The bill splits openly into legends and discovery, and the legends tier spans Brazilian bossa nova, Jamaican reggae and a 2007 alum.

lf.t: Steve Earle headlined 2026; his son Justin Townes Earle played Pickathon in 2009.
Marcos Valle, the bossa nova writer of "Samba de Verão" ("Summer Samba"), played at 82.
Zale on 2026 booking: artists who "are pointing to what's next," not those who are "obvious and everywhere."
Shakey Graves, a 2013 discovery, co-headlined 2026 with Steve Earle, 13 years after his first Pickathon.

1999.th: A KBOO benefit built on Portland pickers
1999.ln: Year one is a local roots party for community radio: Portland bluegrass, Cajun and old-time bands playing for about 90 people.

f.t: Portland's Little Sue and Lynn Conover headlined the first Pickathon; Little Sue would return in 2001, 2003 and 2006.
The Holy Modal Rounders, the 1963 Lower East Side folk band behind Easy Rider's "Bird Song," played Horning's in the early years.
The Holy Modal Rounders had been based in Portland since 1972 and reunited in 1999, the year Pickathon began.
Zale on the first year's turnout: about 90 people, "including performers and dogs."

2000.th: Kelly Joe Phelps gives the bill a name
2000.ln: The first touring-caliber name arrives: Kelly Joe Phelps tops a dozen volunteer acts and attendance more than doubles to about 220.

f.t: Kelly Joe Phelps topped the 2000 bill; WWeek credits him with drawing about 220 people, a high point of the early years.
Phelps, from Sumner, Washington, was known for lap-style slide guitar; his 1995 debut Lead Me On was critically praised.
The 2000 sets became the first live Pickathon CD, starting a yearly series that ran through 2010.

2001.th: National bluegrass names join the local core
2001.ln: Bay Area bluegrass royalty joins the Portland regulars, and Caleb Klauder appears for the first time, still years before Foghorn Stringband takes its name.

f.t: Laurie Lewis, IBMA Female Vocalist of the Year in 1992 and 1994, played with Tom Rozum; their duo album earned a 1995 Grammy nomination.
Fiddler Darol Anger, a founding member of the David Grisman Quintet and co-founder of Turtle Island String Quartet, played in 2001.
The Caleb Klauder Band played 2001; Klauder kept returning, as late as 2018 with Foghorn bandmate Reeb Willms.
Most acts were local; Zale wanted bands "that don't get much Top-20 radio play but who have a face on KBOO."

2002.th: Dirk Powell and Danny Barnes raise the bar
2002.ln: The early pillars lock in: Dirk Powell, Danny Barnes and Foghorn Stringband share a small canyon stage with an Irish fiddle master.

f.t: Dirk Powell played with Cajun fiddler Courtney Granger; Powell later backed Joan Baez for a decade and has won four Grammys.
Danny Barnes, founder of Austin's Bad Livers, played Pickathon 2002; his "Delilah" is on that year's festival CD.
Kevin Burke, ex-Bothy Band fiddler living in Portland since 1979, played the year he was named an NEA National Heritage Fellow.
Foghorn Stringband, formed at the Weiser fiddle contest, took that name in September 2002, the month it played Pickathon.

2003.th: Otis Taylor brings blues to the lake
2003.ln: Pickathon moves to August and adds a weekend of music; a nationally rising bluesman headlines over the Portland old-time and swing scene.

f.t: Otis Taylor played 2003, a year after DownBeat critics named his Truth Is Not Fiction the 2002 blues CD of the year.
Zale counts Otis Taylor, Dirk Powell and the Holy Modal Rounders as legends who played to about 200 people at Horning's.
Danny Barnes returned for a second straight year; Foghorn Stringband and the Crooked Jades also made the 2003 CD.

2004.th: Last Horning's year seeds future Grammy talent
2004.ln: The last Horning's year stays small and local, but it books a young band whose co-founders link straight to the 2005 breakthrough bill.

f.t: Po' Girl, formed in 2003 by Allison Russell and the Be Good Tanyas' Trish Klein, played 2004; Russell later won a 2024 Grammy.
Danny Barnes played his third straight Pickathon in 2004, making him the steadiest early anchor of the bill.
Portland's Hillstomp and the Shiftless Rounders played 2004; the Rounders returned in 2005 and Hillstomp in 2009.

2005.th: The biggest bill yet, built in a hayfield
2005.ln: The lineup jumps a tier: alt-country and Canadian folk headliners with national followings, around the Portland pillars, at a new site built from scratch.

f.t: The Be Good Tanyas, a Vancouver trio formed in 1999 with Frazey Ford, Samantha Parton and Trish Klein, headlined 2005.
Former Be Good Tanya Jolie Holland played the same day as her old band; she returned in 2008 and 2014.
Freakwater, the Louisville duo of Catherine Irwin and Janet Bean on Thrill Jockey, brought alt-country credibility; they returned in 2015.
The Hacienda Brothers, Chris Gaffney and Dave Gonzalez's "western soul" band produced by Dan Penn, played 2005 and 2007.

2006.th: Pendarvis opens with the Avett Brothers rising
2006.ln: The first farm year pairs established songwriters like Iris DeMent and Greg Brown with a band about to break: the Avett Brothers.

f.t: The Avett Brothers played their first Pickathon in 2006; two years later they signed with Rick Rubin's American Recordings.
Iris DeMent, twice Grammy-nominated and John Prine's duet partner on In Spite of Ourselves, helped open the farm era.
Kelly Joe Phelps and Darol Anger came back for the first Pendarvis year, carrying the Horning's lineage to the farm.
Martha Scanlan played 2006 and kept returning through 2019, one of the longest threads in Pickathon booking.

2007.ln: A third day arrives and the festival names its sound "indie-roots," booking young bands like Trampled by Turtles and Alela Diane beside the old-time core.

f.t: JamBase's 2007 listing defined Pickathon's "Indie-Roots" as indie rock and singer-songwriters mixed with bluegrass, blues, folk, country and swing.
Trampled by Turtles played 2007 and 2008; their 2010 album Palomino went to No. 1 on the bluegrass chart.
Alela Diane debuted in 2007 and is billed as a 2026 legend, a 19-year arc from discovery to headliner tier.
Langhorne Slim was a 2007 discovery; he returned in 2008, 2010, 2012 and 2015.

2008.th: Ten years old, and arguing over the barn
2008.ln: Pickathon turned ten with a fight it didn't see coming: a July plan to make the late-night Galaxy Barn all-ages drew so much pushback that the team posted "damage control" two days later and put it to a vote. Fans chose to keep the barn 21-and-over after 9:30, and the beer moved outside to a new barn-side garden beside the first Pickathon Cafe, where al Forno Ferruzza baked pies and Sicilian pastries. Rain hung over the opening, then cleared on Saturday. A visiting writer who had been up since 5 a.m. dozed off on the dry grass during Crooked Still, stepped in horse manure, and was jolted awake by the Hackensaw Boys.

f.t: On the barn vote, the team wrote that "it was clear that we needed to keep this 'adult time' environment sacred."
Saturday's post opened: "The weather became our friend." The rain stopped and the sun came out.
Loch Lomond played without amplifiers and called the crowd in close. The blog's verdict: "Think Andrew Bird times nine."
In March the blog asked readers to help Hacienda Brothers singer Chris Gaffney, a festival regular, through his fight with liver cancer.
Willamette Week billed the 2008 Bad Livers set as a reunion of "Austin punkgrass legends"; the band had dissolved in 2000.
Kelly Joe Phelps, who topped the 2000 bill at Horning's, returned in 2008 for the tenth festival.
Seattle's Cave Singers and Portland's Laura Gibson, both playing 2008, show the bill tilting toward Northwest indie-folk.
Trampled by Turtles were invited back because their 2007 sets were among the festival's most delightful, WWeek wrote.

2008.lu: The tenth festival honors its roots, reuniting Danny Barnes's Bad Livers and bringing back Kelly Joe Phelps, while indie-folk bands keep moving in.

2009.th: A ninety-degree weekend and the search for Marty
2009.ln: The farm got ready by hand that spring, with volunteers meeting at the red Galaxy Barn to burn brush along the fern trail before the burn window closed. The festival opened into heat in the low 90s, with tickets sold only at the gate, in cash. On Saturday night Blitzen Trapper's Marty Marquis vanished before the band's barn set, and his bandmates, staff and Zale walked the woods calling his name tent by tent. At 1:48 a.m. the radio crackled "Marty's in the Barn!"; he had dozed off after a backstage massage, woken in the dark, and walked toward the light and straight onto the stage.

f.t: Opening-day post: "The sun is shining, the crew is out busting their humps," with highs forecast in the 90s.
Searchers looked for a "tall, curly redhead with a rattail" among about a thousand tents on 80 acres.
From the blog's press roundup, a photo caption: "Joe Pug making time stand still in the Galaxy Barn."
Work-party rules: bring loppers and bow saws, no chainsaws, and stay for Al Forno Ferruzza pizza after.
Eugene Weekly: "every year, the Pickathon line-up gets a little less hillbilly-twangy and a little more indie-folk-strummy."
Portland's Blitzen Trapper played 2009, a year after Furr, their first Sub Pop album.
Justin Townes Earle, son of Steve Earle, played 2009, the year he won the Americana Music Award for emerging artist.
X's John Doe played with the Sadies in 2009; Doe returned with X in 2014.

2009.lu: The crossover year: Dr. Dog, Blitzen Trapper and Thao bring indie-rock audiences, and a punk legend plays with the Sadies.

arcSpine: Pickathon began in 1999 as a small benefit for community radio, built by volunteers, friends and family, and it grew until that first home and partner could no longer carry it. In 2006 it found Pendarvis Farm and made a choice it kept for fourteen years: stay small, every band plays twice, and grow outward instead, first with zero-waste firsts and student-built stages, then with cameras on every stage and sponsors paying for videos that reached millions. That idea worked for a long time, until COVID closed the farm for two years and ad tech took the sponsorships that paid for the videos. Pickathon came back in 2022 rebuilt as neighborhoods, and in 2024 it split the mission from the weekend: Creative Neighborhoods, a nonprofit, now builds the stages with architects, builders and students, Pickathon uses them for one weekend, and each structure moves on to a permanent home in the community. Through every chapter the lineup did the same job, putting artists in the woods just before they broke, next to deep cuts and living legends.

legacc.Blind Boys of Alabama: Gospel royalty: an NEA National Heritage Fellowship, the Gospel Music Hall of Fame, and a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award.
legacc.Bonnie “Prince” Billy: I See a Darkness earned a perfect review from Pitchfork and ranked ninth on its list of the best albums of the 1990s.
legacc.Built to Spill: Pitchfork put three Built to Spill albums in its top 50 of the 1990s, with Perfect from Now On at No. 22.
legacc.Jonathan Richman: His Modern Lovers debut sits on Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums of All Time.
legacc.GZA: Liquid Swords is on both Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums and Pitchfork's top 100 of the '90s.
legacc.King Sunny Adé: The juju king was Nigeria's first Grammy nominee and the first African nominated twice.
legacc.Ernest Ranglin: Jamaica has twice honored the ska guitar pioneer with national orders.
legacc.Mavis Staples: A Rock & Roll Hall of Famer, Kennedy Center honoree and NEA National Heritage Fellow.
legacc.Preservation Hall Jazz Band: Awarded the National Medal of Arts in the Oval Office, the highest honor the U.S. gives artists.
legacc.Phil Lesh & The Terrapin Family Band: Led by the Grateful Dead's founding bassist, inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 1994.
legacc.Tinariwen: The Saharan Tuareg band Tinariwen won a Grammy for Tassili and has been Grammy-nominated three times.
legacc.Taj Mahal: Taj Mahal swept four Blues Music Awards in one night in 2018, including Entertainer of the Year, the same year he won a Grammy.
legacc.Steve Earle: Steve Earle has three Grammys for Best Contemporary Folk Album from 16 nominations.
legacc.Yo La Tengo: Yo La Tengo is on Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums list, and The Wire named their 2023 record the year's best.

Kevin Burke & Casey Neill.t: Lucy Cambell and the Jolly Tinker

1999.headline: Year one: a radio benefit with freak-folk forebears and Portland string bands
1999.story: Pickathon began in 1999 as a KBOO benefit at Horning's Hideout, with about 90 people there, performers and dogs included. The Holy Modal Rounders, whose "Bird Song" opened Easy Rider, played the year Robert Christgau said of a reissue, "freak folk started here." Portland's own Dickel Brothers, punk-fast old-time players with a new debut on eMpTy Records, played too.

scenes.name: Freak folk and old-time roots
scenes.blurb: Formed in 1963; critics later traced freak folk to them. Their album Too Much Fun! came out in 1999.

scenes.name: Portland string bands and local acts
scenes.blurb: The Dickel Brothers brought punk-fast old-time music from their 1999 debut, Volume One, and local player Seamus Eagan filled out the bill.

scenes.name: Portland songwriters
scenes.blurb: Little Sue and Lynn Conover headlined a local bill; Sue later entered the Oregon Music Hall of Fame.

1999.legends_note: The Holy Modal Rounders, in Portland since 1972 and the source of the Easy Rider song "Bird Song," chose a 90-person benefit for a community radio station.

acts.proof: Formed 1963 on the Lower East Side; "Bird Song" opened Easy Rider (soundtrack No. 6, gold). Christgau on the 1999 reissue: "freak folk started here." Oregon Music Hall of Fame, 2008.
Local Portland performer on the Pickathon lineup sheet. Not the Solas founder Seamus Egan.

Little Sue (Susannah Weaver) was inducted into the Oregon Music Hall of Fame, class of 2019; her album Crow is called an acclaimed country-folk record. Identity match to the sheet's Little Sue is assumed.
Portland old-time band whose punk-fast debut Volume One (eMpTy Records, 1999) drew praise from Country Standard Time; Volume Two earned three of five from NOW in 2001.

2000.headline: A slide-guitar master and a Colorado jamgrass bassist play a 220-person bill
2000.story: In 2000 a dozen acts played Pickathon's makeshift stage for about 220 people. Kelly Joe Phelps, a Rykodisc slide guitarist whom Jason Isbell later named an influence, topped the bill. Tye North, a Leftover Salmon bassist until 2000, and Casey Neill, a Portland songwriter on Appleseed Recordings, were new. Seamus Eagan and Little Sue came back.

scenes.name: Acoustic blues and slide guitar
scenes.blurb: Phelps moved from jazz bass to lap-slide country blues; a collaborator called him one of the deepest improvisers he had seen.

scenes.name: Colorado jamgrass in Portland
scenes.blurb: North played bass for Leftover Salmon 1993-2000 and led his own Boulder trio; his father played in the bill's Freak Mountain Ramblers.

scenes.name: Portland folk-punk and string bands
scenes.blurb: Casey Neill's band and local country and Cajun groups filled out the field.

acts.proof: Rykodisc albums Roll Away the Stone (1997) and Shine Eyed Mister Zen (1999) preceded Pickathon. Jason Isbell later claimed him as an influence; Steve Dawson called him one of the deepest improvisers he had heard.

North was Leftover Salmon's bassist 1993-2000; the band's 1999 Nashville Sessions (Hollywood Records) had Waylon Jennings, Jerry Douglas and Lucinda Williams as guests. He left about late 2000 and led his own trio.

Appleseed Recordings albums 1998, 1999 (Skree, produced by Johnny Cunningham) and 2001. A 1998 Pete Seeger tribute he appears on won Top Independent Release from the American Association of Independent Music.

2001.headline: A Grammy-winning bluegrass singer, a Cajun fiddle prodigy and Portland's string bands
2001.story: Horning's Hideout hosted the 2001 Pickathon months before O Brother, Where Art Thou? won Album of the Year. Laurie Lewis, a Grammy winner with the True Life Blues bluegrass album, came as a legend with Tom Rozum. Dirk Powell brought a teenage Cajun fiddler, Courtney Granger; Terry Robb carried acoustic blues; and the Caleb Klauder Band started a long line of Northwest string bands.

scenes.name: Bluegrass
scenes.blurb: Lewis and Rozum, and Darol Anger with Scott Nygaard, arrived as bluegrass went mainstream through a movie soundtrack.
acts: Laurie Lewis, Tom Rozum, and Tom Sauber
Darol Anger / Scott Nygaard / and Tye North

scenes.name: Cajun
scenes.blurb: A 19-year-old Cajun fiddler with a Rounder debut at 16 anchored the dance-music end.
acts: Dirk Powell, Courtney Granger, & the Cajun Crew

scenes.name: Blues and Northwest string bands
scenes.blurb: Robb carried acoustic blues; the Caleb Klauder Band, Jackstraw and the Dickel Brothers kept the bill rooted in Portland.

2001.legends_note: Laurie Lewis was a national figure in bluegrass, and played a benefit for a community radio station.

acts.n: Laurie Lewis, Tom Rozum, and Tom Sauber
acts.proof: IBMA Female Vocalist of the Year 1992 and 1994; Grammy winner 1997 for contributing to True Life Blues; 1995 Grammy nominee with Rozum. Wikipedia also lists Opry and Prairie Home Companion appearances.

Cascade Blues Association Muddy Award for Best Acoustic Guitar 19 years running (1992-2010), Hall of Fame 1998, Oregon Music Hall of Fame 2009; Stop This World topped the Living Blues Radio Chart in 1997.

acts.n: Dirk Powell, Courtney Granger, & the Cajun Crew
acts.proof: Powell played banjo on the Cold Mountain soundtrack (2003). Granger, grandnephew of NEA fellow Dewey Balfa, made his solo Rounder debut at 16 (1999). Granger source: Saving Country Music obituary.

acts.n: Darol Anger / Scott Nygaard / and Tye North
acts.proof: Anger was a founding member of the David Grisman Quintet (1977 debut) and co-founded the Turtle Island String Quartet in 1985; later led Republic of Strings with Nygaard.
Vancouver folk-rock, bluegrass and Celtic band formed in 1993; seven independent albums, two on Nettwerk, and decades of touring the U.S. and Canada.

2002.headline: An Irish fiddle legend, banjo masters and a Seattle circus fill the third Horning's year
2002.story: Kevin Burke played the year he received a National Heritage Fellowship, with Casey Neill. Two-time national banjo champion Tony Furtado and Bad Livers founder Danny Barnes brought the banjo, and Dirk Powell, later the banjo player on the Cold Mountain soundtrack, played with 20-year-old Cajun fiddler Courtney Granger. Seattle's Circus Contraption and Baby Gramps brought the vaudeville; Foghorn Stringband's run began; Laurie Lewis, Tom Rozum and Terry Robb returned.

scenes.name: Irish fiddle
scenes.blurb: A Bothy Band fiddler, in Portland since 1979, played in the year the NEA named him a Heritage Fellow.

scenes.name: Banjo, Cajun and Appalachian
scenes.blurb: Furtado and Barnes on banjo; Powell and Granger brought Louisiana and Appalachian dance music after O Brother put old-time on the Grammy stage.

scenes.name: Circus and vaudeville
scenes.blurb: Circus Contraption came down from Seattle; Baby Gramps brought the old-time novelty songs.

scenes.name: Northwest string bands and songwriters
scenes.blurb: Foghorn Stringband, Spigot and Caleb Klauder, plus Casey Neill and Little Sue, kept the local base on the bill.

2002.legends_note: Kevin Burke, an ex-Bothy Band fiddler, received the NEA's highest folk and traditional arts honor in 2002 and still played a community-radio benefit.

acts.proof: Powell played banjo on the Cold Mountain soundtrack (2003), was Joan Baez's band for about ten years, and co-produced Rhiannon Giddens's Freedom Highway (2017), a Grammy nominee, and Songs of Our Native Daughters (2019).

Received a 2002 NEA National Heritage Fellowship, the highest U.S. honor in folk and traditional arts; Bothy Band 1976-79, Patrick Street nine albums 1987-2007; TG4 Musician of the Year (Gradam Ceoil), 2016.
Mandolinist in the original Foghorn Stringband lineup; the band took that name in Sept. 2002 and put out Weiser Sunrise on Nettwerk America in 2005.
Neill: Appleseed albums 1998-2001, Pete Seeger tribute credit (1998 AAIM award). Little Sue: Oregon Music Hall of Fame, class of 2019.
Won the National Bluegrass Banjo Championship at Winfield in 1987 and 1991; signed to Rounder in 1990 for six albums; toured with Gregg Allman.
Founded Austin's Bad Livers (Quarterstick, Sugar Hill); played on Bill Frisell's The Willies (2002); Steve Martin Prize, 2015; Grammy nominee for Best Bluegrass Album, 2021 (Man on Fire).

Formed after the 2000 Weiser fiddle contest; took its name Sept. 2002; Weiser Sunrise (2005) came out on Nettwerk America; toured the Shetland and Orkney folk festivals. Eight Pickathons on the sheet.
Street-musician and 'stunt guitar' performer active since 1964; per the Wikipedia article he opened for Phish in Portland in 1993; that line cites video notes, not a primary source.

2003.headline: Banjo blues and an old-time revival fresh off O Brother, on a small stage
2003.story: Pickathon moved to August with Otis Taylor, whose trance blues won DownBeat and Handy honors, as the deep cut. The Crooked Jades, Danny Barnes with ex-Leftover Salmon bassist Tye North, and Dublin-born Johnny B. Connolly made their first Pickathons. Foghorn Stringband and Little Sue came back. All of it landed a year after O Brother won Album of the Year.

scenes.name: Trance blues and banjo
scenes.blurb: Taylor's minor-key banjo blues drew DownBeat and Handy honors; Barnes took the banjo from Austin punk-grass to jazz-guitar company.

scenes.name: Old-time and string band revival
scenes.blurb: O Brother won the 2002 Album of the Year and sold millions; Pickathon booked the West Coast bands carrying that music.

scenes.name: Swing and Irish roots
scenes.blurb: A hot-jazz crooner and a Dublin-born button-accordion player showed the bill reaching past string bands.

acts.proof: DownBeat critics named Truth Is Not Fiction Blues CD of the Year (2002 poll, per Wikipedia), then Double V (2005). White African won a W.C. Handy Award for best new blues artist; Living Blues readers' pick, 2004.

Barnes founded the Austin Bad Livers (Quarterstick, then Sugar Hill), played on Bill Frisell's The Willies (Nonesuch, 2002), later got a 2021 Grammy nomination (Best Bluegrass Album) and the 2015 Steve Martin Prize.
Boulder bassist who had left Leftover Salmon about a year and a half before April 2002; led Theory of Everything and regularly played gigs with Danny Barnes.
San Francisco old-time band begun at a 1994 kitchen jam; founder Jeff Kazor produced music Sean Penn chose for Into the Wild (2007). A reviewer called their past six albums critically acclaimed.
Dublin-born accordionist who toured Europe with the band Anam by 17, moved to Portland in 1997, and made Bridgetown for Green Linnet with Bothy Band fiddler Kevin Burke on three tracks.
MacGill's bio says the trio played the Edinburgh Jazz Festival and Ronnie Scott's in London, and quotes a New York Times line on his swing-era charm. Self-published bio, no outside confirmation.

2004.headline: The last Horning's year: a future Grammy winner's band and a Portland stomp duo
2004.story: The final year at Horning's stayed small and regional. Po' Girl, which Allison Russell co-founded the year it formed, played; Russell later won the 2024 Grammy for Best American Roots Performance. Hillstomp, a Portland drum-and-guitar duo, made its first Pickathon and later landed in Sons of Anarchy and a Coen brothers trailer. Danny Barnes Collective, the deep cut, anchored the bill.

scenes.name: Banjo from the edges
scenes.blurb: Barnes had run banjo through punk and jazz; the Shiftless Rounders and Freak Mountain Ramblers kept the bill rooted in string-band fun.

scenes.name: Roots-folk and stomp
scenes.blurb: A Canadian folk band with three future solo names and a Portland punk-blues duo showed a new generation arriving.

scenes.name: Irish traditional
scenes.blurb: Connolly, back from 2003, kept Portland's Irish session scene on the bill.

acts.proof: Formed in 2003 by Allison Russell and Be Good Tanyas' Trish Klein. Russell won the 2024 Grammy for Best American Roots Performance (Eve Was Black), a 2022 Juno for Contemporary Roots Album, and Americana Album of the Year 2022.
Bad Livers founder; played on Bill Frisell's The Willies (2002); Grammy nominee for Best Bluegrass Album (Man on Fire, 2021); Steve Martin Prize, Sept. 2015.
Portland duo toured nearly year-round at its peak; a song ran in Sons of Anarchy season three and Meet Me at the Bottom was in the 2016 Hail, Caesar! trailer, then licensed by Yeti.

2005.headline: The biggest bill yet: alt-country, western soul and a Mercury-nominated songwriter
2005.story: At the new Woodburn site, Pickathon booked six first-time deep cuts: Be Good Tanyas, Freakwater, Jolie Holland, Hacienda Brothers, Tracy Grammer and Mary Flower. Waits nominated Holland for a Shortlist prize, Dan Penn produced the Haciendas, and Freakwater's harmonies influenced alt-country. Danny Barnes Collective and Foghorn Stringband returned.

scenes.name: Alt-country and western soul
scenes.blurb: Freakwater's Louisville harmonies and the Hacienda Brothers' Dan Penn-produced western soul covered the country edge.

scenes.name: Roots-folk women
scenes.blurb: Be Good Tanyas, Holland and Grammer each had a national following, from Vancouver to Anti- Records to Joan Baez's tour.

scenes.name: Blues and string band
scenes.blurb: A Piedmont fingerpicker joined returning old-time bands.

acts.proof: Catalpa made the San Francisco Chronicle's 10 best albums of 2003; Tom Waits nominated her for the 2003 Shortlist prize; it reached the top 10 at WFMU and drew Sub Pop interest before Anti- reissued it.

Blue Horse called 'one of the most beguiling debuts' by The Independent; praised by Emmylou Harris and Joe Strummer; Juno nominee (Roots & Traditional Album, Group) in 2007 for Hello Love; songs in Breaking Bad and Weeds.

Dan Penn produced their 2005 debut and What's Wrong with Right, which No Depression ranked in its top 60 of 2006; 2007 Group of the Year nomination; Dave Gonzalez on Guitar Player's unsung-heroes list.
Louisville duo formed 1989; Trouser Press says they helped spark indie-rock interest in early country and folk, encouraging Bad Livers and Uncle Tupelo. Returned to Pickathon in 2015.
